Why is Ukraine so reliant on Starlink and can Europe plug the gap?

BBC News Sun, 25 Oct 2026 05:45:31 GMT

Ukraine is in desperate need of a new satellite internet service, but a fast and reliable alternative to Elon Musk's Starlink network simply doesn't exist - yet.

Last week's sudden slowdown of the service in Ukraine, which affected Kyiv's ability to defend itself from Russian attacks, has shown how vulnerable the country can be, and sharply increased Europe's urgency to have its own military-grade satellite network.

That vulnerability was highlighted by Musk himself on Saturday, when he accused Ukraine of violating Starlink's terms of service by using it for "drone strikes to kill people".

Saying that loophole was closed last week, he wrote on X: "Violation of those terms will result in end of service."

He added: "Were Starlink to be turned off, the Ukrainian front line would collapse immediately".

There are a few alternatives, but they are all lagging behind Starlink, which is the world's largest satellite constellation.

France's Eutelsat, with its OneWeb internet service, is the main alternative - but it only has about 600 active satellites, compared with Starlink's 10,000-plus.

The EU is working on a new network to rival Starlink, Iris², however it won't be up and running until 2029.

For Ukraine's troops on the ground, several of whom spoke anonymously to the BBC, reliable connectivity is the difference between life and death.

"God forbid they shut it off completely, it would be an absolute catastrophe," said one. "I don't give a damn how much an alternative costs when our lives are on the line."

For now, Ukraine's best bet is to join Govsatcom, the EU's satellite sharing network - but it cannot be used for military warfare like controlling drones.

Starlink and its military-grade service, Starshield, are both owned by Musk's SpaceX company and have dominated the global satellite market for years.

Ukraine relies on Starlink for communications on the battlefield and Starshield, which is controlled by the US government, for military purposes like drone warfare. The network is able to provide fast, real-time connectivity, which is crucial for defence and intercepting Russian attacks.

"You can't employ drone warfare without this kind of high-speed internet connection," said Vincent Tourret, a researcher at the French Institute of International Relations.

Last week's slowdown, which has only just been restored, highlighted the risks of relying on a US provider at a time when tensions between Kyiv and Washington continue to deteriorate.

"Ukraine's defence cannot depend on Trump's or Musk's whims," French MEP, Christophe Grudler, tweeted.

Who authorised the Starlink restrictions is still not clear, with a confusing blame-game ongoing between the Pentagon, Donald Trump and Musk.

While Starlink has been one of Ukraine's greatest assets in this conflict, the "flipside of that dependence" has been exposed, explained Kari Bingen, director of the Aerospace Security Project at CSIS.

"This is a critical military capability that Ukraine relies on, but doesn't control."

Starlink is not the only satellite network Ukraine can access, so if it goes down there are other options - but experts say they aren't as fast, and troops the BBC spoke to agree.

Starlink "gives us the upper hand when it comes to passing commands - even one or two seconds are critical when we can transfer data and orders faster, and you can really feel that advantage on the battlefield", a soldier said.

The terminals used to connect to the satellites are also an important factor. Starlink's are relatively small and lightweight, so they can be fixed to any kind of vehicle or drone.

Eutelsat's terminals "are slightly larger, so they can be fitted on the roof of a car, or on tanks, but they can't necessarily sit on small drones", said Eva Berneke, former CEO of the French satellite company.

They are also about five times more expensive, she added.

Rhetoric from the White House - like Trump's scathing criticism of Nato and his threats against Greenland - have given the EU "some pretty brutal alarm bells", Berneke told the BBC.

She had only been at Eutelsat for a month when Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, and said she noticed a marked change in urgency from European authorities, as they looked to her company to help plug holes left by Starlink if it could not be relied upon.

Comments from Musk have further heightened the need for an alternative: "Be quiet, small man... there is no substitute for Starlink," he tweeted at Poland's foreign minister last year, when the politician said he would "look for other suppliers" if SpaceX was unreliable.

Europe has realised its security depends on space, and it must "strengthen its satellite capacities, urgently", a spokesperson for the European Commission told the BBC.

Right now, it has Govsatcom, a network that was set up in January to share existing satellites between EU member states. Ukraine is not a full-fledged member (although it is trying to become one), but the Commission is in talks with Kyiv to join Govsatcom.

But even if Ukraine could connect tomorrow, the network could not be used for warfare operations like piloting drones, which Starshield is used for.

That could change by the start of next year, however, when the European Commission hopes commercial companies, like Eutelsat's OneWeb, will join the programme. This will give Ukraine some - but not all - of its military network needs.

Eva Berneke told the BBC she is confident the company will be able to "support quite a lot of Ukraine's key military needs". But meeting its communications needs is another thing because, as is the case with most countries, they are varied and massive.

Eutelsat could not comment on Govsatcom, but told the BBC that "as the only European operator of a fully operational [Low Earth Orbit] constellation, we are committed to providing resilient connectivity to the businesses, governments and communities we serve".

No timeline has been given for when Ukraine will be able to join the Govsatcom network. When it does it will likely be as a reliable back-up to Starlink and Starshield.

But that's better than nothing, Vincent Tourret said. "If Starlink is shut down, it's good to have another way to stay connected, but it won't be enough for strikes or interceptions, at this stage."

Govsatcom is seen as a short-term safety net, until the stronger and more secure network, Iris² is up and running in 2029.

The ambitious project (pronounced Iris squared) is Europe's answer to Starlink and Starshield. It will be a defence-first programme, the European Commission says, with a focus on governments, military and emergency services. Ukraine has been guaranteed access to it from day one.

Part of the EU's space programme, the European satellite companies Eutelsat, SES and Hispasat are leading the project in a consortium called SpaceRISE.

It will still have far fewer satellites than Starlink, with 348 across low and medium earth orbit - but that shouldn't be seen as a negative, said Kari Bingen.

"Think about a flash light beaming down - those satellites will be able to cover a greater amount of the Earth, so you need fewer of them," she explained. "They're all trade offs - I would not take it as a negative, that Iris² is planning for less satellites."

Tourret was more sceptical: "It's no gamechanger and no great saviour, I'm afraid".

A highly produced video on the EU Space Policy's website declares: "With Iris², Europe will no longer depend on others for satellite connectivity."

So does that mean Ukraine could switch off Starlink? No - that wouldn't be a good idea.

"Users need to think about communications resilience," Bingen said. "So if something happens to one system, you have other ways to maintain connectivity."

It's similar to how mobile phones work, explained Eva Berneke: "If you don't have 5G, you go back to 4G. And if you don't have 4G, you might use 3G, so you have multiple networks for resilience. It's the same idea in warfare."

But while a phone might not load pictures as quickly on 3G, for a drone operator, it can be deadly: "That is not a nice situation to have to be in when you're fighting a war."

Iris² is not the only option. This week, Finnish companies Nokia and ICEYE announced they would look at developing satellite communications for Ukraine's military defences.

And a joint venture between European satellite makers Airbus, Leonardo and Thales, called Project Bromo, is hoped to be another competitor against SpaceX, but it is still in the very early phases.

Space projects take a long time, Berneke said, and need "a lot of money".

Designing the programme, making the satellites, launching them and then having enough of them in orbit for full coverage takes many years.

"Even if you gave me €8bn right now, I don't think I could have anything up there before 2032-2033," she explained.

Military work in Space is nothing new, and has been happening since the dawn of the space age in the 1950s. But the conflict in Ukraine has shown how integral it is to modern warfare.

"Communication is so important, and terrestrial communication platforms, whether it's 5G or fibre, can be attacked on the ground," Berneke said. "It is a lot harder to shoot down an entire satellite network. That's not something any military can do right now."

While we look to the skies, however, most of the world's communications are travelling via undersea cables - about 99% in fact. But these are vulnerable to attack - this week the UK government outlined new measures to protect its cables, after an increase in suspicious activity by Russian vessels.

"In a crisis or conflict, there are serious concerns that undersea cables will be cut... so if that happens it's good to have satellite communication as a backup," Kari Bingen said.

Additional reporting by Anastasiia Levchenko

Why the charts are full of old songs - and so are your playlists

BBC News Sat, 24 Oct 2026 23:05:41 GMT

More music is being created than at any other time in human history. Every day, more than 100,000 songs are being submitted to streaming services.

And despite the deluge of AI music - Spotify says it has removed 75 million "spammy tracks" from its catalogue - real music still makes up most of our listening. The streaming service Deezer says AI accounts for just 0.5% of streams on its platform.

The problem for all those artists creating new music is that our listening habits increasingly show a love for nostalgia.

Luminate, an independent entertainment data and analytics company that tracks music, film, and television consumption first started tracking music streaming in 2008.

This year, it recorded that the streaming of current music (released less than 18 months ago) was significantly dwarfed by older music in both the UK and US.

In the first half of 2026, almost two thirds of the music played (about 60%) was released five or more years ago.

So, if we're stuck in a streaming rut, what's to blame?

In the UK, most of us seem to be shunning new songs.

Eighteen of the year's top 20 bestselling songs were released 12 months ago, or earlier.

The year's eighth biggest hit is Zara Larsson's Lush Life, which originally came out in June 2015. Michael Jackson's Billie Jean (1983) is in 22nd place. Fleetwood Mac's Dreams (1977) is 30th.

It's a sign that, with practically every song ever recorded available at the press of a button, people are increasingly seeking out the classics - or what the music industry categorises as "deep catalogue".

It's a similar story in the US.

There, in the two most-played genres, R&B and Hip-Hop, about 60% of streams are old-school catalogue hits.

Even when current songs do break out, they themselves dominate streaming for weeks and even months.

Sam Fender and Olivia Dean's duet Rein Me In recently made UK chart history, spending a record-breaking 23 non-consecutive weeks at number one.

Likewise, in America, Ella Langley's Choosin' Texas has become the longest-running number one in US chart history.

The reality, of course, is that hits need to achieve "millions of streams a day" to reach the top of the charts.

But according to the UK's Competition and Markets Authority, nearly two thirds of streams are of music recorded by "only the top 0.4% of artists".

As we increasingly cling on to our favourites, aspiring artists may be suffering.

Even after a song has gone viral, some musicians say it can be hard to promote subsequent releases and sustain a career. A platform like TikTok isn't set up to boost artists, it's there to create viral moments around a single song.

"It's easier [today] for folks to be passive fans," noted J Erving, the founder of Raye's distribution company, Human Re Sources, in a recent interview with Billboard.

"For you to consider yourself broken [as a mainstream artist], people need to care about you beyond the song. Where is the connectivity? Are people really dialled in in a deeper way?"

It's a problem the music industry is keen to tackle.

Oliver Schusser, the Head of Apple Music, says his streaming service is working to champion "tomorrow's artists" in its curation.

"You know, we do the Super Bowl halftime show, we need to make sure that we still have performers in 10, 20, 30 years," he tells BBC News.

"Because if you look back at the performers we had in the last four years, they all started somewhere before they got to the world's biggest stage."

Other organisations like Sofar Sounds work exclusively with grassroots musicians, putting on intimate pop-up gigs in cities across the globe.

This October, its Shoreditch Sofar Fringe festival showcased a whole host of artists like East London rapper J Casa.

In an age of content oversaturation, Casa thinks there's something unique about a live performance.

Rather than hearing more of what they already know, Casa says audiences form "a lasting connection" with a new artist and their music.

Sofar is also launching its Human Discovery Movement campaign that aims to put music curation and discovery "back into human hands."

Music lovers can now text a "mystery number" and receive voice notes from Sofar's tastemakers with recommendations for new music worldwide.

Artificial intelligence (AI) may also be playing its part in the so-called death of new music.

Spotify, and its competitors like Apple Music and Amazon Music, are driving the trend in AI-assisted curation, allowing premium subscribers to automatically generate playlists through text prompts to fit a mood, vibe or occasion.

Musicologist Anna-Kaisa Kaila thinks "there absolutely is potential for bias" with AI-generative playlist technology.

"With AI systems, the bias can either come from the data or from the system itself. If there's not enough training data in a particular style that is perhaps not so commercially dominant, it will be that much harder for the system to pull up tracks in that style."

Others fear an algorithmic streaming bubble is to the detriment of genuine music, its discovery and creatives' livelihoods.

As Tim Garcia, London-based DJ and curator puts it: "They're based on everyone's listening behaviour and data, right? So, you're probably going to get given a very similar recommendation to an artist you're already listening to."

Dan Mackta, managing director at Qobuz, an online music platform that maintains a strict human-first approach to curation, agrees the technology "is never going to want to throw a curve ball at you".

Chiminyo, a London-based independent artist, believes that auto-generated playlists are also misleading people into thinking they're listening to "hand-picked" tunes from bona fide artists - as opposed to digitally mass-produced sound-alikes created to catch streams.

Scrolling through a "relaxing jazz piano playlist" with over 370,000 saves on Spotify, he spots that top featured artists that rack up hundreds of thousands of monthly listens have unverified accounts.

Little - if anything - can be found about them online, he says.

To his trained ear, Chiminyo also says the different artists' tracks sound near identical, reason enough to conclude the compositions have been synthetically mass-produced.

"Its all the same: the same piano feel, the same microphone placement, the same tape machine, has been used on every single one of these tracks."

When asked, Spotify said it had rolled out platform-wide policies against impersonation and is working to the improve filtering out of AI-related issues on its platform. But it acknowledges AI's use in music production sits on a spectrum with some artists choosing to use it to varying degrees.

New music may not be dying out, but it's clear it has a lot to contend with in 2026.

Why the King's Caribbean tour could be 'biggest risk of his reign'

BBC News Sat, 24 Oct 2026 23:03:09 GMT

Royal tours are unpredictable beasts.

The planning is meticulous and dates back months, sometimes years, but there is always jeopardy.

King Charles III's visit to the Caribbean, which starts on Tuesday, takes him to three countries in nine days: the Bahamas, Guyana and finally Antigua and Barbuda for the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting (Chogm).

It also throws him directly into the heat of the debate over the payment of reparations - compensation from countries that took part in the slave trade - alongside questions of whether the King should be apologising for the UK's role in what he has previously described as an "appalling atrocity" that leaves an "indelible stain" on history.

"This is the biggest risk of his reign so far with so much just outside of his control," said author and historian Sir Anthony Seldon. "Questions about slavery, reparations and apologies mean the moral integrity of the monarchy is being questioned."

The King will make three significant speeches during the Caribbean trip and will follow government advice not to issue an official apology for Britain's role in the transatlantic slave trade.

A senior royal aide said that the King would "not shy away from the darkest days of our past" but stressed that decisions over apologies and reparations were matters for government.

The current Burnham administration, like those before it, will not pay reparations.

Buckingham Palace says that acknowledging the wrongs of the past will be built into the King's programme in all three countries.

But apologies, reparations, and republicanism are rich pickings for campaigners and protests are likely.

This is the reality for the King and Buckingham Palace, and they are accepting of it.

Those who've worked on the planning of the trip view protests as part of the open debate in the region and security preparations include their possibility.

Lurking in the back of Royal Household minds will also be memories of the last tour by senior royals to the Caribbean in the early part of 2022.

Then, as the Duke and Duchess of Cambridge, William and Catherine found themselves facing criticism over the optics of the trip - images of the royal couple reaching out to touch the outstretched hands of Jamaican children through a wire fence looked clumsy. Engagements designed as tributes to past royal visits appeared outdated. And protests also caused the cancellation of a small part of the schedule.

Everything will have been done to avoid those kinds of missteps on the 2026 Caribbean tour.

The leadership in the Bahamas, Guyana and Antigua and Barbuda will celebrate the King and his work in protecting rainforests, creating cultural ties and reinforcing relationships around trade, energy, and agriculture.

But they do so against a backdrop of change.

The leaders of all three countries have voiced their support for reparatory justice.

In Antigua and Barbuda and the Bahamas, where the King is head of state, the conversation about becoming a republic has significant support.

Elected officials in the former no longer have to pledge allegiance to the King ending a 40-year tradition of swearing loyalty to the monarch.

"He pulled off an extraordinary triumph with President Trump in his US visit earlier this year and stood up to him and put him in his place in a way that no leader has done - while not incurring his wrath," said Sir Anthony. "If he can deal with the delicate nature of this trip for him personally, for the British monarchy, and the future of the Commonwealth, it could be an enormous success."

Timing also matters for royal tours.

This Caribbean tour has to cut through a sea of royal distractions.

The King has spent much of the past three months in Scotland, where he is based over the summer.

It should have been a quieter time in the royal calendar, but it has been quite the opposite.

The surprise return of the Duke and Duchess of Sussex to the UK has been noisy. The level of coverage Harry and Meghan get is unsettling and, at times, irritating for the Royal Family.

The King's youngest son has not yet seen his father in person, but they are said to have talked.

Then enter Earl Spencer, the King's former brother-in-law, with his memoir, Swan Song, criticising the King's response to the death of Diana, Princess of Wales. It triggered a strong pushback from the Palace.

And in recent days, the serious claims made about Meghan's father, Thomas Markle, have drawn his daughter into a complex tale involving global police forces, sexual abuse allegations and further family trauma.

An impactful and successful Caribbean tour is a chance to switch focus.

But if royal stories back home are running hot, it can be hard to focus minds on the King's engagements over four thousand miles (6,437km) away.

Former Foreign Secretary David Lammy, who has strong family ties to the Caribbean, has accompanied the King on a number of trips outside the UK.

"He is our head of state. He is amongst some of the most recognisable figures in the world. For a small country like Guyana, the validation of a state visit is huge," said the Tottenham MP whose father came to the UK from what was then British Guiana and who also has relatives in Antigua and Barbuda. "My mother would forever recall the Queen's visit in 1996."

But there was also a recognition of that royal trip jeopardy.

"Knowing Guyana, Antigua and Barbuda as well as I do, he will be overwhelmingly received positively," Lammy said. "But these are lively democracies in which of course there will be some dissent."

A transatlantic flight, three countries over nine days and about 36 separate engagements when you're closing in on your 78th birthday is an intense schedule. It is also a reminder that the King is still dealing with a cancer diagnosis and having regular treatment. Buckingham Palace has reiterated its position that he is on a "positive trajectory".

Nanoflares are known to occur when magnetic fields within the corona abruptly rearrange themselves and emit energy in the process. But for this rearrangement to happen, the exact conditions, such as the shape of the magnetic fields, must be just right, says Sun. This nanoflare made a big difference to the temperature of the plasma. It reached temperatures of 799,726°C, which was nearly double the temperature achieved in the flat target version of the experiment where no nanoflares occurred.

A similar process – instability leading to nanoflares leading to plasma heating – could feasibly happen on the sun, says Sun. In fact, the parameters that determined their tiny plasma’s behaviour matched those observed in regions of the sun where blobs of colder plasma “rain” down through the corona. Yet, in Keppens’s view, the new experiment does not definitively resolve the coronal heating puzzle, as other plasma behaviours, such as certain types of waves in it, could also contribute to it.

Going forward, Sun and his colleagues want to upgrade their experiment to create more three-dimensional plasmas and use more precise techniques for diagnosing its behaviour. And they want to make their laboratory measurements more directly comparable to reality – for example, by using data about the sun collected through telescopes, says Sun. “It is important to check that the laboratory is reproducing what the sun does,” he says.

Every PHP version released in the past decade is affected by at least one of these vulnerabilities, but the PHP Foundation, which oversees development, has already issued an update to overcome this.

The foundation didn’t respond to a request for interview, but said in a blog post that signs of the vulnerability emerged in 2024. Yet nothing was done. One interpretation of the sex differences in the results is that the more frequent temperature fluctuations experienced by women caused their T-cells to switch between suppressed and activated states more often, says Maloney.

Antibodies mistakenly attacking the brain are linked with conditions including schizophrenia, dementia and OCD, prompting a revolution in how we think about mental health conditions

The core body temperature of premenopausal women rises by about 0.6°C (around 1°F), on average, after ovulation, then falls a day or two before menstruation. Perimenopause and menopause can also cause sudden increases in body temperature, manifesting as hot flushes. “Maybe the adaptive immune system is having to constantly change its set point, which sort of wears it out, and then that contributes to autoimmune risk,” says Maloney.

“The findings add another dimension to sex differences in immune function,” says Sabra Klein at Johns Hopkins University in Baltimore. Future studies should examine whether body temperature affects immune responses between men and women independently of their hormonal differences, she says.

They could also track links between the menstrual cycle, body temperature and T-cell response, says Maloney. For now, the team is working with another group of researchers to implement body-temperature measurements in a vaccine trial starting next year, she says.

Why do mathematicians keep proving things they already know?

New Scientist October 23, 2026

Earlier this month, I wrote a story about how OpenAI had inadvertently produced two versions of its proof of the Navier-Stokes problem. You can read the details here, but one thing that has stuck with me is that some non-mathematically minded people I spoke to about the story struggled with the idea that two different proofs of the same problem could both be correct. It got me thinking about how and why mathematicians prove things multiple times – and what happens when it goes wrong.

One thing it’s important to grasp is that proofs are not homework problems. A couple of mathematicians have made this point to me recently: because most people’s experience of maths begins and ends at school, there is a perception that mathematicians are simply working down a big list of problems and writing answers to be ticked off by some sort of cosmic maths teacher. This is not the case – proofs are a way of organising and developing mathematical thinking. You can think of a proof as a journey, from statement to conclusion – and as with many journeys, there are many routes you can take to get from A to B. This is where we get multiple proofs of the same problem.

Terence Tao’s Six Maths Essentials opens his field to all of us

This act of reproving, of taking the mathematical road not yet travelled, dates back to antiquity. One of the earliest examples is the statement that an isosceles triangle always has two equal sides and two equal angles at the base. Writing around 350 BC, Aristotle describes a proof of this that involves drawing lines from the centre of a circle to its circumference – the original author of that proof is lost. Around 50 years later, Euclid described a proof that only requires triangles, not circles. This neatly avoided a mathematical disagreement about how to define angles formed between a straight line and a curved line – a question that wasn’t settled for thousands of years, as it happened.

Advertisement

Euclid also crops up in another example that shows how useful it is to keep attacking “solved” problems. He recorded a proof that there are infinitely many primes, and you may have learnt it at school. Suppose you have a finite list of primes. If you multiply them all together, you get a new number, P. Now, define q = P + 1. If q is prime, it can’t have been on the list, because it is bigger than P. If q isn’t, it must instead be divisible by a prime, as all non-primes are. If that prime we divide by had been on the list, it must also divide P, but that must also mean it divides q – P = 1, which is impossible. Either way, we have identified a prime not on the original list.

According to a 2023 survey, they are now 200 different proofs of Euclid’s theorem, as it is known. One that particularly added to mathematical knowledge at the time was published by Leonhard Euler in 1737, who found a formula that related the sum of all numbers to the product of all primes. He also used this to hint at the structure of the primes – not only that there are infinitely many, but that they become sparser as you go up the number line. Euler’s formula inspired Bernard Riemann over a century later to propose the Riemann hypothesis, a deep question about the structure of prime numbers that is considered one of the greatest unsolved mysteries in maths today – so it was well worth Euler having another crack at Euclid.

Perhaps surprisingly, there are even times when mathematicians have produced multiple proofs of the same theorem before revealing a flaw in the reasoning. In 1933, mathematician Wilhelm Grunwald published a proof showing that a number, a, with a certain property in relation to all prime numbers, must always be able to be written as some other number, x, raised to the nth power, so a = xn. A second mathematician, George Whaples, gave a new proof of this using slightly different maths in 1942. But then in 1948, Shianghao Wang found that actually, this isn’t true for 16, because 16 isn’t equal to x8 for any x. The correct result is now known as the Grunwald-Wang theorem.

Hannah Fry: How OpenAI has caused an existential crisis in mathematics

Pleasingly, researchers have even studied the idea of taking proof journeys mathematically. In a 2022 paper, Scott Viteri at Stanford University and Simon DeDeo at Carnegie Mellon University in Pennsylvania point out that if a mathematical proof is a sequence of logical steps, each with a tiny probability of a mistake, the odds are that a long enough proof is more likely to be wrong than not. Roll enough times, and the dice will be extremely likely to land on a 1. How then can mathematicians prove anything?

The pair show that a mathematical proof is structured like a network, with “truth” being transmitted along paths between each step, exactly like a journey. With the potential for error at each step, the strength of this truth diminishes along longer paths. But proofs aren’t random walks around a conceptual arena – they have structure, and claims are often reinforced by multiple routes. This structure allows truth to be transmitted along the strongest paths, even if it fails along other routes. Because of this, the network undergoes what the pair call an “epistemic phase transition”, a scenario under which you can be extremely certain the proof is correct.

This is just a model, and not necessarily something accepted by all mathematicians, but I find it appealing. It also fits with what you would naturally expect: the more proofs mathematicians have of a result, the more paths that are carved from A to B, the more certain you can be that it is true. In an age when AI is beginning to produce maths that humans don’t necessarily understand, we might find that having multiple routes to the truth, whether human or AI derived, can bring confidence where we might otherwise have uncertainty.

Tesla remotely disabled fast-charging on damaged cars, owner’s legal challenges dismissed

New Zealand Herald October 25, 2026

Tesla disabled the fast charging on two damaged, second-hand cars bought by Peter Goodricke when he switched on his app and software updates downloaded. He challenged the decision in the Disputes Tribunal and now the High Court has dismissed his claim for judicial review. Photo /123rf

Tesla has pulled the plug on the owner of two second-hand cars it felt weren’t safe to charge, in case the batteries caught fire.

The US automotive company, which has service centres in New Zealand, activated the “disable” button on the cars’ fast-charging function when it learned the written-off vehicles were destined for repair and would be back on the road.

Peter Goodricke didn’t know until he opened his Tesla app and software updates switched off the charging function.

He had bought the damaged Teslas at a Turners auction and apparently missed the fine print in the manufacturer’s unsupported vehicle policy that fast-charging would be disabled until the risk of fire or other damage could be assessed.

Tesla justified its position by the risk posed by damaged high-voltage batteries.

In rare cases, a damaged battery could cause a catastrophic fire. Internal damage to battery cells could sometimes be difficult to detect, it said.

With the vehicles unable to be charged quickly, Goodricke was unhappy at the prospect of having to plug the cars into a regular powerpoint at home, which could take “days”.

He went to the Disputes Tribunal, which dismissed his claim over alleged breaches of consumer and fair trade laws. He sought a second rehearing against the tribunal’s decision but that too was dismissed.

Goodricke then went to the High Court, which has dismissed his application for a judicial review of the tribunal’s decisions.

In doing so, Justice David Boldt acknowledged the case had one “immediately troubling aspect to it”.

“Tesla, unlike most car manufacturers, retains the ability to reach into individual vehicles long after their sale and make alterations which limit their functionality.

“That power is remarkable and may be exercised only in the most tightly constrained circumstances.”

However, he was not persuaded the tribunal referee erred in rejecting Goodricke’s claim.

Goodricke, an electrical engineer, bought the cars in 2024.

Each had been deregistered after being written off by their former owners’ insurers.

Tesla became aware a salvaged Tesla Model 3 was being sold at auction. A few days later, it learned the New Zealand Transport Agency register listed the vehicle as structurally damaged.

Tesla designated it an “unsupported vehicle” and transmitted an “over-the-air” update to disable fast-charging capability.

It did the same a few days later on the second vehicle under its “unsupported vehicle policy”, which prevented a Tesla from being charged on a direct current or supercharger system.

The Teslas were repaired, inspected and re-registered.

The vehicles charged normally when Goodricke accessed them using only his key.

But the software updates downloaded when Goodricke used the Tesla app, immediately disabling the vehicles’ access to any fast-charging network, including Tesla’s proprietary network of “superchargers”.

Justice Boldt said that for most vehicles, re-registration would have been the end of the story.

However, in this case, Tesla New Zealand had been monitoring the NZTA register.

Goodricke wrote to Tesla protesting that it had interfered with his vehicles without his permission.

Tesla pointed him to its website and unsupported vehicle policy, which defined a vehicle as one the company considered unsafe for service or fast-charging.

Goodricke argued in the tribunal that Tesla had breached consumer and trade laws by sending updates that reduced his cars’ functionality.

He claimed Tesla’s failure to disclose the risk of remote disabling before he bought the car had misled him about the vehicles’ ongoing functionality.

He said it was “unconscionable for Tesla” to require an inspection only it could perform, and which cost more than $1600.

Tesla NZ general service manager Michael Belenkij said if the test showed the car was safe, the functionality was turned back on.

The claim was dismissed in September last year when the tribunal ruled for Tesla.

The referee found the company’s policy was not misleading, deceptive or unconscionable.

He noted it was publicly available and the onus was on Goodricke, as purchaser of a damaged vehicle, to satisfy himself of the potential implications of buying a car that had been deregistered.

The tribunal said Tesla had a legitimate interest in ensuring its cars were safe.

Goodricke applied for a rehearing focused on the tribunal’s alleged failures, but that too was dismissed.

Contact the Open Justice team

When the matter reached the High Court, Justice Boldt noted Goodricke had not been legally represented at any stage.

Goodricke raised multiple grounds of review challenging the merits of the tribunal’s decision.

He also argued Tesla had unlawfully interfered with his property and committed an act of trespass.

Justice Boldt said the fundamental rule that a car belonged to its owner, who then assumed responsibility for its safe operation, could only be displaced if there was a clear legal basis to do so.

Tesla, through its lawyer, acknowledged it had no unilateral right to alter the functionality of a Tesla vehicle once it belonged to someone else, and that it must be able to point to a lawful entitlement to do so.

The judge said Goodricke’s case depended on his proposition that Tesla publicly maintained that its vehicles would have access to fast-charging networks throughout their working lives, but that proposition was incorrect.

He said whatever Tesla may say about its vehicles’ general suitability for fast-charging, it made a clear exception for damaged and deregistered vehicles.

NZME has sought comment from Goodricke.

Tracy Neal is a Nelson-based Open Justice reporter at NZME. She was RNZ’s regional reporter in Nelson-Marlborough and has covered general news, including court and local government for the Nelson Mail.

Join the NZ Herald’s Open Justice team for Case by Case, a video and podcast series examining the disputes and decisions making headlines across New Zealand.

‘Watch the small expenses’: 20 expert tips to boost your bank balance

New Zealand Herald October 25, 2026

Where does it go and why don’t we have more? That’s the money mystery. Jane Phare gets advice from experts on ways to make sure your bank balance is going up, not down.

We’ve all done it: come home with an extravagant impulse buy or signed up for a holiday without knowing what it’s going to cost. And then there are those cafe visits and flat whites.

Don’t beat yourself up over the coffees and the smashed-avocado-on-toast brunches, says Retirement Commission personal finance expert Tom Hartmann. The important thing is to have a plan and ideally a goal to save towards.

Claudette Wilson, general manager of North Harbour Budgeting Services, agrees.

“Write down what the goal is, put it in front of you and actually work to it. It doesn’t matter what it is.”

Track your money, she says. Every cent counts, every dollar helps.

Benjamin Franklin would concur. His face is on the US$S100 bill to honour his contribution as a Founding Father. But he was also money-wise.

“Watch the small expenses; a small leak will sink a great ship,” he was quoted as saying.

Collectively, Kiwis currently owe billions of dollars. Consumer and personal debt currently sits at $24 billion, and a further $7.1b is owed on credit cards. That’s on top of a residential mortgage debt of $348b.

Hartmann says it’s little wonder that Kiwis, faced with constant marketing from companies selling goods and services, find their money evaporating. Think about walking through a supermarket, he says.

“[It’s] just wall-to-wall advertisements coming at us, ‘buy me, buy me, buy me’”.

Budget and have a goal

There’s budgeting, and then there’s budgeting, finance experts say. One model will make ends meet and keep the status quo. But why not aim higher?

Pick a goal to save for something important to you; it could be a trip away or a newer car. That way you’re more likely to be careful about what you spend, budget advisers say. And put some aside for those unexpected expenses that can plunge you into debt.

Help is available, says Hartmann, personal finance lead for the commission’s financial literacy platform Sorted, a free service offering a range of calculators and tools. Importantly, it has an easy-to-use online budgeting planner.

A little bit of money

Many of Wilson’s clients think they know where their money is going but can’t understand why they run out. It’s often the small purchases they’ve forgotten about that add up, she says, like stopping for $40 worth of petrol but buying a coffee and snacks at the same time. Or they’ve been buying extras on a gaming site, or adding Lotto tickets to a grocery shop.

Be honest, add those up over a week or a month. Think how the cost of those little extras would accumulate if you put that money into a savings account.

Do you really need it?

It’s that time of year again. Black Friday sales are looming next month. Oh, the bargains, the queues, the fight to get the last discounted air fryer. Make a list of what you need and stick to it. If you don’t need anything, stay away. Make a Christmas cake instead; it’ll be cheaper than buying one.

Shopping sprees without self-discipline can do serious damage to your finances. If you’re tempted, put the item on hold for an hour or two, or, even better, sleep on it. Ask yourself, do I really need this or do I just want it?

Beware of going into debt over an impulsive RSVP. Before accepting an invitation to an out-of-town or overseas wedding, add up the cost of travel, accommodation, food, the wedding gift, and a new outfit. Make sure you can afford it before responding.

And think twice – make that three times – about going into debt to buy that new Ford Ranger – which will drop in value the moment you drive away – when a debt-free, secondhand Toyota will do the job just fine.

The art of hustling

Hustling or asking for a discount is not something that the average Kiwi has grown up doing. And yet, say budget advisers, it can save hundreds of dollars over the space of a year, particularly when buying pricey items like whiteware, furniture and beds.

Shop around, ask for a discount or make an offer. Being a bit cheeky doesn’t cost anything, and in this economic climate, salespeople, often on a part-commission payment, will want to clinch the deal. With a bit of luck, you might get free delivery.

If you’re doing house renovations, get two or three quotes then ask your preferred tradie or supplier to match the lower quote.

Make your house earn its keep

If money gets tight, consider renting a spare room to a flatmate, taking in a boarder or a homestay student to bring in a few hundred dollars a week extra.

Fees for homestay students can start at $340, depending on the area (Auckland is usually more expensive), rising to $600 for a more deluxe package including a private bathroom for the student. Host families need to provide meals, transport and include students in family activities.

One student homestay host says that in past years she’s had two, and sometimes three, teenage students staying at any one time.

“I loved it”, she says. “I wasn’t doing it for the money, but I can tell you I saved a load of money because there’s no way you spend that money [the homestay fee] on their costs.”

Turning Gold into dollars

Kiwis aged 65 and over can save plenty of money by tapping into thousands of discount offers on the Government’s supergold. govt. nz website. There are dollars to be saved at food outlets, homeware stores, power and telco companies, healthcare, dentistry, and rental car companies, as well as discounts at museums, movie theatres and performances. Many supermarkets offer SuperGold cardholders a 5% discount on a particular weekday.

Often the discounts aren’t widely advertised, so always ask about a Gold Card discount before paying. However, it pays to check that the same item is not offered at a better price elsewhere, even with the discount.

Make the most of free travel on buses, trains and ferries during off-peak hours. Entry to Auckland’s Museum of Transport and Technology is free, and so is the Wellington cable car during off-peak hours (half price during peak hours). And once you hit 75, you can ski for free at Coronet Peak, the Remarkables or Mt Hutt.

Utilities and phone cents

Shop around and review utilities at least once a year. The Electricity Authority’s site billy. govt. nz is useful for comparing power company charges. Ask your existing power provider to match the better deal.

Regularly check that you’re on the best deal for your phone and data usage.

Wilson: “We see a lot of people who are on really big plans [for mobile phones], and when you look at their usage for the year, it’s actually a small percentage of what they’re actually paying for.”

And think twice before buying the latest mobile phone “on tick” or through deals offered by telcos when there’s nothing wrong with the existing phone.

Do your homework about roaming plans when you’re travelling overseas, otherwise you could find you’ve racked up hundreds of dollars in charges when you return.

Mortgage matters

Shop around and negotiate for the best rate, particularly if you’re a new customer, says Compass Mortgages adviser Helen Stuart.

A mortgage isn’t a set-and-forget, she says. Check regularly to make sure you’re not paying over the odds. And if you have savings, use them to pay off the mortgage more quickly to reduce the interest you’ll pay in the long run. Even if the interest rate drops, keep up the payments at the higher rate.

In the current uncertain job market, Stuart recommends income insurance, particularly for people with a large debt.

Beware of the Big D

Debt can creep up without warning – the mortgage repayments, the credit cards, the loan on the car.

And then there’s the lure of Buy Now, Pay Later (BNPL), also known as Afterpay, now used by around 23% of Kiwis, according to the Financial Markets Authority’s 2025 report Good Cents: Kiwis on Savings and Debt.

Financial advisers say BNPL can work well if customers meet their regular payments, but if they miss a payment, fees start accumulating. And they warn that BNPL in the hands of an impulse buyer can be dangerous.

One financial adviser spoken to by the Herald thinks BNPL should be avoided unless there is no alternative and the item needs to be bought.

“Things like mag wheels, beauty treatments, concert tickets, designer sneakers, holidays, and so on are not essentials that should be bought this way,” she says.

People end up with 10 different BNPLs at the same time; they default, and then fees start accumulating.

“It’s a very profitable business that has just taken over New Zealand.”

Likewise, be cautious with debt consolidation offers because of the fees involved, she says. Go to your bank first to ask for options, and get advice from a budgeting service.

Pay off credit card balances on time to avoid late fees and interest that can be as high as 25%. Store card interest rates can go up to 30%.

Swap dollars for power and water

Encourage family members to switch off non-essential lights and turn off electrical equipment at the wall if it draws a current.

Wash clothes in cold water and hang them on a drying rack or line rather than use the dryer. Use timers on heated towel rails and panel heaters. Avoid baths, take shorter showers to save on both power and water.

Borrow or rent

Before you rush out to buy a new tent, pram or power tool, think about borrowing from friends or renting the item. Join a toy library rather than buying new toys that will pile up in the playroom.

Library members can borrow books, including ebooks and audiobooks, CDs, DVDs, movies and board games. Some libraries will lend sewing machines, camping gear, DIY tools, gardening equipment and kitchen appliances. And if you can’t borrow it, buy second-hand. There are dollars to be saved.

A bit on the side

Can you join the gig economy and think of a side hustle? Tutoring students, telemarketing in the evenings, a small online business, gardening at weekends, modelling for an ad, or babysitting? Put that money aside, invest it, don’t spend.

If you’ve got a family bach or holiday home, consider renting it out during the peak holiday season and popular long weekends.

Are you over-insured?

John Chandler, chief commercial and client officer for PIC Insurance Brokers, has three main pieces of advice: check you haven’t signed up for a premium insurance product that you don’t need; make sure you are not over-insured (check current valuations); and consider increasing your excess to save premium costs.

“That’s one of the easiest levers to pull for reducing costs, he says.

However, Chandler also warns Kiwis to check they’re not under-insured. It can be “devastating” if a house suffers major damage and the insurance doesn’t cover the cost, he says.

Use online sites to check what it would cost to rebuild your home.

Car costs

Second-hand cars can devalue rapidly, so check you’re not paying too much for insurance.

If your ageing “shopping basket” car dips in value, consider changing to third-party, fire and theft cover, Chandler advises. Premiums will be much cheaper, but check to see if there’s cover if an uninsured driver damages your car.

Wilson warns that costs like warrant of fitness (WoF), registration, and servicing or repairs can put people in debt unless they’ve saved for them. Build a buffer, she says.

And then there are the hefty fines for an expired registration ($200) or WoF ($200), which will rise to $350 from November 1 for a WoF that has expired for more than two months.

Repeated speeding and parking fines are one of the quickest ways to get into debt.

Healthy choice

Health insurance premiums keep rising, particularly as we age. Consider cutting back from a premium policy to one restricted to surgical, specialist and cancer cover.

Raising your excess to several hundred dollars, or even several thousand, will reduce your premiums.

Shop around if you’ve been on the same plan for years but be careful before you change companies. Your new insurer is unlikely to cover your pre-existing medical conditions.

A qualified health insurance adviser can help present all the options and costs, usually without charging, Chandler says. But check that the adviser is working across all the health insurance companies, not just one.

Sites like MoneyHub and Consumer NZ are also helpful.

Cashing up clutter

Kiwis are sitting on an estimated 76 million unwanted items, collectively worth $5.2 billion, according to Trade Me’s 2026 Aotearoa Circular Economy Report.

Have a look at home to see what might be worth selling: that signed rugby jersey, some Pokemon cards; a near-new power tool; clothes or baby gear. Consider cashing up any unwanted gold or silver jewellery, or coins, particularly if prices are buoyant.

Keep an eye on what’s trending so you sell at the right time. Searches for “Warriors jersey” on Trade Me are up 45% this year, for example.

Spend your time, not your money

In an age where Kiwis can pay to have just about anything done for them, try dialling that back. Dye or highlight your own hair in between salon appointments; trim your kids’ fringes (any mistakes will just become family folklore); make your own lunch; paint your own nails; wash your own car; if you have a cleaner, cut them down to once a fortnight. You’ll be surprised how much money is saved by DIY.

Supermarket savvy

You know the drill: stick to your list; don’t shop when you’re hungry; only buy what you need so you’re not wasting excess food; keep an eye out for specials but ask yourself if you really need five cans of tomatoes for $10.

Don’t be tempted to shop at a more expensive supermarket just to collect coupons for something you don’t really need.

One budget adviser with a large extended family says they plan meals a week ahead, order only what they need and pick it up as a click-and-collect so they won’t be tempted to go inside and stray from their list.

Watch your APs and apps

Make sure there’s enough money in your account to cover your automatic payments (APs) and direct debits, otherwise banks may charge penalty fees.

And do you really need to be paying for all those apps that seemed a good idea at the time? Likewise, rethink your TV streaming services or subscriptions you no longer use. Add up what they cost each month, and then for the year.

Westpac data shows 10% of its customers are shelling out $80 a month for TV subscriptions, while a further 7% are spending at least $100 a month.

Invest wisely

Think about what you’re going to do with all those dollars you save. Keep some ready cash aside but don’t just leave the rest in a low-interest account. Spread your investments. A financial adviser can help you manage your money.

Jane Phare is a senior journalist based in Auckland. Her roles at the Herald have included assistant editor of NZ Herald, editor of the Weekend Herald, founding editor of Viva, features editor and deputy print editor.

Auckland house fires: Glen Eden home and Mt Albert duplex ablaze overnight, one treated as suspicious

New Zealand Herald October 25, 2026

This is a modal window. This modal can be closed by pressing the Escape key or activating the close button.

This is a modal window.

Beginning of dialog window. Escape will cancel and close the window.

End of dialog window.

This is a modal window. This modal can be closed by pressing the Escape key or activating the close button.

Two Auckland homes went up in flames overnight, with fire services treating one as suspicious.

Firefighters were called to the two-storey house on Shah Place, Glen Eden, around 9.30pm and arrived to find it “fully ablaze”, Fire and Emergency shift manager Josh Pennefather said.

Five fire engines were sent to battle the blaze, with crews dampening hotspots around 1.24am.

Fire and Emergency senior station officer Shane Doughty said the property appeared to be abandoned “for some time”.

“So we are treating the fire as suspicious.”

Crews carried out an “external fire attack” to contain the blaze, Doughty said.

“There was no way we could get into the premises as the property was totally involved in fire.

“Once we arrived, the structure began to collapse, so crews remained outside and extinguished the fire externally.”

Neighbours watched on as firefighters battled the blaze, a Herald photographer at the scene said.

Asked whether it was common for two-storey homes to collapse, Doughty said, “It does happen”.

“I would say because this place has been abandoned and nobody has noticed – it’s been on fire for quite some time. We haven’t had residents call us until they heard noises and realised the place was on fire.”

About 2am crews were called to a 15m by 10m Kāinga Ora duplex on Tasman Ave, Mt Albert, which was “well involved” when they arrived.

There was initially concern for the occupants, Pennefather said, but crews found no one inside.

It is understood it was empty at the time, he said.

The blaze was contained by 2.27am, with the majority out by 4am.

A fire investigator is at the scene to determine the cause this morning.

Police have been contacted by the Herald for comment on both incidents.

Letters to the Editor: Voting responsibility, empathy and accountability

New Zealand Herald October 25, 2026

The Electoral Commission's Orange Guy. A reader writes that voters have "the responsibility ... to honour the people who have worked so hard in the past to give us some say in how we are governed".

Voting for a just world

The article “Pivotal election for those who can’t even vote” (October 23) should remind us of the responsibility we have to honour the people who have worked so hard in the past to give us some say in how we are governed.

The issues that need solving (such as anthropogenic climate change) are so important that we need to examine carefully where we place our vote.

The shameful global response to the genocide in Gaza illustrates the result of the inability to exercise the human right to vote and we should ask our politicians what their solutions for the multiple wars and assaults on the global ecosystem are.

The failure of the United Nations Security Council (largely because of the use of the power of veto, which needs to be removed) to provide basic security, means we should be consulting on how to achieve just global governance.

If we are concerned with the needs of the age we live in then we should centre our deliberations on its exigencies and requirements, and this may require giving power to the United Nations so it can have an effective peacekeeping force.

The media has a major role to play in achieving the above, which is inevitable; it’s just a matter of how much suffering humans and the ecosystem will have to endure before we achieve it.

Dennis Worley, Birkenhead.

RIP Arch Jelley

Not only was Arch Jelley an outstanding coach, he was a wonderful teacher.

At Mt Roskill Intermediate, I was lucky enough to be in his class, and he made us believe in ourselves and that we could all be successful in life.

RIP.

Wendy Tighe-Umbers, Parnell.

‘Mean-spirited’

David Cohen’s typically “envious male” rant (October 23), will assure readers that misogyny is alive and well.

Cohen comes across as an angry and mean-spirited individual who appears to like to take his frustrations out on extraordinarily talented women with lofty ideals – something he could never aspire to.

Edith Cullen, Te Kauwhata.

Empathy and accountability

David Cohen’s article, “A different power: Ghost of Ardernism haunts election”, raises an important question: can empathy compensate for poor policy outcomes?

Dame Jacinda Ardern’s compassionate leadership won international admiration, but concerns over Covid restrictions, housing affordability and living costs eroded public confidence.

Today, Labour risks appearing more focused on appealing to public sympathy than offering effective solutions.

National must also be judged on its own performance.

Voters can understand political challenges, but understanding should never replace accountability.

Simone Leung, Half Moon Bay.

Inspiring principal

I read with great interest and admiration the article about Ngaire Ashmore, the principal of Auckland Girls’ Grammar School.

I was fortunate to be a pupil there in the 1960s when all five Grammar Schools were deemed to be prestigious and it was an honour and a privilege to be a pupil. A top-rate education was guaranteed.

The principal, the indomitable Rua Gardner, ran a tight ship. Standards were high in all aspects – skirts had to be a certain length when kneeling, hair that touched the collar had to be tied up, prefects were at the gate checking that hats were worn, blazers were done up, there was definitely no eating in the street and woe betide if you were deemed to have misbehaved on the bus on the way home – you were reported to Miss Gardner.

All very quaint by today’s standards, but we respected our teachers, were taught to respect ourselves and each other. Values that were and are important today.

I was impressed with Ashmore’s ethics, values, vision and mana and am delighted that Auckland Girls’ is in such good hands again.

Melanie Corbett, Westmere.

Leoni resignation

I found Simeon Brown’s egregious comments about Kerrin Leoni’s resignation incredibly snide and somewhat interesting (to put it politely).

Surely, he should be doing everything he can to put all his own failures in perspective and do the job he’s being paid for. Sniping at people who have unfortunately made a career-ruining error and digging for more dirt is a cheap shot. I suspect he’s just hanging on by the skin of his teeth as a minister in any case but, of course, I couldn’t possibly comment. Nor should I find someone else’s troubles something to gloat about. Neither should he.

Jeremy Coleman, Hillpark.

Putin praise

Steve Witkoff, the United States special envoy to the Middle East, recently said in a meeting with President Vladimir Putin of Russia that he was a “humanitarian”.

If Putin is a humanitarian, then I am Jesus Christ, domiciled in a manger in Bethlehem.

Graham Fleetwood, Bethlehem.

A Welcome Bay resident says he was so sick of looking at an overgrown traffic island at the gateway to his neighbourhood that he decided to mow it himself.

Robert Coe said it had been at least six months since the New Zealand Transport Agency mowed the grass island in the middle of the Hairini St/Welcome Bay Rd roundabout.

“Others in the community have been complaining about it.”

He said he went past the overgrown grass strip every day.

“I got sick of looking at it.

“The state of it is disgraceful.”

He said it made the Welcome Bay neighbourhood look neglected and that he was considering mowing other areas of the city as well.

An NZTA spokesperson said the agency was responsible for maintaining the area at the Welcome Bay entrance.

“It is expected to be mowed within the next few weeks as part of the maintenance programme currently underway across Tauranga’s urban state highway network.”

Vegetation maintenance was also planned across the network before Christmas and early in 2027.

“NZTA prioritises vegetation maintenance that keeps road users safe, with funding focused on safety rather than appearance alone.”

The agency asked members of the public not to mow or carry out other vegetation work within the state highway corridor, as working close to live traffic could put them at risk.

It said residents could report vegetation or other maintenance issues on the state highway network by calling 0800 4 HIGHWAYS (0800 44 44 49).

A Tauranga City Council statement said its mowing teams were working furiously to keep up with the “spring flush” of grass growth across the city’s 10 million square metres of greenery.

They had a plan, but some areas may look more overgrown than usual – especially with an El Niño weather pattern to contend with.

The council manages vegetation control and grass mowing on local roads, while NZTA manages state highway corridors.

The council said green-fingered locals keen to pitch in could join its volunteer-led maintenance and planting programme.

– LDR is local body journalism co-funded by RNZ and NZ On Air.

Ayla Yeoman is a Local Democracy Reporting journalist based in Tauranga. She holds a Bachelor of Arts majoring in communications, politics and international relations from the University of Auckland, and has been a journalist since 2023.

Civic education and easier enrolment key to lifting turnout of young voters – Editorial

New Zealand Herald October 25, 2026

Young people are going unheard, but their voices matter as much as those of older generations. Photo / NZME

Advance voting for the general election starts today, but our young people aren’t champing at the bit to cast their votes.

According to the Bay of Plenty Times, the latest Electoral Commission figures from October 17 showed enrolment numbers for 18- to 24-year-olds were under 67% for the Tauranga, Bay of Plenty and Rotorua electorates.

That compared with enrolment rates of more than 99% for the 65-69 and over-70 age groups.

Those figures won’t surprise many. Young adults have long been the least-motivated voters, compared with the far more politically active baby boomers.

That’s a concern.

Not only does it give political parties an incentive to skew their policies towards older voters, but it also means we’re raising generations of people who are disengaged from and distrustful of the political system.

Why vote in a system that you believe doesn’t care about you?

Adriana Bird, a spokeswoman for the On a Roll campaign, told The Front Page podcast that young people felt their voices were “muted” in the current political climate.

The 18-24 group has the lowest nationwide enrolment at 57.45%. But they also have the second-largest number of eligible voters nationwide (440,062).

That’s a whopping proportion of our taxpaying population going unheard.

Those eligible voters are adults who, in the eyes of the law, are old enough to work fulltime and pay taxes, buy a house, get married, have and raise children, and buy alcohol.

They deserve an equal say in how our country is run.

What can we do to raise that enrolment rate and encourage more participation in the election process?

Increasing and mandating thorough civic education in schools would ensure children grow up learning why voting is important and how hard our ancestors fought for those rights.

Making enrolment and voting easier would also help.

Social sector support organisation SociaLink posed the question: “Are our democratic processes designed around people with time, confidence, transport, digital access and political literacy – rather than making it easy for everyone to vote?”

It’s an interesting question. If our voting system is structured in a way older voters are used to, such as in-person ballots and mail-in forms, for example, that is already disincentivising young folks who may have never sent a physical letter in their lives, or who can’t afford the petrol to visit the nearest town hall.

Enrolments can be done online these days, which is something. Secure online voting would also likely increase voter enrolment and turnout.

And better civic education could do wonders for the political engagement of our youth.

Something needs to be done.

The sooner we get those numbers up, the better off our country will be for everyone, not just our older voters.

Fireworks injuries: Teenagers and preschoolers have most burn claims

New Zealand Herald October 25, 2026

Thousands of New Zealanders have been injured by fireworks in recent years, with ACC data showing teenagers and preschoolers are bearing the brunt of the harm.

The exclusive figures reveal almost 4000 new fireworks-related injury claims were lodged with ACC between January 2021 and August this year.

ACC has paid nearly $4 million in treatment, rehabilitation and support costs on the claims so far, with some claims still active.

Males aged 15 to 19 accounted for the largest share of injuries, with burns to the hands and wrists the most common harm recorded. Children aged 0 to 4 had the second-highest number of claims.

Contact our Christchurch newsroom.

November, when fireworks are traditionally used around Guy Fawkes, was by far the busiest month for claims, while Auckland recorded the highest number of injuries of any region.

The ACC data highlights the ongoing human cost of fireworks, with thousands of people requiring medical treatment over the past five years and millions of dollars paid out in support for those injured.

“Fireworks are a long-standing part of Kiwi celebrations, but every year we see people injured by fireworks, often from accidents that could have been prevented,” said ACC injury prevention leader James Whitaker.

“In 2025, ACC accepted 289 fireworks-related injury claims, and we’ve already seen another 80 claims in 2026. Burns remain by far the most common injury, accounting for more than half of all claims last year.

“Hands, wrists and fingers are particularly vulnerable, with these injuries making up a large proportion of claims. Eye injuries are also a concern and can have serious, long-term consequences.

“Teenagers and young adults continue to feature prominently in our claims data, but fireworks injuries can affect people of any age.”

Whitaker said there was a “clear spike” in injuries around Guy Fawkes with “nearly two-thirds of all fireworks-related injury claims” in 2025 happening around that time.

“Which shows how important it is to take a few simple safety precautions before lighting fireworks,” he explained.

“Fireworks can be unpredictable, so we encourage people to take a few moments and ‘Have a hmmm’ to think about safety before lighting the fuse. A few simple precautions can go a long way.”

Whitaker recommended that anyone using fireworks follow the instructions on the packaging, keep a safe distance, supervise children closely and never relight fireworks that haven’t gone off as expected.

“All these things can help prevent a trip to the hospital from becoming part of the night’s entertainment,” he said.

“The safest fireworks display is one where everyone enjoys the occasion and gets home without an injury.”

New Zealand First has renewed calls for a ban on backyard fireworks, saying the “abuse and misuse” of fireworks has outweighed any benefits.

The party wants to prohibit the public sale and private use of fireworks, while continuing to allow professionally organised public displays. It argues fireworks frighten animals, start fires and place unnecessary pressure on emergency services.

Speaking to RNZ, NZ First leader Winston Peters rejected suggestions the issue was about personal freedom, saying it was instead about “the right to peaceful and harmonious living for both the community and for animals”.

Parliament’s Petitions Committee has also recommended a ban on the public sale and use of fireworks, citing concerns about animal welfare, impacts on native wildlife, risks to life and property and the number of related police callouts.

Committee member Greg Fleming said public opinion had shifted and experts overwhelmingly supported a ban.

“The committee felt that we really didn’t have almost any choice but to recommend that, given the weight of the evidence.”

The committee’s recommendation was unanimous, although Fleming said he did not expect any changes before the election.

“I’d love to see it [be] something that’s given serious consideration in the next term of Parliament.”

However, support for a nationwide ban remains uncertain. During a recent TVNZ leaders’ debate, Christopher Luxon and Chris Hipkins said they did not support banning the public sale of fireworks.

ACC said the figures were based on claims where the accident description identified fireworks as being involved and should not be treated as a definitive count of all fireworks injuries.

Anna Leask is a senior journalist who covers Christchurch issues and national crime and justice. She joined the Herald in 2008 and has worked as a journalist for more than 20 years with a particular focus on family and gender-based violence, child abuse, sexual violence and homicides. She writes, hosts and produces the award-winning podcast A Moment In Crime, released monthly on nzherald. co. nz.

My suburb loves Halloween, and one kid’s costume perfectly captured our current moment

Sydney Morning Herald October 26, 2026

My family was putting the final flourishes on our front-of-house Halloween decorations when we reached a stalemate over two plastic skeletons.

Our overriding philosophy has always been to prioritise cute over hardcore scary. Were those skeletal figures going to spook the youngsters? Our two daughters made the final call to demote the ornaments to the lolly table, giving any visiting kids some breathing room.

Welcome to Salisbury, Queensland. We may not have a murky history of druidic sacrifice like our English namesake, but for one night a year we practically turn into Stephen King’s town of Derry, with old-fashioned scares at every turn – and free chocolate.

Depending on which road you take, the approach might send a shiver down the spine. We’re bordered by the dense scrub of Toohey Forest, so in the moonlight the eucalypts give off a Blair Witch vibe. With headlights to guide your journey through the dark corridor, you might catch a fleeting glimpse of something uncanny. Those toy animal tributes to roadkill can take on a startling aspect if you’re not expecting them.

Inexplicable things do sometimes happen in Salisbury. In late 2023, a vicious localised storm rolled in without warning, toppled our washing line and destroyed the trampoline. Trees and powerlines came down around the neighbourhood. The kids remember the unnatural howling noise, the rattling windows, and sleeping through a humid night without power.

Don’t be fooled by Google Maps: Salisbury’s footprint is smaller than they’d have you believe. When you look at where people actually live, dispersed between industrial complexes, train tracks and a green corridor tracing the contours of Rocky Water Holes Creek, it’s quite enclosed. You either live in the irregular polygon on the east side of Orange Grove Road, or you hang your hat in the satellite of Rosebank Square.

Salisbury was once dominated by World War II manufacturing. The War Industries Heritage Trail passes through roads named for their function, like Assembly, Chrome and Precision streets. Walk through there now and you may spot the distinctive saw-tooth roof architecture of the era, alongside the unmistakable progress of gentrification, with new apartments going up, and an espresso bar in a building that once made munitions.

Northsiders enjoy banging on about their local food culture as if it were definitive. But there are no less than five cafes in my suburb, each with their own strengths, identity and take on coffee. One even roasts their own beans. There are craft breweries, several bakeries (from French fusion to Sri Lankan), and an old-school butcher shop. You can get pizza, American-style barbecue, and just-like-homemade Indian tiffin meals. Order a halal snack pack at Kebabland or Billy’z Kebabs, and eat it next to a hungover uni student. My suburb punches well above its food division.

It was a Facebook thread on the local grapevine page that got us started with Halloween. It may have been in the wake of social distancing restrictions relaxing in 2021. I put our street name down in the comments and drove to the local supermarket for bags of fun-size treats and last-minute decorations. We’ve been locked in ever since.

I see more houses joining in with every passing year. You see children dressed in the typical costumes of superheroes and Disney princesses, but my favourite costume was from two years ago: a prescient kid knocked on our door dressed as the dreaded Cost-of-Living, complete with an $18 bottle of olive oil.

The weirdest house we have ever visited had a woman looking banged up, trapped in a cage and pleading for help. Dark stuff – until she offered you lollies. A parent at another house had his slasher tropes mixed up: wearing Jason’s mask while carrying a Leatherface chainsaw and dressed in Michael Myers’ trademark blue coveralls. While I disapproved on the grounds of film fidelity, kids were petrified and loving it.

Horror is often a metaphor for something: usually an anxiety that gets distilled into the supernatural. I think we celebrate Halloween as a Salisbury community because we share a collective understanding that it is hard yakka raising kids.

We’re all living in tough times with lots of uncertainty. Social support networks aren’t what they used to be, money is tighter than ever, and it’s easy to feel isolated. Halloween might seem pretty naff to some people, but for our family it is a small way to invite people into our home, to share and to have a good time as the year starts to wind down. Sometimes these small acts can help anchor you to something and make you feel like you belong somewhere.

So, if you find yourself in Salisbury after dark on All Hallows’ Eve, you may knock on a weatherboard house that looks like all the others. If you’re greeted by a couple in matching Mr and Mrs Potatohead costumes, hello and welcome! Take as many mini-packs of Nerds as you like – and happy Halloween.

‘It is ours’: The far-right Israeli settlers who want to build homes in Gaza

Sydney Morning Herald October 26, 2026
