The Simhoni Forest: While many Palestinians dream of escaping the ruins of Gaza, Israeli Tchiya Chaim cannot wait for the chance to move there – and take her 11 children with her.

For the past week, the settler activist and hundreds of comrades have been living in an outpost in southern Israel, just a few hundred metres from the Gaza border. Working quickly overnight to avoid detection, they established what looks like a squatter campsite with rows of tents, tarpaulins, demountables and caravans. There is also a jumping castle for young children and a classroom lined with religious texts. They have called the encampment Halutzei Aza – “the Pioneers of Gaza”.

“God willing, we will stay here until the government will take this settlement and put it into Gaza,” says Chaim, a member of the controversial Nachala settler organisation led by Daniella Weiss, known as the godmother of the Israeli settler movement.

“It’s part of Israel, and we are going back there. On a basic level, it is ours.”

And what should happen to the two million Palestinians who live there? “They have so many places they can go,” she responds with a grin. “For example, Australia. Such a big place. Don’t you have room for them?” As we speak, children run around wearing T-shirts saying “Gaza’s Jews”.

Chaim speaks glowingly of Gaza as a place of tranquillity and natural beauty, not mentioning the fact that most of its buildings have been destroyed or damaged during Israel’s war against Hamas, which killed more than 74,000 people, according to Gaza’s Health Ministry. Locals there speak of rodent infestations and infectious diseases running rampant amid the rubble.

The Pioneers of Gaza have nestled themselves between Kfar Aza and Nahal Oz, two of the kibbutz communities that came under brutal attack by Hamas on October 7, 2023. It’s a vivid display of the competing ideologies at the far ends of Israel’s political spectrum. The kibbutzim are famously left-leaning, pro-peace and secular; the Pioneers of Gaza and its supporters are right-wing, mostly religious, and committed to establishing a Jewish presence across all of what they call Greater Israel.

In the West Bank, settlers commonly use hastily built outposts to establish a foothold that later becomes a more developed and permanent community – despite the settlements being regarded as illegal under international law. This one, inside Israel’s 1948 borders, is designed as a way station to the Gaza Strip. Its arrival just days before Israelis vote in their first election since 2022 sends a message from the settlers that they want this to be a priority for the next government.

The Nachala settlers had no permission to set up their camp in the forest, which is controlled by the Jewish National Fund, a major charity. But authorities are showing no haste in moving them on. When we visit, there are a handful of police at the scene watching passively. Eventually, the officers politely ask someone from the camp to join them for questioning at the station. When the settlers decline, they quickly give up.

“We’re working together,” Chaim says, evincing no concern at being evicted. Israel’s police force is controlled by the ultra-national National Security Minister, Itamar Ben-Gvir, himself a radical right-wing settler.

The mayor of the nearby town of Sderot, a stronghold of Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud party, has visited to express solidarity and support for the settlers’ cause.

Twenty-one Jewish settlements were built in Gaza between 1967 and 2005, before Israel dismantled them under a policy known as the unilateral disengagement. Israel evacuated 8000 settlers from Gaza and relocated a cemetery containing 48 graves, while retaining control of the strip’s sea and airspace. The policy was deeply polarising at the time, with critics arguing it would expose Israel to more terror attacks.

Soon after the disengagement, the Iran-backed Islamist militant group Hamas gained power and began smuggling in rockets and building an elaborate underground tunnel network. Two decades later came the October 7 attacks, which killed an estimated 1200 Israelis.

Rabbi Duv Fendel, who has travelled from Sderot to teach Torah classes to the would-be Gaza settlers, says: “It’s outrageous that the only place in the world that by law a Jew is forbidden to live is in the Gaza Strip. Uprooting the settlements was one of the most hideous crimes in Zionism, and they need to be restored immediately.”

As for the Palestinians living there, he peppers his speech with comparisons between Hamas and the Nazis. “They lost the war and when you lose you have to face the consequences. Relocating is the least they could do,” he says.

The activists at the camp say they speak for a large part of Israeli society, and they are correct. While not commanding majority support, resettling Gaza is not a fringe position either. A poll by the Israel Democracy Institute last year found 40 per cent of Jewish Israelis support Israeli settlement of the Gaza Strip.

Two of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s most senior ministers, Ben-Gvir and Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich, are campaigning for re-election on a platform of returning Jewish settlers to Gaza. Both have been sanctioned by Australia and other Western nations for inciting violence against Palestinians.

“I want all of Gaza. I want Gaza to be ours, I want it Zionist, I want it secure,” Smotrich told a campaign event this month. Ben-Gvir told Time magazine in a recent interview: “If Israel wants to continue to live and not be destroyed, we have to capture all of Gaza ... Israel is a tiny country. We have to be wider, broader.”

Defence Minister Israel Katz, a member of Netanyahu’s Likud party, said in July that he intended to set up three military outposts in northern Gaza, a move that has traditionally been a prelude to civilian settlements.

When Eliyahu Aton saw a story about the Pioneers of Gaza encampment on Channel 14 – Israel’s equivalent of Fox News – he drove from his home 45 minutes away to offer his solidarity. Resettling Gaza, he argues, will improve Israel’s security and ensure an attack like the October 7 massacre can never happen again. He believes the kibbutzniks living nearby who still believe in the possibility of peace with the Palestinians are dangerously naive.

Danny Rahamim, a leader of the Nahal Oz kibbutz, counters that the settlers are “crazy” for wanting to resettle Gaza. “That would be like poking two fingers in their eye,” he says.

Critics argue resettlement would stretch the Israel Defence Forces to breaking point, drain the budget and expose Israel to international opprobrium. Netanyahu has repeatedly insisted that Israel has no intention of permanently occupying Gaza or displacing its civilian population. US President Donald Trump’s peace plan states that “Israel will not occupy or annex Gaza”.

This is why Aton, who served with the Israeli military in Lebanon in the 1980s, says Netanyahu needs ideologically committed coalition partners who will push him further to the right. The 63-year-old used to vote for the left-wing Labor Party until the early 2000s but is now backing Ben-Gvir’s Otza Yehudid (Jewish Power) party. “He knows how to treat the terrorists. He speaks our language,” he says.

Aton’s shift reflects a broader ideological trend in Israeli society accelerated by the October 7 attacks. Nearly two-thirds of Jewish Israelis identify now with the political right and a quarter identify as strongly right-wing, according to a study released this month by the Jewish People Policy Institute. Just 22 per cent of Israelis now identify with the left.

Ben-Gvir is expected to win about eight seats on Tuesday (Israel time), up from the previous election. That’s a massive turnaround from 2020, when his party failed to win a single seat. Younger voters, in particular, have been rushing to his campaign events, and conservative towns like Sderot are plastered with posters of him in front of handcuffed prisoners. Ben-Gvir drew international condemnation, including from Australia, earlier this year when he was filmed taunting pro-Palestinian detained after trying to enter Gaza on a flotilla carrying humanitarian aid.

Many at the Pioneers of Gaza camp say they back Smotrich, who is more calculating and less bombastic than Ben-Gvir but equally hardline. The problem for the far-right parties is that while they are holding and even gaining ground, support for Netanyahu’s less extreme Likud party has plummeted.

The latest polls show the pro-Netanyahu bloc hovering around 50 seats, significantly down on its haul at the last election and below the 61 required to form a government. Rabbi Duv Fendel is praying for a miracle on election day so his dream of resettling Gaza can be fulfilled. “I hope it will be a landslide for the right-wing,” he says.

NFL roundup: Falcons spoil Niners’ undefeated start; Steelers win in Paris

The Guardian Sun, 25 Oct 2026 20:48:11 GMT

Bucs rout Panthers in Baker Mayfield’s return

Browns move to 5-2 with late win over Titans

Jets hand Dolphins their first win of the season

Michael Penix Jr threw three touchdown passes, Atlanta scored 13 points off four turnovers and the Falcons handed the San Francisco 49ers their first loss, 29-20. San Francisco were already thin at wide receiver before its offense faced additional limitations when running back Christian McCaffrey missed much of the first half with a thigh injury. Brock Purdy threw two interceptions, one of them by rookie linebacker Kendal Daniels. Daniels also recovered a fumble by George Kittle. Penix threw scoring passes to Nick Muse, Kyle Pitts and Drake London as the Falcons snapped a two-game skid.

Harrison Smith capped another dominant performance by Minnesota’s defense with the game-sealing interception, and the Vikings overcame another sluggish start to stay unbeaten with a 16-10 victory over the spiraling Indianapolis Colts. Linebacker Blake Cashman led the onslaught of pressure on Daniel Jones all afternoon with 12 tackles, two sacks, four passes defensed and three quarterback hits as the Vikings improved to 6-0 despite minimal production from the offense. The Colts fell to 2-5. Jones went 13 for 122 for 108 yards and lost 44 yards on four sacks, and Spencer Shrader missed two field goals in the second half.

Malik Willis lead the Miami Dolphins to their first win of the season with a 28-25 victory over the New York Jets. It was the first win for Jeff Hafley as coach of the Dolphins, who avoided an 0-6 start for the first time since 2019. They scored on their first two drives and controlled most of the game. The Jets are 2-5 and made a late push, but Willis sealed the victory with a first down on fourth-and-1. Willis threw two touchdown passes and ran for a score. Geno Smith threw three touchdown passes and an interception for the Jets.

Aaron Rodgers threw one touchdown pass and Chris Boswell kicked three field goals in Pittsburgh’s 16-10 win over the New Orleans Saints in the NFL’s first regular-season game in France. Jaylen Warren rushed for 101 yards and Rodgers completed 19 of 30 passes for 212 yards and scrambled for a key first down late in fourth quarter as the Steelers (5-2) won their third straight game. Linebacker Payton Wilson had a red zone interception of Tyler Shough in the third quarter and the Saints (2-5) couldn’t recover. New Orleans rushed for just 18 yards.

Devin Singletary’s 30-yard touchdown run in overtime lifted the New York Giants to a 27-21 win over the Houston Texans on Sunday. Cam Skattebo had a 16-yard touchdown run in the fourth quarter and his 42-yard scamper to set up Singletary’s game-winning run. He had 17 carries for 124 yards after not having a carry last Sunday following a costly fumble two weeks ago. JJ McCarthy moved the ball effectively for the Giants (4-2-1) in his first start of the season after coach John Harbaugh benched Jameis Winston. He was 20 of 28 for 252 yards in the stadium in which he won the national title with Michigan in January 2024. The Texans (2-5) got the ball first in overtime, but New York’s defense forced a three-and-out with Kayvon Thibodeaux dropping a potential interception on second down.

Joe Burrow threw four touchdown passes in the second half, and the Cincinnati Bengals rebounded from a desultory first two quarters to beat Baltimore 35-13, handing the Ravens a second straight divisional loss with Lamar Jackson sidelined. Baltimore dominated the first half but led only 13-0 after settling for a couple short field goals. Then the Ravens blew a double-digit second-half lead for the second straight week and 10th time since the start of the 2022 season. Baltimore has outscored opponents by 65 points in the first half this season, while being outscored by 70 in the second.

Deshaun Watson has led his fifth game-winning drive in the fourth quarter this season. Park’s powerful, driven shot clipped the top of the crossbar around the hour mark, after Yamashita had saved well from Terland, one-on-one. At the other end, Shaw cut inside and forced Phallon Tullis-Joyce into a smart stop at her near post. Soon afterwards, though, last season’s WSL Golden boot winner delivered the breakthrough with her ruthless, low strike that was struck with too much venom for Tullis-Joyce to react.

Shaw, who had been booed by the home fans after exchanging robust challenges with Maya Le Tissier in the first half, ran across to celebrate in front of the travelling City fans, many of whom were waving inflatable bananas in the air. She almost had a second moments later but whipped a close-range, rising shot just over the bar.

Emmanuel Macron has been accused by trade unions of trying to curb the fundamental French right to protest as the government fast-tracks a bill to make protesters pay for damage caused by vandalism at street demonstrations even if they did not directly cause it themselves.

The French president, who leaves office next spring, has faced more than a month of protests in which high-school students have blockaded schools demanding a response to teacher absences, repairs to decrepit buildings and changes to the university applications platform.

Trade unions and gilets jaunes (yellow vest) anti-government protesters are now joining sustained street demonstrations in a growing social crisis over schools, as well as the cost of living and public services. Authorities have increased security measures and placed restrictions on demonstrating after France saw one of its worst days of violence in years earlier this month when largely peaceful demonstrations were marred by looting, fires and vandalism of state buildings.

The senate will this week debate the government’s proposed “vandals pay” law. The legislation would mean that a person protesting could be held liable to pay up to €10,000 for damage and vandalism even if they did not directly cause it themselves, if they were continuing to demonstrate nearby or as part of the same group as perpetrators. The bill also provides for greater use of drones over protests.

The prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, said the bill, which was originally prepared in the wake of violent clashes after Paris Saint-Germain’s victory over Arsenal in the football Champions League in May, was “absolutely essential” after looting and burning during recent demonstrations across France.

The bill comes as the government struggles to contain the current crisis. Marine Le Pen, of the far-right, anti-immigration National Rally (RN), has seen her frontrunner status in next spring’s presidential election boosted as she seeks to reinforce her law-and-order credentials and back police.

Le Pen, who has lodged an appeal to France’s highest court over her conviction for embezzlement of European parliament funds, launched her presidential campaign on Sunday at a rally in Orléans, promising to “bring back order to France”.

The RN has claimed the “vandals pay” bill was originally its idea and Le Pen said she would ensure damage to property was paid for by rioters. Le Pen told a cheering crowd of more than 8,000 people at the rally: “Vandals will pay and if it takes their whole life to pay, then they will spend their whole life paying.”

She said: “We are going to restore the rule of law. Who can claim that there is rule of law when hordes come to ransack and burn our buildings?”

Éric Coquerel, from Jean-Luc Mélenchon’s radical left La France Insoumise, said on Sunday that the “vandals pay” law “would mean the end of street demonstrations” in France because people would not want to take the risk of being held responsible and made to pay up to €10,000 for vandalism they had not committed. The Communist senator Fabien Gay told the parliamentary TV channel Public Sénat: “No demonstration could take place again in our country.”

In an open letter to Le Monde, leftwing trade unions and France’s Human Rights League wrote: “This unfair law, which is a serious attack on the freedom to demonstrate, should be abandoned, or risk a major step back for the rule of law.”

At this weekend’s protests there was widespread anger at Macron for banning non-union demonstrations that his government deemed “illegitimate” and for keeping all protesters away from city centres.

Although Macron has not put in place a state of emergency, the government and local authorities have introduced limits on demonstrating, including bans on gatherings in front of schools and demonstrating in city centres, as well as curfews in some places and extended periods of police custody for the record number of people arrested.

At demonstrations this weekend, many said they had come out to defend the French right to protest in the street. Street protests in France, which are seen as a fundamental way for people to make themselves heard by a centralised state, have regularly been used to express criticism of changes to the law, from pension changes to same-sex marriage.

Serge Slama, a professor of public law at Université Grenoble Alpes, told Telerama magazine: “Although a state of emergency has been ruled out [by Emmanuel Macron] at this point, we have seen a number of decrees bringing a wide restriction on public liberties.”

He said this was “unprecedented” and would benefit the far right if they won elections next year, allowing them to put in place further crackdowns without changing the law.

Lecornu will meet representatives of protesting high-schoolers on Monday as the government comes under pressure to respond to their demands with funding and school repairs in order to avoid further school blockades.

The prime minister made his plea for an “honest discussion” about freedom of movement in an interview with the Sunday Times, making clear that staying out of it would no longer be a red line in talks with the EU.

Burnham also revealed his belief that rejoining the single market and accepting free movement could be done without the need for another referendum, if Labour put it in their manifesto. In contrast, he said fully rejoining would need another in-out poll.

The prime minister said: “Freedom of movement had very significant challenges associated with it and I spoke about them in my previous time in parliament. But, at the same time, it was a type of immigration that perhaps wasn’t as difficult [as now].

“Revolving-door migration where people would come and then go back is different. The balance of migration has changed, hasn’t it, since then? I think we’ve just got to have an honest discussion about those things.”

His remarks were supported by Angela Rayner, the housing secretary, as well as Stella Creasy, the chair of the Labour Movement for Europe. However, Shabana Mahmood, the home secretary, is among those Labour MPs who previously has been more cautious about closer ties with Europe, while a number of backbenchers with heavily pro-Brexit seats in the north and Midlands are wary about reopening the arguments for free movement or rejoining the EU.

Rayner told the BBC’s Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg she would “like to have an honest conversation about what the trade-offs could be, and then put that to the people at a general election”, and Creasy, the Labour MP for Walthamstow, said Burnham was right that the UK was “long overdue for a grownup conversation about what EU freedom of movement actually means”.

A number of senior cabinet ministers are keen for the UK to form a much closer relationship with the EU to help boost growth, potentially involving a return to the single market and accepting free movement as a result. Those in favour of reopening the discussion include Ed Miliband, the foreign secretary.

At a New Statesman event during the Labour party conference in September, however, Mahmood said rejoining the EU would not be a “simple, straightforward thing” and there were “quite hard trade-offs”, such as eliminating trade friction without “some of the burdens that also brings”.

One senior minister under Keir Starmer said the reopening of the debate on free movement was “brave” given how divisive it had been in the Brexit years. “It’s a question of timing. Public opinion is of a place where you can start to have this debate,” he said. “Theresa May, Rishi Sunak, Keir Starmer: what they were all trying to do was get as close as possible without freedom of movement. There is now the a possibility of being brave and making the case on single market and free movement without going for rejoin.”

Labour MPs with pro-Brexit seats have expressed scepticism about rejoining the bloc, including Jonathan Hinder, the MP for Pendle, who recently pressed the prime minister in parliament to rule out a return to free movement.

One red wall MP said they thought debating free movement was the right thing to do but many colleagues in the north-east, especially in coastal areas, had begun to raise serious concerns. “These MPs are definitely raising the alarm,” they said. “Andy may have to work out if he can win without them, which is brutal but true.” Another Labour MP from a Brexit-voting area said it would “undoubtedly put seats at risk to Reform” but that Burnham was making an argument from a position of strength, having taken the party to higher poll ratings in recent weeks.

Worries were brought up publicly on Sunday by Richard Walker, the Labour peer and executive chair of Iceland, who told Times Radio that restarting the debate would be a “dangerous precedent” and that opening the borders would not help the “1 million young people that are out of work”.

In his party conference speech last month, Burnham fired the starting gun on the argument about rejoining the EU as one potential route, but his latest comments suggest he appears to be favouring the option that would avoid a referendum.

Although Labour’s manifesto pledges no return to free movement and the single market, Burnham signalled it could still be up for discussion at next month’s EU summit.

Burnham’s comments at the weekend drew an immediate response from the right of politics, with the Conservatives and Reform UK criticising the idea of reopening the debate. Kemi Badenoch, the Conservative leader, said the idea of reopening free movement was “another example of Burnham’s foot-in-mouth syndrome”.

Nigel Farage, the Reform UK leader, called it a “total betrayal of Brexit Britain and his Makerfield pitch”. “He is also deluded to say immigration was different when we were members of the EU. We will fight this dishonesty,” he added.

Polling suggests voters in the UK are increasingly open to rejoining the EU or a single market arrangement involving free movement. The concept of free movement was that British and EU citizens could move more freely for jobs within the bloc, which also shared a single market for goods and services.

Luke Tryl, a polling and focus groups expert at the More in Common thinktank, said on Sunday that people tended to be less concerned about free movement given years of high non-EU migration but would be more exercised about EU budget contributions or joining the euro.

During the Brexit referendum, the topic was hotly debated, with the leave campaign arguing that the UK would be able to take control of its borders if it voted to exit the EU. However, in the years that followed, net migration rose to a peak of 944,000 in the year ending March 2023 under a new points-based system, up from 330,000 before the Brexit vote.

Burnham’s decision to open the debate on free movement was welcomed by some businesses, which have grown frustrated at the lack of progress on the issue, as well as reducing the extra paperwork required to do business with EU customers since Brexit – both seen as obstacles to faster economic growth.

The British Chambers of Commerce lobby group called for the Treasury to analyse the various economic options for different forms of EU-UK relationships. Most economic studies have concluded that a closer EU relationship would benefit the UK economy.

William Bain, head of trade policy at the BCC, said the common understanding strategy agreed by Keir Starmer in May 2025 was “approaching the ceiling of what can be achieved”.

This week’s budget is expected to underscore the damage to the economy from Brexit, including from a drop in net migration. The Resolution Foundation, a thinktank, said that if migration falls by 300,000 over the next five years it would translate to a hit to government tax revenues of £4.7bn in 2029-30, reducing chancellor John Healey’s room for manoeuvre.

The Institute for Fiscal Studies, another thinktank, estimated that lower net migration estimates would reduce the chancellor’s “headroom” by between £1bn and £5bn by 2031-32, depending on how the government’s Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) chooses to model the expected reductions in population.

The OBR has previously estimated that Brexit barriers to trade and free movement have caused a long-term hit of about 4% of UK output.

Has Healey’s military-style budget secrecy really played out so differently to past budgets?

The Guardian Sun, 25 Oct 2026 19:35:17 GMT

Chancellor was said to be worried about market-sensitive leaks, yet significant policies have been heavily trailed in the media

The public has been told repeatedly that John Healey is so concerned about budget leaks that he has set up defence-style “compartmentalisation” to prevent the Treasury’s financial secrets escaping.

The macho military analogies began in mid-August when Healey was said by the Telegraph to be “on a war footing” to stop the drip of information that he believed had beleaguered Rachel Reeves.

The Financial Times added that “military-style protocols” were being deployed, while the Spectator was excited about the use of “classified computer systems” and the i newspaper described a process where officials could sign in to only their parts of the document and could not access the sections they were not working on.

This weekend, the Observer reported that Healey was “flabbergasted” by the lack of security around financial information when he became chancellor and “it was so different to how we did things in the MoD”.

The chancellor is known to have been worried that market-sensitive leaks cost Britain billions in the run-up to the last government’s budgets. But has this time around been so different after all?

Despite the heightened “security” around Wednesday’s budget, many of its announcements have been leaked already from a clear mixture of authorised and unauthorised sources.

It emerged well in advance that there will be a higher tax on banks – a deeply market-sensitive policy – and a package of energy support for the most vulnerable.

There will also be billions of pounds in extra defence spending, directed towards the British Business Bank and National Wealth Fund, as well as a £1bn crackdown on online VAT sales, with big retailers such as Amazon, eBay and Temu to be responsible for collecting what is due from smaller merchants selling on their platforms.

On top of that, there have been stories indicating the level of headroom the chancellor will be looking at – in the region of £15bn – known in the political trade as “pitch rolling” to avoid alarming the markets or the public.

The Treasury and No 10 have also undertaken their traditional stream of embargoed announcements by press release in the days before the fiscal event, such as a new £1.5bn borrowing facility for local authorities and £1bn for social housing, as they seek to build a sense of action and momentum about what the government is trying to achieve.

Former Treasury advisers believe the rigamarole around budget security is partly designed to deter civil servants and gossiping MPs from thinking they can embark on unauthorised chatter before a policy is ready.

But they also say it is unhelpful for the chancellor to produce a hermetically sealed budget, which could cause a backlash over surprise measures – in the markets, the media, among the government’s own MPs and the wider public.

It is often the less-trailed policies that have tended to go wrong, from George Osborne’s pasty tax in 2012 to Philip Hammond’s surprise national insurance hike for the self-employed in 2017 that had to be abandoned within seven days after a furore among Conservative MPs about breaking their manifesto promise.

Aides say there is a balance to be struck – and it’s not always a good idea to hoard information until budget day. “If everything is kept tight, then you end up surprising people. And that’s called a Liz Truss situation,” says one former strategist from the Tory years.

Healey has been shutting down speculation about various tax rises, from higher capital gains tax on certain assets to lowering the mansion tax on properties worth more than £1.5m – showing he has begun to see the virtue in expectation management and limiting surprises on the big day.

There may still be a few fiscal “rabbits out of the hat” on the day, as Healey seeks to combine a “steady-as-she-goes” budget with some eye-catching measures designed to show the public that the government is on their side.

But if the Treasury really has aimed for military levels of secrecy around its budget, the Ministry of Defence might have something to worry about.

An Emirati diplomat who as UAE ambassador to the UN helped secure the delivery of humanitarian aid to Gaza has entered the race as a late contender to succeed António Guterres as the world body’s secretary general.

Lana Nusseibeh, who is of Palestinian heritage, is widely noted for her advocacy of the Palestinian cause and the two-state solution and has won the endorsement of the state of Palestine.

She is however facing criticism over the UAE’s contested role in arming the Rapid Support Forces in Sudan, a group that has been accused of genocide by two successive US administrations.

Nusseibeh, 48, has been one of the leading UAE diplomats denying reports that the UAE supplied weapons to RSF leader Mohamed Hamdan “Hemedti” Dagalo in defiance of a UN arms sales ban.

A grouping of Latin American and Caribbean states, CELAC, has also sent a letter of objection to the security council, claiming her late entry came just as a consensus was emerging behind their region holding the UN top job.

Nusseibeh, who was educated at Cambridge University, was born in 1978 in Abu Dhabi, where her father, Zaki, had emigrated after the Arab-Israeli 1967 war made it difficult for him to return to his birthplace, Jerusalem.

She is the niece of Sari Nusseibeh, a distinguished Palestinian intellectual and author of a widely admired book on Palestine, Once Upon a Country.

She has justified her late – but widely predicted – entry into the race on the grounds that the UN security council appears to be close to deadlock on the six remaining candidates in the race, with no one as yet able to establish a clear lead after six rounds of voting, the latest on 16 October.

The latest straw poll – the first in which it was revealed whether any of the five permanent members of the 15-strong UN security council objected to a candidate – ended with Rebeca Grynspan of Costa Rica holding the lead spot.

But Grynspan faced objections from two unidentified permanent security council members, making it harder for her to claim she is a breakaway consensus candidate. She has support from nine security council members and objections from five. Guterres is due to stand down at the end of the year

Other candidates include: the Argentine diplomat Rafael Grossi; the UN envoy from Guyana, Carolyn Rodrigues-Birkett; Olara Otunnu, a distinguished veteran Ugandan diplomat; and Ecuador’s former foreign minister María Fernanda Espinosa. Two previously declared candidates have pulled out.

In her vision statement, Nusseibeh said: “At the heart of the UN sits a wager: that states will give up a little today to gain a great deal together over time.

“States have not stopped needing to partner with one another, but they no longer trust that cooperation will yield sufficient returns. Rebuilding that trust, with faster, more certain, and more realistic results, is the work of the UN.”

Brett McGurk, who served in the Biden administration as a top national security adviser, backed Nusseibeh for her work on Gaza.

“How did UAE become the largest global provider of humanitarian aid to Gaza, according to UN data? Because of Lana Nussaibeh – a diplomat who knows everyone and works with them … she would be an inspired choice for this impossible job,” he said.

Nickolay Mladenov, the Bulgarian diplomat who heads Donald Trump’s Gaza Board of Peace, said Nusseibeh “has always understood that the UN works when someone is willing to systematically build the bridges nobody else wants to build”.

He added: “In the Security Council [as UAE representative] she did that quietly and consistently and with great professionalism. She now has the chance to take that same spirit and ethos to the UN secretariat.”

But there is a fierce backlash from human rights activists who point to the UAE’s domestic human rights record and its alleged funding of the RSF in Sudan, the group responsible for killing thousands, including in the capture of El Fasher in October last year.

A January 2024 report by the UN panel of experts described allegations from sources in Chad and Darfur – including those of arms being smuggled into the RSF from the UAE – as credible.

One of the strongest attacks on Nusseibeh’s candidacy has been mounted by Kenneth Roth, the former executive director of Human Rights Watch, over her denials of UAE provision of any “military, logistical, financial or political support to any faction in Sudan”. The UAE says it supports the formation of a civilian-led government in Sudan.

A spokesperson for the force said: “We were made aware of a 60-year-old man having been struck by a falling tree on a minor road at Mid Kelton at about 10.30am on Sunday, 25 October 2026.

“The man was pronounced dead at the scene. There are no suspicious circumstances and a report will be submitted to the procurator fiscal in due course.”

Engineers had restored power to 344,900 customers but 82,600 remained disconnected, the Energy Networks Association (ENA) said on Sunday morning. The figure included more than 30,000 homes across Scotland.

The ENA said: “The networks have been focused on reconnecting customers this morning, though the continuing severe weather in some regions is limiting network engineers’ opportunities to safely start the work of restoring customers’ power today and access to certain areas remains difficult. Engineers are working around the clock to identify and fix faults.”

Train travel was disrupted on Sunday. Network Rail Scotland shared an image of flooding from the tracks to the platform at one Glasgow station, and fallen trees above the lines near another. Speed restrictions were in place across Scotland and several sections of its railways were closed, the operator added.

Network Rail shared images of a trampoline beneath a train and a shed by the tracks, and it reminded people living near rail lines to firmly secure objects in their gardens.

Some flights were diverted from landing at Leeds Bradford airport and others were cancelled.

The Met Office advised people in affected areas to secure loose items in gardens and to stay indoors as the storm posed a danger to life from flying debris and crashing waves.

The Met Office chief forecaster, Jason Kelly, said: “Storm Boelo will be felt across the UK this weekend, with the strongest winds and greatest potential for disruption in the north.

“Amber warnings are in place across mainland Scotland, parts of Northern Ireland and the far north of England, where gusts of 60-70mph are expected widely, with the potential for 80mph in exposed coastal locations.

Fernandes gamble leaves Carrick to carry the can for United’s institutional failures

The Guardian Sun, 25 Oct 2026 17:56:06 GMT

Leaving out his captain was doomed to fail but so are the club under the current leadership and the fans at Old Trafford know that all too well

Dropping your captain, who has held the team together for most of the past five years, is a bold move from a man whose job is on the line. It was very much a make-or-break decision from Michael Carrick to leave out Bruno Fernandes against Bournemouth. It did not work and Carrick knew the consequences if it failed and will probably pay the price for it, but he should not be alone.

Carrick said the decision to drop the Portuguese playmaker was purely based on football reasons but criticising his manager after the desperate defeat to Como cannot have helped. Clearly Carrick disagreed with his captain’s comments on the lack of pressing in the Champions League fixture. It was somewhat telling that Lisandro Martínez kept his place despite pointing out the director of football, Jason Wilcox, was a hindrance to the club the previous week.

Fernandes has been a long way from his best this season, with three goals and one assist in the Premier League, all in one game against Ipswich. It would have been justifiable to give someone else an opportunity in the No 10 role, especially when the squad contains far too many of those. But then, no one at United is in form, so keeping an angry Fernandes in position may have made more sense. United have won almost half the Premier League fixtures Fernandes has started since he joined in 2020, and less than a third when he is absent.

Some question Fernandes’ attitude based on his complaints when things are not going right, but that is his way of showing he cares. He may not be a leader in the Bryan Robson or Roy Keane mould but is certainly the one who sets the example, shown by a banner in the Stretford End depicting the two former captains and Eric Cantona alongside the word “STANDARDS”. Those have dipped here. This is a mid-table team, made worse by a lack of desire.

Everything was pedestrian in thought and execution. One promising attack lost momentum and United decided the most sensible course of action was to pass the ball all the way back to Senne Lammens, resulting in deserved boos. It felt like a moment that indicated Carrick’s days were coming to an end.

Hypotheticals are pointless, as was Youri Tielemans, Fernandes’ replacement. The central midfielder has not impressed since joining from Aston Villa in the summer and the extra responsibility for an experienced player did not spur him on. He was ponderous in midfield, repeatedly losing the ball as he struggled to cope with the pace of the game against a Bournemouth team eager to press and hunt in pairs. The No 10 is supposed to be a creative influence in the final third but the Belgian was a lost boy against men.

A poorly defended first goal resulted in the inevitable cutting by the cameras to a sullen Fernandes sunk into his seat on the bench. It was a goal that summed up the mood at Old Trafford, Rayan was left in space to volley home at the back post after Ayden Heaven needlessly gave away a free-kick. He looked miserable and the majority inside the ground felt exactly the same.

United lack pace across the pitch so require someone in key areas to speed up play, but Tielemans is not capable of doing so. His main influence on the match was getting booked in the first half, which all but confirmed his exit at the break. It was telling that Carrick turned to Matheus Cunha to take over the duties behind the labouring Bryan Mbeumo in the desperate hope he could spark his team into life.

Carrick has been left with an unbalanced squad, lacking quality in key areas. It would be hard to suggest on Sunday’s viewing that United were the Champions League team and Bournemouth in the Europa League. The Cherries can boast a wealth of smart recruitment, acquiring the likes of Adrien Truffert and Rayan – two players who would walk into the United team – for half a Harry Maguire.

The shambles of the third goal was on Lammens and Maguire, the former for running out too fast and the latter for not knowing how to run fast. Evanilson nipped in and flashed in the definitive game-ender. It sent Fernandes back to the bench with the expression of a man who had sipped sour milk. The final insult came when Carrick sent on the academy graduate Shea Lacey and left his captain to brood.

It is not solely one bottle; the whole dairy has curdled. Carrick can take some of the blame; the Glazers, Sir Jim Ratcliffe, Wilcox and Omar Berrada should receive more. United are not fit for purpose and the supporters’ ire was largely aimed at the directors’ box, demanding the owners sell up and go home, with slightly less savoury language. The Old Trafford faithful know where the fault lies, offering more creativity than any of their team with a fine repertoire of chants against the hierarchy, most pointedly at Wilcox, whose signings left Carrick in trouble before the season started.

Carrick had his name chanted, the full-time boos not for him. The manager – for now – did a lap of honour, cheered by the fans who jeered the players. Another era is nearing an end and finding reasons to be optimistic would be a greater waste of time than playing up front for United. Change will almost certainly come but it will not be enough.

Marcus Smith produces timely reminder of his class as Harlequins sink Saracens

The Guardian Sun, 25 Oct 2026 17:30:59 GMT

Harlequins 33-15 Saracens

England fly-half marks 200th appearance in style

Marcus Smith celebrated his 200th Harlequins match in magnificent style. Perhaps there is a danger, at times, of taking his immense talent for granted, but he was unstoppable here. A powerful visiting Saracens side barely got a look-in, with Smith reminding us all of his ability on the day Steve Borthwick named his England squad for a packed November.

Smith’s sensational running, distribution and tactical kicking masterfully controlled Quins’ attack for a badly needed success. They were nought from three in the league and this was a vital result for reasons more important than Smith’s personal prestige.

Defensive discipline and forward muscle was as significant as the customary soft hands and creative vision. It is only one victory but the storm clouds gathering around Jason Gilmore, the head coach – and the rest of the club’s hierarchy – have cleared to some extent.

Gilmore paid tribute to Smith: “The work he puts in, the way he cares about the club, he’s only 27 and played 200 games for us. We’re so lucky to have him. He led us around the park and I’m really proud of Smithy.”

Saracens – despite the presence of Maro Itoje, George Martin and Ben Earl – struggled to make an impact, hardly helped by their indiscipline; Earl and Fergus Burke were shown yellow cards before half-time.

Brendan Venter’s rotation policy may begin to raise eyebrows: Noah Caluori, Owen Farrell and Charlie Bracken were doing shuttle runs 10 minutes before kick-off. There are not many clubs who would ignore players of that quality as a matter of course.

“We have chopped and changed, so I understand why people are asking that,” Joe Shaw, the Saracens head coach, said of his side’s obvious lack of cohesion. “It’s not some random thing we’re trying to be quirky with. We believe there is merit in what we’re doing.”

The Prem weekend had been characterised by stormy weather and old-fashioned wrestles at Welford Road and Ashton Gate, in conditions that did not favour free‑flowing rugby.

A stiff breeze remained but the appearance of the sun appeared to play into Quins’ hands. Smith proved the point within three minutes, launching an attack down the left before capitalising on slick handling from George Furbank and Cadan Murley to sprint over. The crowd were on their feet. The tone was set.

The prop Fin Baxter, returning from a 10-month injury layoff, soon demonstrated Quins are about more than silky skill, producing a muscular carry in the 22 before a delightful one‑handed offload for the openside Seb Driscoll, who smashed through the Sarries No 9, Tomos Williams, and over the line.

The wing Rotimi Segun did get Saracens on the board with a fine twisting finish after the visitors worked through the phases into the Quins’ 22, with Martin, Rhys Carré and Theo Dan making inroads before Williams’s looping pass to the left.

But Quins, as if to prove a point, soon went to the driving maul at the other end, culminating in a penalty try and Earl in the sin bin for collapsing it.

Smith’s afternoon got better when Max Malins was sent cantering over the line on 26 minutes thanks to more sharp work by Segun. The England back, hungry to make a difference at both ends, chased a seemingly lost cause and batted the ball out of Malins’s hands.

Saracens’ media strategy has been debated recently and a three-word message on social media last week – “Their cup final” – raised the pre-match temperature. Rather like Northampton’s Henry Pollock and his embarrassing involvement in a scuffle at Leicester on Saturday, that only served to motivate the opposition, it was a provocative move from Saracens that seemed to backfire. Before half-time, Burke was shown a yellow card for an upright tackle on Rodrigo Isgró before Murley pounced for Quins’ fourth: bonus point secured, 26-5 at half-time. Saracens had missed 22 tackles and conceded 10 penalties.

On 55 minutes Quins twisted the knife. Williams flung a long pass out for Segun on the Saracens left where he knocked it on: Will Porter, the No 9, kicked ahead, collected and took advantage of some halfhearted defending to score Quins’ fifth and final try. It was a ragged effort from Sarries and will be a horrible one for their post-match analysis.

Tottenham’s 2-0 win against Chelsea on Saturday – another significant London derby – was distinctly un‑Spursy. Here was a heartening, notably un‑Quinsy, victory for Smith, the player of the match, and his suddenly resurgent team.

“He’s brilliant isn’t he?” Shaw said of Smith, adding the derby defeat left him with an “awful feeling”.

“We planned for him not to be that brilliant. He can pick you off. It’s a disappointing day at the office.”

The Guardian view on adult education: learning should be for all ages

The Guardian Sun, 25 Oct 2026 17:30:07 GMT

Teenagers and young adults are not the only people in need of new skills and a sense of purpose

The neglect of adults was, David Blunkett said in a recent interview, his biggest regret about education policy under New Labour. Spending on classroom-based adult learning in England has fallen steadily, from a high point of more than £5bn in 2003-04, to less than £2bn last year. We should not expect two decades of decline to be reversed quickly. But the upcoming report from Alan Milburn on young people who are not in education, employment or training is widely expected to result in a boost for colleges, as well as apprenticeship changes so that more are offered to new recruits rather than existing staff.

A timely report from MPs aims to ensure that older learners are included in these reforms. The all-party group for further education recognises the need to tackle the low level of labour market participation among young adults, which is particularly pronounced in smaller towns and cities. But the MPs take a longer view of the current system’s failings. Their report makes a persuasive case that an overall vision for adult education has been missing for a long time.

Economic and employment outcomes are important. If people are being trained in construction or IT or social care, their ability to find work afterwards matters. But adult education has a broader purpose that is harder to measure. Acquiring new skills, the MPs point out, can be a first step on a longer journey – a way to “begin to imagine different futures”. Learning can contribute to health and wellbeing, as well as income and productivity. One of the consistent themes from research was the importance of relationships – highlighting the role of education as a social glue, and of classrooms as a potential source of the people skills that employers want.

It is right for ministers to prioritise help for young adults who have yet to find their feet. But mid-career adults facing redundancy, or aiming to come off benefits, or to transition out of manual roles due to declining health, also need support. And while the promised modular alternative to maths and English GCSEs should be useful to future cohorts, the low literacy level of up to 8 million older people must also be addressed. In some areas, English language lesson providers urgently need more resources to meet demand. So does prison education, which has faced damaging cuts.

Adult education is not helped by the complicated administrative and funding arrangements that sit behind it. Overall responsibility for skills, including the £3.3bn apprenticeship budget, was transferred to the Department for Work and Pensions last year. But the Department of Education retains a role in further education, while the division of powers between Whitehall and the mayor-led regions is expected to be clarified in the budget.

This report proposes an England-wide minimum standard, which could then be developed by local partnerships. The lack of incentives for employers to invest in training is among the most serious problems at the moment. Uncompetitive pay is another, which makes recruitment of qualified instructors difficult. Careers advice is yet another gap.

Given these interlinked shortcomings, the proposed “renaissance” in adult education sounds optimistic. But at a time when the benefits of social and economic participation are being vigorously advocated, MPs are right to resist overly narrow prescriptions, and to champion the freedom to learn at any age.

The Guardian view on Oxford Street’s pedestrianisation: cities should be designed around people, not cars

The Guardian Sun, 25 Oct 2026 17:25:07 GMT

The transformation of Europe’s busiest shopping street should be a case study in making cities greener, less congested and more inviting places to live

Sadiq Khan has been trying to pedestrianise Oxford Street since he first became the mayor of London in 2016. On Monday, after numerous setbacks, his plan will finally come to fruition. The busiest stretch of the nation’s famous shopping street will be closed to traffic in a scheme designed to improve the area and make it more attractive to pedestrians. It should be an emblematic case study in making cities greener, less congested, more inviting places to live and visit.

The Greater London Authority hopes it will rejuvenate a high street fallen on hard times. Since the pandemic, the number of vacant shops on Oxford Street has more than quadrupled. It estimates that the scheme will generate £82m of value a year in the area by increasing footfall and encouraging visitors to linger. This impact remains to be seen, but research from other cities suggests that shops experience higher sales once an area is pedestrianised. Given the prime minister’s focus on rejuvenating British high streets, whose dilapidation is correlated with support for Reform UK, he should be watching with interest.

The benefits of pedestrianisation are far greater than increased shopping. Domestic transport remains the largest contributor to greenhouse-gas emissions in Britain. This sector’s emissions have fallen more slowly than others largely because too many people still rely on cars. Mr Khan’s city is an outlier: 59% of all journeys in Britain were made by car in 2024, while in London cars accounted for 34%. This is hardly surprising when the Treasury spends twice as much on London’s transport system as it does on other regions in England, and the capital’s bus fares are cheaper. In Leeds, which has no mass-transit system, nearly half of people drive to work. Car use cannot be reduced without simultaneously improving public transport.

The critics of pedestrianisation – including Westminster council – suggest it merely displaces traffic elsewhere. But the evidence on this is more nuanced. One study from the University of the West of England suggests the closure of strategic roads causes some traffic to disappear permanently, as people switch to public transport or walk. Low-traffic neighbourhoods (LTNs), the pedestrianisation schemes that were rushed through in the capital during Covid-19 and have since been introduced in Manchester and Birmingham, were fiercely criticised for causing a buildup of road traffic elsewhere. Yet one study of 46 LTNs in London suggested their impact on traffic elsewhere was minimal.

Car-free areas should be accompanied by other policies that reduce pollution on surrounding roads, such as the low-emissions zones introduced in London and Oxford. Mr Khan was criticised by the then leader of the opposition, Keir Starmer, for the expansion of Ulez in 2023, and also suffered racial abuse. He has since been vindicated by research from Imperial College suggesting Ulez has significantly improved the health of primary school children in the capital, whose lung growth had been stunted by pollution.

That Transport for London estimates the pedestrianisation of Oxford Street will have only a minimal impact on nitrogen dioxide emissions, which were already decreasing as a result of Ulez, is testimony to the policy’s success. In 2014, Oxford Street had the highest concentration of nitrogen dioxide pollution in the world. Its pedestrianisation should be an inspiration to other cities to embrace policies that work for people, not cars.

Cutting welfare to pay for work support is all wrong

The Guardian Sun, 25 Oct 2026 17:14:58 GMT

Priya Sahni-Nicholas on a proposal by Alan Milburn to help those not in education, employment or training. Plus letters from Ruth Lister and Alan Coppin

Alan Milburn correctly identifies that the nation’s 1 million young people not in education, employment, or training (Neet) represent a crisis of “youth detachment” deeply intertwined with mental ill health (Cut benefits to fund work support for young people, says Neet review author Alan Milburn, 18 October).

However, his proposal to cut welfare benefits to fund employment support both misdiagnoses the problem and points to a solution that will worsen it.

Framing welfare as something that is “plunging far too many young people into a life on benefits” ignores the fact that nearly half of Neet young people do not claim benefits.

The modern social security system is experienced as a regime of surveillance and scrutiny rather than a safety net. Paternalistic approaches that treat structural disadvantage as a personal failure actively drive vulnerable young people away from public institutions. Squeezing benefit safety nets further will deepen inequality, increase mistrust and worsen the problem, not alleviate it.

Rather than robbing Peter to pay Paul, we need the government to invest directly in reducing inequality. Creating the conditions for young people to thrive requires a fairer economic model that eradicates poverty and tackles gross disparities in income, wealth and power.

Health and employment support funding must come from progressive taxation on extreme wealth and corporate profits, not from threatening to withdraw support and further impoverishing already underresourced and vulnerable people.

We need government action that actively reduces inequality and builds security, giving every young person the structural foundation required to live a good life. Priya Sahni-Nicholas Co-executive director, Equality Trust

Thank you, Frances Ryan, for the call to arms in defence of our social security system (The right’s scrounger rhetoric dominates the benefits debate. Labour must fight back – and win, 16 October). But while it’s true that the right’s attack has been largely focused on disabled people’s benefits, the underlying hostility to social security and those reliant on it runs wider and deeper.

Fuelled by false claims that spending is out of control, the calls for cuts are relentless. And any attempt to start repairing the damage wreaked by the previous government’s cuts and restrictions – for instance, through the recent abolition of the two-child limit – are vilified with the kind of rhetoric she warns against. Cutting benefits to promote jobseeking is a false economy, as research suggests that impoverished people are ill-placed to seek and gain employment, and the costs are likely to fall elsewhere, including on the NHS.

The fightback needs to emphasise that social security, adequately financed, is both an essential weapon in combating poverty (including child poverty) and, as the name suggests, a key element in any strategy to promote the financial security of a wider population at a time of widespread insecurity. Ruth Lister Labour, House of Lords

Your article (Who exactly will be affected by the UK review of benefits for young people?, 20 October) again uses the term “Neets”. When I chaired the young people’s social inclusion charity Cities in Schools, we recognised that a new name was needed. Interbrand gave us Include, free of charge, with a modern logo: a lowercase “i” with a jagged line running through it, positive yet honest about the challenges our young people faced. The name mattered. It shaped how those young people saw themselves, and how others saw them.

Neet does the opposite. It defines young people by what they are not: in education, employment or training. Surely a government with all the resources at its command can find a less negative, less stigmatising term for the young people we need to help build a future. Alan Coppin Bourne End, Buckinghamshire

Plague risks in Russia and a dangerous delay on WHO pandemic agreement

The Guardian Sun, 25 Oct 2026 17:13:58 GMT

Responding to an editorial on a potential plague outbreak, Dr Darren Mann deplores delays to the agreement, while Kent Buse says Britain could do more

Your editorial on the silence from Siberia after a worker died at a plague research institute there is right that the lack of information is the real worry (The Guardian view on plague in Russia: what is most worrying is the lack of information, 18 October). But the deeper failure is not Russian. It is that, six years after Covid, we still have no agreed system for sharing pathogens, or for sharing what is made from them.

I spent three decades in Hong Kong, through bird flu, Sars and Covid, working on outbreak surveillance and sample-sharing between Hong Kong and the UK. It is also where this territorial argument began. In June 1894, two bacteriologists arrived to investigate the plague. Kitasato Shibasaburō was given lab space and immediate access to the bodies. Alexandre Yersin was refused access to the dead, and worked from a straw hut, having to appeal to the governor for his share of cadavers. Access to the material was allocated by favour, not by need. The organism carries the name of the man who was shut out: Yersinia pestis.

The pathogen access and benefit-sharing annexe to the World Health Organization pandemic agreement is the same argument in modern dress, and it has stalled on the same point. Poorer countries are asked to detect and share dangerous pathogens quickly. In return, they want a binding guarantee of what follows: 20% of real-time production of vaccines and treatments, half donated and half sold at cost. In article 13, the global supply chain and logistics network provides for a more equitable distribution of personal protective equipment. Richer countries prefer all that sharing to stay voluntary. The agreement cannot open for signature until this is settled, and it has now been deferred to 2027.

All pandemics start with a rumour. The next pandemic is likely to be something we have never seen before, and whoever first holds the samples will not be us. If we cannot agree what they get in return, we should not be surprised when they are slow to hand them over. Dr Darren Mann Former medical director, Cabinet Office Covid-19 PPE taskforce

Your editorial on plague in Russia is right that the system is fraying, but wrong to treat Moscow’s silence as an aberration. It is the predictable product of rules that member states built without teeth. The International Health Regulations oblige governments to notify the WHO within 24 hours, yet provide no verification, no sanctions and no independent monitoring. States mark their own homework through annual self-assessments. The amendments in force since last September add an implementation committee that is, by design, consultative only. Member states, Britain included, chose this. They then starved the WHO of assessed funding, leaving it dependent on the goodwill of the governments it is meant to hold to account.

Britain accepted the amended regulations in July 2025 and, with the United States gone, is among the WHO’s largest government funders. Ministers should raise Russia’s non-reporting formally within the WHO rather than leave Washington to make the only public request. The UK should table proposals for independent verification and a public compliance register when the pandemic agreement’s pathogen-sharing annex returns to the assembly, due by May 2027. And it should volunteer for the WHO’s Universal Health and Preparedness Review, a peer review that only 11 countries have joined and Britain has not. A government cannot demand transparency it declines to practise. The recent UN declaration on pandemics will mean little unless the governments that signed it are held to account. Kent Buse Co-CEO, Global 50/50

On dementia, we need to tell it how it is

The Guardian Sun, 25 Oct 2026 17:12:58 GMT

David Lee responds to a letter questioning the use of language about people with dementia

Sally Byers takes Polly Toynbee to task (Letters, 19 October) for using what she considers to be “deeply troubling language” about people with dementia, in particular the phrases “glazed stares or sleeping mouths agape” and “that terrible human vacancy” in Toynbee’s article (In Liverpool I saw the tough choices Louise Casey faces on social care – starting with who will pay?, 13 October).

I looked at the Dementia Engagement and Empowerment Project language guide for journalists highlighted in the letter. It gives a list of words and descriptions to avoid, including “dementia sufferer”, and lists alternative phrases to be used as “person/people with dementia”, “person/people living with dementia” or “person/people living well with dementia”.

I disagree. Toynbee described what she saw and wrote it, and her words had impact. In all the care homes I have been into to see elderly relatives, people with dementia weren’t “living well with dementia”; they were suffering. So why can’t we all tell it how it is rather than pretending otherwise? David Lee Staveley, Cumbria

Tech firms should pay the creators whose work they use

The Guardian Sun, 25 Oct 2026 17:11:34 GMT

It could raise up to £300m a year, providing UK creators with additional income, write Barbara Hayes, Tayyiba Nasser, Christian Zimmermann and Paul Seheult

Anthropic’s proposal (AI firm Anthropic to commit 5% of shares to fund for ‘public good’, 19 October) raises an important question: who should benefit from technological progress? Before pledging money for the public good, AI companies such as Anthropic should first pay the creators whose work they use.

Device manufacturers have a separate responsibility under the same principle: creators should share in the value their work generates. Smartphones, computers and other devices enable creative work to be copied and stored, yet UK creators receive no private-copying payments, unlike their counterparts in more than 40 other countries.

The proposed Smart Fund would require manufacturers and importers to make modest contributions on devices used to copy or store creative work. It could raise up to £300m a year, providing creators with additional income and supporting skills, cultural programmes and affordable workspaces.

For creators on persistently low and falling incomes, these payments would make a tangible difference. Visual artists’ median annual earnings are just £12,500 – 47% lower in real terms than in 2010. Authors earn a median of only £7,000 from writing, down from £11,300, according to surveys published in 2022 and 2018 respectively. Audiovisual performers report median annual earnings from performing of £17,500. Yet it is creators’ work that attracts people to technology, sustains their engagement and drives innovation. Those creators should share in the value their work helps generate, so they can continue creating and powering that cycle. The government should turn this principle into action by introducing the Smart Fund. Barbara Hayes Chief executive, Authors’ Licensing and Collecting Society (ALCS) Tayyiba Nasser Chief executive, British Equity Collecting Society (BECS) Christian Zimmermann Chief executive, Design and Artists Copyright Society (DACS) Paul Seheult Chief executive, PICSEL

England stunned after Shadab Khan’s miraculous century delivers one-wicket win for Pakistan

The Guardian Sun, 25 Oct 2026 16:49:49 GMT

England blow victory chance after hosts were 154 for nine

Shadab makes unbeaten 113 in thriller

Shadab Khan whipped the rug from under England’s boots with an ­eye-popping 113, a blitz of boundary peppering when hope was lost, the one-wicket win guaranteeing Pakistan a place in the tri-series final. England, for the second time in four days, watched a sure thing swirl down the drain.

With Pakistan 154 for nine in their run chase, 88 away from victory, queues were beginning to build at the Gaddafi Stadium exits. But Shadab had other ideas, and with No 11 Haris Rauf providing adhesive company, went on the rampage. Balls disappeared over this boundary and that as England giggled nervously into their hands. The drama doubled when Shadab was given out lbw on 97, slamming his bat into the turf in frustration, hands shaken with England, before an inside edge was discovered on a what-the-heck review.

From there 21 were needed, and 21 were hit, nail-nibbling minutes encompassing Rauf arguing a Sam Curran wide with Will Jacks having to be placated by Joe Root, a first ­hundred in any international cricket for Shadab, and Rauf driving Henry Crocombe for four to win the game by one wicket. Their partnership of 89 was the highest for the 10th wicket in any successful ODI chase.

After the cut-throat chubbiness of Thursday’s 859-run glut, this was pared-down cricket. Pakistan, in West Indies World Series salmon pink for breast cancer, had looked in command at the halfway stage, after England left runs in the middle, all out with 20 balls to spare for just 241. But England’s bowlers kept their nerve and Pakistan’s batters faltered, until Shadab and Rauf’s last stand.

Pakistan’s chase started under a purple Lahore night sky, with the ground filling up late. Like England earlier in the day, Pakistan had a tricky power play.

A frustrated Fakhar Zaman flashed a drive straight into the giant paws of Jamie Overton at slip in the fifth over to give the immaculate Gus Atkinson his first wicket.

The debutant Crocombe, all baggy shirt and rosy cheeks, coltish arms and legs working overtime, shared the new ball. He was on the money with his first over, and a more erratic nine-ball third finished with the wicket of Saim Ayub, who ladled the ball straight to Overton as Crocombe was mobbed. The crowd had one name on its lips and Babar Azam, at his home ground, made them sing with a pure off-drive matched by something equally majestic on the on-side. But just as the glory hit the veins, Atkinson whistled through the gate, firing the top of off, wagging his finger in celebration.

Saad Baig picked up the pace with an otherworldly 32, until a bullet was collected by Jacks at backward point off Overton, who had pulled up in his delivery stride earlier in the over.

From there, it was cat and mouse: could England frustrate Pakistan into giving wickets away? Yes they could, as Liam Dawson and Overton bowled on a button, and finally Hasan Nawaz yahooed Dawson into the stratosphere, Harry Brook waiting for his prize. Arafat Minhas lasted just three balls before directing Overton to Root, who had just been ushered to short fine leg by Brook.

Salman Ali Agha had a meaty slog at Dawson, Razaullah, also on ODI debut, got a gorgeous ball from Jacks between bat and pad to leave Pakistan nine down. It looked like game over.

Earlier, Ben Duckett’s fifth ODI century was the backbone of an ­England innings that sparked in places but was blotted by clusters of wickets. His second century at Lahore was dominated by sweeps of various hues, but after Pakistan won the toss and bowled, England’s first four wickets lined up like a pin number: 4, 5, 1, 6.

Tom Banton clipped the superb Shaheen Shah Afridi’s fifth ball to cover to give him a 150th ODI wicket. Root had time, just, to dispatch Afridi to the boundary before leaning back and enveloping him to point.

Brook, fresh from 202 against Sri Lanka, was undone coming back for a second, fractionally too slow for an inspired Razaullah pick up and throw. Then Jordan Cox tried to nuzzle Rauf to third man but was met by Babar diving to his right at slip.

In Curran, Duckett at last found sticking power, and the pair added 93 until Shaheen brought himself back on and Curran took on his shorter ball. As the black kites circled above, England’s last five wickets added 96, Duckett celebrating his first hundred against Pakistan with a low-key kiss of the badge, but they looked underdone and so it proved. To reach the final, England need Pakistan to beat Sri Lanka on Tuesday before thrashing Sri Lanka on Thursday.

Todd Blanche, Donald Trump’s attorney general, lashed out during an interview on Sunday while defending the justice department’s pre-emptive lawsuit to block certification of Alaska’s US Senate results if the GOP incumbent loses, calling a TV host’s question “crazy”.

The testy repartee unfolded on CNN’s State of the Union over the DoJ’s unprecedented legal action, which alleges that there could be “voter confusion” due to two candidates named Dan Sullivan on Alaska’s ballot. Trump told reporters, “I’m the one that said do it” when asked about the suit.

Dana Bash, State of the Union host, said “one of the big questions is whether or not “Trump tries to overturn the election, and the result of that could be, God forbid, what we saw after January 6”.

“Oh, stop it,” Blanche said. “Oh, you got to stop it with that. You are not being a real person. Come on, man.

Bash said, “it is not crazy.”

“I would have said that before January 6,” Bash said, referring to election-denying Trump supporters’ shocking attack on the Capitol. A bipartisan Senate report said there were seven deaths in relation to this incident.

“Because the president, because the Department of Justice, is concerned that there is an absolute fraud happening in Alaska, and he wants to do something about it, you’re saying, Mr Attorney General, because the president of the United States wants to stop a fraud and confusion in Alaska, is he going to do something crazy? That is not, that is not a real question.”

“We’re not laying any groundwork for the president to do that,” a fiery Blanche insisted. “What I said is the groundwork that we are laying is for Alaska, for the state of Alaska.”

“If it becomes an issue after the election, we’ll have the ability to determine whether there was confusion that violates the law in determining who the senators should be.”

Blanche also appeared irked during an interview with Margaret Brennan on CBS’s Face the Nation after she summed up the litigation and asked whether Trump directed him to file suit.

While Trump’s DoJ has claimed there might be “voter confusion” on Alaskan ballots, potentially propelling Democratic Senate candidate Mary Peltola to victory, election experts maintain that this position is legally weak.

“The legal claim is so absurdly thin, there’s essentially no likelihood of success,” said Derek Mueller, a law professor at the University of Notre Dame, in a blogpost.

The lawsuit, Becker said, “raises serious concerns about political interference” and that he could not remember “ever attempting to stop the certification of an election – and certainly not 11 days before polls close”.

Richard H Pildes, a law professor at New York University who focuses on elections, told the New York Times: “It is one of the weakest election lawsuits I’ve ever seen.”

“It should have no realistic chance of success in the courts,” Pildes said.

Is having urine the color of Mountain Dew normal?

The Guardian Sun, 25 Oct 2026 16:00:06 GMT

A Trump administration doctor says neon yellow urine is normal because of diets consisting entirely of meat and fermented foods. Here’s what experts say

A doctor who advises several Trump cabinet members on their diets rhapsodized this summer about having urine the color of Mountain Dew, thanks to a diet consisting entirely of meat and fermented foods.

What you consume does determine what you see in the toilet. But should urine be neon yellow – or some other hue? Here’s what you need to know.

Urine is normally a shade of yellow owing to a pigment called urobilin, which your gut bacteria produce. The more diluted it is by extra fluid intake, the lighter its shade – so urine is typically darker in the morning or when you’re dehydrated.

You may have seen charts that indicate what color and shade urine “should” be, but “they are considered imprecise” and experts don’t rely on them for serious purposes such as managing kidney disease, says Suzanne Watnick, a nephrologist at the University of Washington. Urine’s darkness or lightness loosely corresponds with hydration status, but for most people, it’s best to rely on your sense of thirst rather than what’s in the toilet to determine when to drink water.

That said, in people who need to stay highly hydrated, urine shade can be a helpful hydration indicator. For example, people prone to kidney stones should aim for very pale urine, Watnick says.

Your kidneys constantly filter blood to remove excess water and waste products, which trickle down to the bladder to get peed out as urine. These organs’ goal is to ensure your blood consistently has exactly the right balance of fluid, minerals, salts and acid.

“Your kidneys are really smart,” says Sharon Moe, a nephrologist at Indiana University School of Medicine. As long as they’re healthy, you can’t really override their settings. For instance, if you consume more water-soluble nutrients than you need, anything “extra” ends up in the toilet. This includes the by-products your body makes when it breaks down food and medicines, as well as the majority of any vitamins and supplements you might be taking.

Some of these compounds won’t visibly change urine – for instance, digesting a lot of beef is likely to turn urine more acidic but not change its color, says Watnick. But some can change the color of urine or make it exceptionally bright. B vitamins (like riboflavin) can turn it fluorescent yellow, rhubarb a reddish-brown, and beets a festive pink.

Anything but the usual yellow – including Mountain-Dew-adjacent hues – may signal your body is consuming something it can’t use. “If you get super fluorescent or super red, you’re eating too much of something or taking too many supplements,” says Moe.

For most healthy people, urine color changes are rarely an emergency. Notable exceptions include people with kidney disease, or if the color change is accompanied by other concerning symptoms like new pain, a new rash or severe leg swelling. These types of changes might signify a medical problem – get it checked out.

Otherwise, to troubleshoot a strange new urine hue, first stop any supplements you’re taking, says Moe. If it doesn’t go back to normal, cut out brightly colored foods next.

Sign up to Well Actually

after newsletter promotion

Additionally, look over your medication list. If you recently started a new drug, ask your clinician whether it could cause urine color changes. But don’t stop taking any prescribed medicines before that conversation, as urinary changes are an expected and harmless side-effect of some drugs.

If your urine is red or brown, you haven’t had any red flag symptoms, and the color persists after you’ve ruled out any recent dietary or medication changes, get checked out.

Bleeding in the kidneys, the bladder or the urinary tract can also turn it red or brown, and your clinician can assess that with a simple urine test. (In people who menstruate, it can occasionally be challenging to determine where blood in the toilet is coming from. Talk to your clinician if you’re not sure.)

Foamy urine can mean protein is leaking from your kidneys – a few bubbles aren’t worrying, but you should be concerned if you see anything that looks “like a beer head in the toilet”, says Moe.

Odor, frequency and transparency are also important. A sweet or foul smell, peeing much more or less than usual, and cloudy urine are all reasons to get checked.

Although urine changes can occasionally herald kidney problems, most kidney disease is invisible; 37 million US adults have chronic kidney disease, but only one in 10 of them is aware. Moe says the best prevention is keeping your blood pressure in a healthy range and eating lots of fruits and vegetables, with meat in moderation. “The carnivore diet is not a healthy diet,” she says.
