Matthew McConaughey has read all his bad reviews – and I applaud him

The Guardian Sun, 25 Oct 2026 16:00:06 GMT

The Hollywood actor revealed he once read two-decades’ worth of pans in one fell swoop, during two days in the desert. It’s the kind of preposterous self-flagellation we can all learn from and enjoy

To assume makes an ass out of you and me, but as sweeping generalisations go, this seems fairly uncontroversial: nobody likes hearing themselves being criticised. Obviously there are exceptions to the rule – no kink shaming here – but most people aren’t fans.

Which is why a recent admission from Matthew McConaughey is unusual. The Hollywood actor revealed that he once spent two days in the desert reading 20 years’ worth of negative reviews about himself.

I love everything about this. Each detail is perfect: the setting, the duration of the pursuit and the period spanned by the reviews, the narcissistic/anti-narcissistic intent, the ridiculousness, the pretension, the commitment.

“I read every one,” McConaughey said on the podcast Build or Break, while wearing tinted sunglasses inside and the sort of hat last seen on The Only Way Is Essex. “I sat with them – I spent two days looking. It was hard.”

The mental image this conjures up is a gift – nay, payback. This is why McConaughey is paid the big bucks; why, as the world burns, we need celebrities more than ever. Thinking about a 56-year-old tortured artist-millionaire, hunkered down in a barren landscape, nobly forcing himself to pore over his harshest critiques, is a wonderful distraction from proper news. It’s like a ludicrous minibreak from reality.

There are a few gaps we’ll have to fill in ourselves. When McConaughey says he “collected 20 years” of slatings and “went away to the desert for a weekend and took them all in this thick book”, do we imagine him sitting by the printer with his Pritt Stick, constructing his burn book with his own fair hands? Or is it more likely that this endeavour fell to an assistant in his employ? (In which case, talk about a fool’s errand.) Did McConaughey’s wife and kids join him on the multi-day desert jaunt and, if so, how was his 48-hour absence explained? “Sorry darling, Daddy can’t play Uno, he’s wallowing in painful self-reflection.”

In summary: this column will definitely not feature in any of his handmade tomes of the future. Ten out of 10, Mr McConaughey, no notes. And thank you.

Polly Hudson is a freelance writer

‘I think of it as anti-brain rot’: how our podcast team creates space for thought

The Guardian Sun, 25 Oct 2026 14:01:39 GMT

The journalists behind our new show Radical Thinking wanted audiences to experience a guest’s thought processes rather than simply hear their hot takes. But achieving this required a very different approach

It doesn’t often happen during interviews. Something inside the person starts shifting. Fresh ideas get forged in real time.

Our new podcast series Radical Thinking with Aditya Chakrabortty has already managed to generate many such moments. Each time it happens, you can almost hear the expression changing on the guest’s face. At one point, I switched from audio to video to witness the change and then watch as they refined their thoughts.

The effect is riveting. It’s also by design.

“We didn’t want this podcast to be a boxing match,” says Kirsty Major, a Guardian deputy opinion editor and an executive producer of Radical Thinking. “We hold guests to account where needed, but ultimately it’s about giving them the space to really think.”

The series sees Guardian columnist Aditya Chakrabortty sit down with some of today’s major thinkers to discuss the forces that are transforming our world and how we can meet the myriad challenges that are confounding conventional wisdom.

Fellow executive producer Maz Ebtehaj likens the approach to focusing on people’s thought processes. “We’re encouraging people to think about why they think a certain thing,” she says. “We’re sort of holding a magnifying glass up to their politics and their values, but in an exploratory way not a confrontational way.”

“We’re also trying to get a better understanding of where a guest’s thinking leads them,” says Aditya. “I might not always agree with what they think, but I’m really interested in how they got there and whether we share any premises. And because the interviews are exploratory rather than accusatory, we get those moments when a guest says something they perhaps didn’t expect to say.”

Whether you are listening to the podcast or watching it, it’s striking how each episode of Radical Thinking leaves you feeling notably nourished. That owes as much to the podcast’s radical approach as it does the radical ideas discussed on the show. By deliberately letting listeners and viewers experience a guest’s thought processes rather than simply hear their hot takes, the team hopes the podcast will feel distinct.

“I expressly think of it as anti-brain rot,” says Aditya. “When people talk about doomscrolling and brain rot, notice that they often slip into the passive voice. What they’re really talking about is how they no longer feel as if they have control over their lives. People want a different way of thinking about what’s going on in their world and that’s what we’re trying to provide.”

This sense of mission is coupled with an urgency that informs the series as the far right continues to gain power around the world by exploiting people’s grievances. “We’re living through some very precarious moments right now, and that requires us to come up with new ideas urgently, or at least to press the ideas people have into service,” says Aditya.

“The systems and the ideas and frameworks that we’re used to don’t work any more, so it does call for radical thinking,” adds Maz. “Some of our guests are inherently radical thinkers. Others have radical thoughts.”

The show’s guests are drawn from across the political spectrum, including former Greek finance minister Yanis Varoufakis, Spectator magazine editor and former Conservative deputy prime minister Michael Gove, Naomi Klein and Astra Taylor, the playwright James Graham, and the writer and Guardian columnist Nesrine Malik.

“That plurality of voices comes from within the Guardian’s own traditions,” says Aditya. “There’s a fascinating bit in the interview with Gove when I ask what his abiding principle in politics is and he says, I want to fight inequality. How does someone on the right explain that to the rest of us? Not with me saying to him, ‘but you did austerity, you backed Brexit and now this new nativism’... I want to know what throughline he sees there. And actually, what he tells us is shattering.”

Another such moment from the first few episodes is when Varoufakis explains how his experience of power radicalised him. “There is the look of defeat on his face,” says Aditya. “There’s also the genuine look of surprise on Naomi Klein and Astrid Taylor’s faces when we start talking about how the left might respond when the AI bubble bursts.”

These sorts of moments are spontaneous, but also the result of the way the whole team carefully plans and structures each episode. “I’ve just come out of an all-day meeting where we were thinking about how to structure our interview with James Graham,” says Aditya. “The really big, guiding question we wanted to discuss was whether stories can heal a divided country. What is it like to be the nation’s playwright at a point when the nation is falling apart?”

Those meetings are key to the alchemy of the series. “We plot it through,” says Maz. “What’s the guiding thought? Where and what are we going to get to? For example, with Varoufakis, we started by asking him about his upbringing and how he felt during certain moments of his life – because the personal can be very revealing about a person’s political views. We have time to draw emotional connections to people’s politics because each episode is an hour long. So the conversation should feel like a story and by the end the audience should feel they’ve arrived at some sort of answer to that initial guiding thought.”

For Kirsty, some aspects of the prep were very different from the kinds of journalism she’s previously done. “I went from editing and writing articles to working with the audio team, and they’ve opened my eyes to how you might structure a conversation and plan it out,” she says. “An incredible amount of work goes into that. We have to know what’s already out there and what a guest might say, but we want to go beyond that. By the end of it, you really feel as if you live in their head.”

As well as being familiar with each guest’s body of work, Aditya has also written about some of them before. “Another thing that helps inform some of these discussions is that I’ve known some of our guests for a while during the course of my reporting,” he says. “So there’s a degree of informality. I’m not trying to impose on our guests; I want to draw out the best of them. I know their work, I know where the broader conversation is, so I can think about how it can be taken to a different place or how we can add different perspectives. Journalism to me has always been about adding value like that.”

One regular feature involves asking each guest what they would do if they had a billion pounds. The answers aren’t just instructive, they are often informed by the preceding discussion. Another feature involves Aditya summing up what he has taken from each interview – underscoring how everyone comes away from the encounter feeling fortified.

Aditya says he hopes this also extends to listeners and viewers and that Radical Thinking proves empowering for audiences – just as he felt empowered by certain news outlets back when he was growing up. “During my childhood and early youth, newspapers and the media always played that role. It was a tool for the rising classes to make themselves better informed about the world.”

The podcast’s combination of informative and informal is also aided by its physical space. “We spent a lot of time thinking about the setting,” says Maz. “It’s very dark. It’s very low-lit. At first, we had two sofas but Aditya said it didn’t feel right because it wasn’t how he’d have a conversation. So we put in a table and chairs.”

Even without the sofas, however, the work and thought that goes into each episode means the interviews very quickly morph into a more intimate conversation. “It feels pretty therapeutic,” says Aditya. “A lot of stuff spills out.”

Watch every episode of the podcast on the Guardian’s Politics Weekly YouTube channel www. youtube. com/@politicsweekly, or listen wherever you get your podcasts.

The joy of veg-maxxing: how to eat many, many more plants – without really trying

The Guardian Sun, 25 Oct 2026 14:00:04 GMT

A new report has found many crops are far less nutritious than they once were, so we need to eat more of them. Here is how to get your five portions of fruit and veg a day, easily and affordably – and potentially increase that to ten

When Eva Humphries first started working as a nutritionist, she met a client who had just found out he had high blood pressure and high cholesterol, and was on the verge of type 2 diabetes. He had no idea how to change his diet or lifestyle.

The man broke down and cried for 45 minutes, leaving Humphries with “no idea of what to do”, she says. In the final 15 minutes of the session, scrambling for a quick but helpful message, she finally said: “When you look at a plate of food, can you just make half of it veg for me?”

The client came back two months later and “the colour was back in his cheeks”, she says. He told her that adding the veg had “started to [make him] feel really good”.

It’s a simple approach to eating more plants – and one we might all need to start emulating, sooner rather than later. Earlier this month, a new report found that, due to deteriorating soil quality, crops including carrots, apples and peas are now 20% to 50% less nutritious than they were in the 1960s. So should we be eating double the amount?

When I was a child, the “five a day” mantra for fruit and veg was drummed into me and, as an adult, I thought I was doing OK. I’m vegetarian, which means that most of my meals revolve around plant-based foods; I subscribe to a vegetable delivery service from a local community farm; and I frequently snack on apples. I actually do eat my five a day, most of the time – and often exceed that.

But even before these findings, there was research suggesting we should aim for 10 portions of fruit and veg per day, instead of five, while some experts advocate for consuming 30 different plants a week. Eating – and affordably sourcing – that kind of volume can feel overwhelming, and the news about declining nutritional value is potentially demotivating.

William Summers, senior associate at Deep Science Ventures, which published the new report alongside charity the Mark Leonard Trust, hopes the findings make farmers and policymakers consider and prioritise nutrient density. In the meantime, he doesn’t want people to imagine that there is no point in eating plants. His research has shown that “whole foods, across cereals, fruit and veg, have definitely got less nutrient dense. That’s a fact – but they’re still way, way better than eating ultra-processed foods.

“There are certain vegetables that are known to be more nutrient dense and that’s tied to their genetics,” he adds. “Broadly, it’s leafy greens. So I’d say the more leafy greens you can get in your diet, the better.”

According to last year’s National Diet and Nutrition Survey, only 17% of UK adults get their five a day, which can include, fruit, vegetables, beans and pulses. So how can we consume more plants without really trying?

A first step could be switching out meat for beans in meals you already make. Dr Shireen Kassam, visiting professor of plant-based nutrition at the University of Winchester, and executive director of Plant-Based Health Professionals UK, suggests swapping a tofu curry for a chicken curry, or a lentil bolognese for one made with mince. Even if you don’t want to lose the meat completely, a “half and half” meat and lentil bolognese is a good way to sneak in vegetables without entirely changing the flavour, she says.

Matt Beardmore, executive chef at the Italian restaurant Legare, also uses pasta sauces to pack in veg. At his restaurant, the focus is on taste, but at home, to get the maximum nutrition, he will double or triple the amount of sofrito (an onion, celery and carrot base for sauces) that he normally puts into a recipe. As the weather gets colder, Kassam and Beardmore both recommend soups as a way to use up any sad-looking leftovers in your vegetable drawer. With a soup such as minestrone, “you can just absolutely fill it with veg”, Beardmore says.

His rule of thumb is “filling half my plate with veg” – which is what Humphries suggests, too. The approach she used with the unhappy client at the start of her career has become a guiding principle for the way she now works. “It’s this concept of: if we look at a plate visually, can we just shove a couple more pieces of veg on it, or maybe add some herbs or a handful of greens? I think we underestimate how far little practices like adding an extra portion of vegetables can go.”

The next step, says Humphries, is to diversify your intake, to ensure you’re consuming as many different minerals and vitamins as possible. “We tend to get into a repertoire of eating broccoli and peppers and peas,” she says. One question she challenges her clients with is “when was the last time you’ve had watercress? Or, when was the last time you added a handful of fresh parsley on top of your food?” Fresh herbs are quite concentrated sources of nutrients, she says, so you don’t need to eat a lot to receive benefits. The idea is to get people thinking about easy ways to add new vegetables and other plants to the diet they already have.

One plant we could be eating more in the UK is seaweed, says Humphries, particularly because it contains iodine, one of the minerals flagged by Deep Science Ventures as having been lost from our soils. “It’s got loads of iodine, iron, calcium and magnesium,” she says. “It’s one of those other plant foods that we don’t often think about.” You also don’t need a lot of seaweed in your diet to reap the benefits, so eating a bit of sushi, which often features a dried version called nori, will give you your fill. “I typically tend to use it in seasonings because it’s got quite a salty flavour,” says Humphries.

The way we cook fruit and vegetables matters, too. “Typically, vitamins C and B tend to go from vegetables if you boil them,” says Humphries. “C is broken down by heat, and then a lot of the B-vitamins leach into the water.” On the other hand, certain vegetables actually improve when boiled: “Say, for example, iron in spinach. We can barely absorb any iron from raw spinach, but we can absorb it really well when it’s cooked or boiled”.

Neither Humphries nor Kassam recommend getting over-worried about cooking methods, though – increasing your quantity of vegetables is the main thing. “For most people, the basic message remains the same: five a day is the minimum,” says Kassam. If you can manage more, that will serve your body well.

To maximise the nutrients you absorb from the food you already eat, choose wholegrain varieties wherever you can – thereby “reducing the reliance on refined grains and going for brown rice, brown pasta”, Kassam says. One surprising thing that Kassam and Humphries tell me is that soaking beans and pulses before you cook them can also increase their bioavailability – which helps you to absorb more nutrients from them.

Beans might be a great source of selenium and zinc, but it can be hard work for us to actually absorb those minerals if they haven’t been soaked for a long period or cooked very slowly, Humphries explains. This is because beans contain phytates, which are “anti-nutrients, and their main job is to bind minerals”, she says. “So when we eat beans or grains, we can’t fully absorb those minerals because they’re bound to these phytates. So the only way that we can get around it is to do things like soaking beans overnight. Because that tricks the plant into thinking that it’s about to sprout, and it releases the phytates.”

This is great news if you’ve got the time and capacity to think ahead and prep your beans in advance – but the reality is that most of us buy beans in cans or jars. Most ready-to-eat beans in cans will have been boiled quickly, Humphries says – so while eating them is still good for you, you’re not maximising their nutritional content that way. For a convenient alternative, Humphries recommends the Bold Bean Co, which sells pre-soaked and slow-cooked beans in jars – but these are approximately four times the price of supermarket own-branded cans.

The most nutritious option does often come with a cost, says Humphries, who says that she can’t afford to eat 100% organic produce, even though she would like to. Does choosing organic actually make a nutritional difference? “Our data on organic isn’t particularly brilliant,” she says. But she wants people to be aware that “when we metabolise pesticides or any kind of artificial chemicals that are left on our food, we use nutrients to detox it” – so there is actually a case for pesticide-free produce allowing us to retain more nutrients.

If you can afford to buy organic and local, that’s great, says Humphries, “because we know that having a farmer down the road who really cares about supporting their local community is ultimately supporting more than nutritional wellbeing – it’s supporting our local economy. We also know that, when things are picked, they start losing nutrients fairly rapidly. So having access to fresher produce does have merit.”

For this reason, if you are able to grow your own fruit, vegetables and herbs in your garden or on your windowsill, you are likely to catch more of the plants’ nutrients before they start degrading. That is probably “the one advantage”, nutrition-wise, that has been proven when it comes to homegrown v shop bought, according to Summers. “There isn’t a huge body of evidence, but from what there is, there doesn’t appear to be any reliable differences” other than “simply freshness”, he says. “The sooner you either eat or preserve it, the better.”

“Ultimately, as a nutritionist, my heart lies with: ‘get the vegetables in’” – in whatever way is affordable and manageable – says Humphries. While Kassam would recommend switching sugary snacks for fruits, nuts and crudités (the third one to pack in even more vegetables outside meals), “ultimately we have to recognise that unhealthy calories are cheaper than healthy calories”, she says. She points to the charity the Food Foundation’s most recent Broken Plate report, which showed that a fifth of UK households would need to spend 85% of their income on food to afford the government-recommended healthy diet, and that the price gap between healthier and less healthy food is now the widest it has been in over a decade.

Because of this, Kassam says, “people don’t always make active choices: their choices are made in the food environment, what’s affordable, what’s familiar. We need to be representing healthier options in our supermarkets and incentivising those purchases.”

There are ways to maximise your plant consumption slightly more cheaply: frozen vegetables still count, and sometimes even contain more nutrients than fresh ones. “There are cases where rapidly freezing veg will give better nutritional quality than fresh veg that has been sat around long enough to have time to degrade,” says Summers.

“I tend to stash three to four different types of vegetables in my freezer,” Humphries says, so she’s always got a handful of spinach or peas to add to her meals.

If you have room, keeping a store cupboard full of “tins of beans and wholegrains and things that are always going to make a nutritious meal” is also a good, and relatively cheap, way to ensure that you always have plant foods on hand, even if you haven’t got anything fresh in, says Kassam.

But, she adds, any increase in fruit and vegetable intake is beneficial. “We’re not talking about being perfect.”

‘There’s nothing interesting about me – and no interest in me’: how Larry David’s new biography nearly didn’t happen

The Guardian Sun, 25 Oct 2026 14:00:04 GMT

He point-blank refused, begged the author not to talk to people who knew him … and eventually relented. Making the first authorised biography of the Seinfeld and Curb creator was no mean feat

Emperor of Nothing: The Making of Larry David might be the most begrudgingly authorised biography ever written. The story of how author Blake J Harris convinced the comedy titan to “tolerate” him begins, of all places, at Fox News.

It was 2020 and Harris’s second book, The History of the Future: Oculus, Facebook, and the Revolution That Swept Virtual Reality, had been published the previous year. Palmer Luckey, the Oculus founder, was “fired for being a Trump supporter” and Harris, anything but a Trump fan, simply reported the facts. Speaking on the phone from his home in Colorado, he explains: “My book ended up doing well because I was all over rightwing media, as they loved having me on. I was the liberal journalist who exposed the truth about how conservatives were treated in Silicon Valley.”

Glenn Beck was one of several rightwing commentators who gave Harris a television platform that helped his book to succeed. He even asked if the author would consider writing his biography. Harris politely declined but started to ponder whether there was a public figure he would like to spend years of his life researching and writing about. One day, while taking a shower, he started to think about the way Seinfeld and Curb Your Enthusiasm had shaped his sense of humour, formative years, his entire worldview. Harris had an epiphany – he would write about the man behind them, Larry David.

Harris had written a lengthy piece for ESPN to mark the finale, at the end of 2015, of The League, a sitcom written and directed by Jeff Schaffer. Schaffer was a Seinfeld writer who would become David’s chief collaborator as Curb Your Enthusiasm wore on. Schaffer liked Harris’s proposal because he felt there should be a biography of his mentor, arguably the most significant comedy writer in American television history. He was also aware that his boss would be reticent given David was the man whom comedy writer Alan Zweibel once described as: “The only person I know who has buyer’s remorse before he buys something.”

Emails flew back and forth in August 2020, with the potential subject informing the potential author that this was a bad idea. In one, reproduced in the prologue of Emperor of Nothing, the subtext is clear – curb your enthusiasm: “There are far better ways to spend your time. There’s nothing interesting about me and there’s no interest in me. That’s not being modest. It’s the truth. So why the book? My parents are dead, so now we’re only left with my kids and my wife to read it. I don’t think three books is making it to the bestsellers’ list. Surely there are better subjects that would welcome a biography.”

Harris was not deterred. He enlisted David’s friends and explained to his hero that this would not be a conventional biography, but rather David as “the protagonist in an ensemble story”. Eventually, to appease his friends in a way his Curb Your Enthusiasm alter ego rarely would, David sent Harris a five-word email: “Oh Jesus. If we must.”

When Harris was eventually introduced to his idol, he had what he considers one of the greatest ideas of his life: a ploy George Costanza (the scheming Seinfeld character modelled on David) could be proud of. He decided to focus on a shared interest: “I really wanted to make a good impression with Larry and show him I’m someone he can just shoot the shit with … I’m not a typical stiff journalist who’s going to make his life difficult … So, I suggested for that first conversation … the only topic I want to talk about is the New York Yankees.” (David is a lifelong fan.)

Steering clear of the work in that initial chat proved an inspired move, even if, six years on, David recently told Harris: “I agreed to do the book, but I immediately regretted it.” Those regrets will be his alone: what started with a conversation about baseball is a 576-page tome that captures the spirit of the comedy great in ways that suggest Harris understands the Davidian shtick so well that this is the closest we will get to a Larry David memoir. Take the story of David’s birth, which reads as a glorious tribute to the late Richard Lewis, his best friend and collaborator: “On 29 June 1947, at Brooklyn Jewish hospital, a remarkable little boy was brought into the world. This boy – who’d prove to be special in so many ways – would by the age of thirty become one of the most influential comedians of his era. Three days later, at that same hospital, another little boy was born. That boy’s name was Larry David.”

The author spoke to friends, family, colleagues and neighbours as he attempted to forensically trace a journey that began in Brooklyn, encompassed years of struggle on the standup circuit and would ultimately produce two of the greatest television comedies in the history of the medium. Few people manage to produce a work of such quality once; to do it twice is almost unprecedented.

The book is especially compelling when covering David’s lean years (a period that stretched into his early 40s). It explains how he found himself picking out potential spots in the street for when he would inevitably become homeless, despite being viewed as the “comedian’s comedian” by his peers. His talent was never in doubt, only his temperament. Harris is skilled at drawing parallels between the art and the life, just as Seinfeld and Curb were at their best when blending fact and fiction. We learn about our hero giggling uncontrollably at a piano recital when confronted with a Pez dispenser, quitting his job at Saturday Night Live in a fit of pique on a Friday only to walk back in the following Monday as though nothing had happened, and taking part in a masturbation contest. All this would become material during the Seinfeld years: Jerry ruins George’s girlfriend’s recital by making Elaine laugh with Pez; George screams at his boss and storms out, then acts as though nothing has happened when he realises the financial implications; and The Contest, in which the four main actors have a wager to determine who can go the longest without indulging in onanism, won David an Emmy. In 2009, The Contest was No 1 in TV Guide’s Top 100 Episodes of All Time.

Indeed, every funny life experience in those early years would invariably find its way into a David sitcom. The urgency of the writing and our awareness of the greatness to come ensures Harris’s biography rattles along like a thriller, but one which, rather than heading inexorably towards a crime scene, instead leads to some of the greatest art of the past century. Harris reassured David, who was afraid of looking egotistical, that he “could hide in his own biography”, due to it including interviews with people other than himself. When he heard Harris was talking to friends and collaborators, David urged him not to “bother them”. Sarah Silverman allayed the biographer’s fears: “That’s so Larry. What he doesn’t realise is what a joy it is for us to speak to you about him.”

Harris describes his subject as the “idealised version of the artist we all wish we were”, a man far more concerned with artistic integrity than financial gain. In the 1980s, long before the fame and fortune, Larry wrote a screenplay entitled Prognosis: Negative. His manager sold the script and was thrilled when she secured a hefty payday for a rewrite. In an unprecedented move, the struggling comic asked for the fee to be negotiated down from $35,000 to $5,000 because he thought the material was good and had no wish to make wholesale changes.

Through Harris’s biography, we learn that this strange combination of unerring belief in his own ability on the one hand and low self-esteem on the other has defined the career of the comic genius. During his standup days, he would routinely open with the following esoteric bit: “You seem like a very good audience tonight. I’m wondering, may I use the tu form with you people? Because I feel very close to you. Do you mind if I jump into the tu form?”

By David’s own admission, it got nothing “60 to 70% of the time”. When Seinfeld asked his future collaborator why he persisted in opening with a routine that rarely worked, the answer was unequivocal: “I think that’s funny! And if that’s not funny, why am I even doing standup? What’s the point?” Typically defiant, he extended it: “You know, Caesar used the tu form even after Brutus stabbed him.” Thus, Seinfeld got an early glimpse of a man who would not be cowed by outside interference.

Harris was grateful that David largely chose not to interfere with his manuscript. His only real notes were asking for sections to be toned down where he appeared “too nice”, especially in relation to his daughters (“What father doesn’t love his daughters?”). He did, however, witness one trademark David rant when he was invited to appear as a background actor in the Curb finale, a story he is delighted to relay over the phone.

Harris and Ken David, Larry’s older brother, were sitting at a table in the background while Larry and Richard Lewis improvised an argument. The pair of extras were instructed to mouth their words, but not speak audibly. Larry’s sibling, however, appeared not to have got the memo and audibly started trying to talk sports with Harris. Harris tells me: “In the middle of the take, Larry seamlessly turned from yelling at Richard Lewis to yelling at his brother and telling him he was supposed to be quiet and that he was ruining the take.”

As an early Curb tagline made clear: “Just because he’s made it, doesn’t mean he’s got it made.” David, it seems, will never stop shouting. Emperor of Nothing perfectly captures the evolution of an artist – even as the man steadfastly refuses to change.

Emperor of Nothing: The Making of Larry David by Blake J Harris is published by HarperCollins (£22). To support the Guardian buy a copy at guardianbookshop. com. Delivery charges may apply.

Your boss might be an idiot – and 12 other things you need to know about work

The Guardian Sun, 25 Oct 2026 14:00:04 GMT

British teenagers are stressing about jobs (or the lack of them). Here is my advice, from owning your mistakes to the importance of biscuits

Young people want to know more about the world of work. A survey of 2,000 13- to 18-year-olds for BBC Radio 5 Live found that they wanted to learn about applying for jobs (42%), managing stress (39%) and developing their communication skills (38%).

It’s sensible stuff – dispiritingly so. Shouldn’t they be drinking BuzzBallz at bus stops? If someone had asked 13-year-old me what I wanted to know about work, I would have stared blankly, or asked: “What job will let me touch Mark Shaw (of obscure 80s band Then Jerico)?” Look at what their French peers are up to!

I asked a French friend what she thought kids needed to know about work and she said (imagine her taking a drag on a Gauloise; she wasn’t, but still): “Nothing matters, nothing is real, hierarchy is a social construct. Burn it all down.” But in mustn’t-grumble Britain, with its nearly 1 million Neets, teens aren’t rioting – they’re worrying about work experience, CVs and LinkedIn. The least we can do is try to help, so I asked what people think kids should know about exchanging labour for money and these things came up again and again:

Anyone who tells you “do something you love and you’ll never work a day in your life” is a cliche-sodden bullshitter. “Do something you love and see your relationship to that thing shift, become ambivalent, maybe even curdle” is more accurate. Most people don’t keep a pure, unsullied passion for the thing they spend 40-plus hours a week doing. “All jobs get boring, even if you’re Mick Jagger,” as a friend says.

You don’t need to know what you want to do yet. Try things out: even jobs you hate are illuminating, and it’s almost always better to do something than nothing. Working somewhere poisonously unethical is the exception.

Your colleagues make more difference – good or bad – to the quality of your life than the work itself. You can’t do much about it, but cherish the nice ones.

You never know who the really important people at work will be. There’s usually someone who makes you want to bang your head against a wall until you pass out, but one day they might be the only thing standing between you and disaster – treat them (and everyone else) accordingly.

Equally, just because someone is in charge, it doesn’t mean they aren’t an idiot.

The best advice on complaining to others about your colleagues (or bosses) is don’t, but we’re only human. Take a tip from someone with two scarring, unforgettable “replied instead of forwarding an email” professional experiences to her name, and always triple check you’re sending the bitchy message to the right person.

Speaking of mistakes, you’ll make them. Own up immediately, because the longer you leave it, the harder and scarier it gets. Most people respect and appreciate an honest admission of fault; anyone who doesn’t is an idiot.

Most difficult work situations are improved by a packet of biscuits (unless you work in a biscuit factory).

Speak up when you don’t understand, and don’t pretend you’re on top of a job when you’re not. Bad managers make this feel almost impossible, but try not to let yourself get steamrollered.

So much is forgivable if you’re enthusiastic and cheerful. I say this as someone who is naturally neither, but I’ve seen how winning these qualities are even in people who are, in all other ways, basically unemployable.

You’ll probably lose your job at some point and it will feel like a shameful, personal rejection and the end of the world. It isn’t.

“Shit on company time,” says a wise acquaintance. That’s her pithy way of explaining you can start believing work is so important you can’t spare time for basic bodily needs. Work is never that important (unless you’re doing brain surgery, which you probably aren’t at 16). You’re a human first and an employee second; you have time for a sandwich and a loo break.

Finally, perhaps the most important tip of all from the same wise woman: “Never tell anyone your living grandparent status – you’ve got at least four days off for funerals that way.” Hope that helps, kids.

Emma Beddington is a Guardian columnist

Cutting ‘red tape’ is nothing but a red herring – and arguably counterproductive

The Guardian Sun, 25 Oct 2026 13:00:34 GMT

Blaming a moribund economy on too many rules is a hackneyed neoliberal trope – UK plc needs smarter regulation, not less regulation

Before becoming prime minister, Andy Burnham pledged to “end 40 years of neoliberalism”. But as he prepares for his first budget on Wednesday, his government is yet to let go of one of its most tedious cliches: red tape.

In the run-up to the chancellor John Healey’s high-stakes Commons address, the government issued a press release last week promising his plans would include measures to “slash the red tape choking firms”.

Named after the tape once used to tie up government bills, and popularised by the historian Thomas Carlyle, the phrase is straight from the neoliberal playbook and has long outlived its usefulness.

Getting the interfering state out of the way of the wealth creators was a trope of Thatcher and Reaganite economics, and on this side of the pond it has been repeated ad nauseam by every government since.

Thatcher unleashed the City with her “big bang” deregulation drive, and her successor John Major was enthusiastic about “hacking back the jungle of red tape”. It was the man he appointed for the job – Michael Heseltine – who coined what has become the most hackneyed description of this particular approach: the “bonfire of red tape”.

With Labour back in power, Gordon Brown celebrated a light-tough regulatory regime for the UK’s hard-driving financial sector – until the Treasury had to bail out the banks after the 2008 financial crisis.

Boris Johnson wanted to unfetter Britain’s businesses from “Brussels bureaucracy” and waffled on during the Brexit campaign about bendy bananas. Yet, after Brexit, business groups said their members would rather comply with longstanding EU standards in many areas than adopt an entirely new UK regime. And bananas are no more or less bendy than before.

Rachel Reeves had a more unpleasantly graphic way of making a similar point, referring to regulation as a “boot on the neck” of British business.

There is nothing wrong with ensuring the interaction between business and the state is smooth. But even during the early years of neoliberalism, the free market good, regulation bad dichotomy was always unhelpful, for several reasons.

First, good regulation – a robust competition regime, for example – is essential to make markets work well. And even most enthusiasts for a laissez-faire approach would acknowledge the need for some basic quality standards – for food and medicines, for example.

When it comes to the labour market, Labour has unashamedly adopted a pro-regulation stance. Its Employment Rights Act is the most significant increase in workers’ rights in a generation – but it inevitably, and deliberately, increases the rules firms must follow.

That is to the benefit, ministers rightly argue, of low-paid employees trapped in insecure work. But a bonfire of red tape it is not. Labour posing as a champion of deregulation will seem unconvincing, given that context.

Second, and ironically, the march of neoliberalism itself is a reason regulation has mushroomed in recent decades. As the Labour MP Yuan Yang argued in a recent lecture for the journal Renewal, as the state retreated from providing important services, watchdog institutions to oversee the private sector became necessary.

As she put it: “The neoliberal illusion, that privatisation liberated markets from state interference, obscures the reality that the state already significantly controls our privatised utilities, but through a maze of arm’s length regulatory agencies which operate outside democratic influence.”

For the water sector, privatised in 1989, these include Ofwat, which sets bills (with the Competition and Markets Authority acting as an appeals body in the event of a dispute); the Drinking Water Inspectorate; the Environment Agency; and the Consumer Council for Water.

Yet, as Yang points out, none are responsible for drawing up a coherent plan for the sector as a whole. “Everyone knows how this story ends: with our rivers polluted and our water infrastructure dangerously lacking.”

Sign up to Business Today

Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning

after newsletter promotion

Hacking away at the regulatory thicket fails to deal with the structural features of the economy that make the rules necessary in the first place.

Mat Lawrence, the director of the thinktank Common Wealth and author of The Productive State, a policy paper influential among those close to Burnham, calls this “the regulatory state”. He cites affordable housing targets for private developers as another example of regulation taking the place of stuff the state once did itself.

The third reason the endless red tape discourse is unhelpful is one raised by Mike Clancy, the general secretary of the Prospect union, which represents workers at many of the regulators.

He has urged the government to lay off these often not lavishly paid staff, who are trying to do their jobs with stretched resources. “Regulators continue to be labelled as ‘blockers’ despite the vital work they do keeping us safe and protecting our natural environment,” he said.

Prospect has been urging the government to ditch a promise to “cut the administrative burden” of regulation by 25% by the end of the parliament, arguing it is arbitrary and potentially counterproductive.

Finally, we would all benefit from some over-mighty businesses being reined in by regulation, not least the tech firms, which insouciantly concede that their AI agents have been busting through safety controls and may be about to start spawning spontaneously.

Embracing the tired idea that red tape is “choking” business is hardly likely to help the government make the case for the more stringent approach that is clearly necessary.

As it happens, Bonfire Night is almost upon us. If Burnham really wants to embrace a different approach to the economy, he could start by consigning the phrase “red tape” to the flames.

‘If it was up to me it wouldn’t end like this’: Jimmy Anderson confirms Lancashire exit

The Guardian Sun, 25 Oct 2026 12:04:15 GMT

England’s all-time record wicket-taker not offered new contract

Bowler has spent 25 years at county

Jimmy Anderson has confirmed he will leave Lancashire when his contract ends this year, after the county decided not to extend his deal for the 2027 season. The 44-year-old has not said whether he will retire or continue playing elsewhere.

Anderson reflected on his Lancashire career on Instagram. “I’ve supported Lancashire since I was a kid, and so to get to play for them for 25 years was a dream come true,” he wrote. “I have always found it special walking out to play at Old Trafford and have some incredible memories of doing so, including the honour of being captain.

“If it was up to me it wouldn’t have ended like this, but I wish the players and fans all the best for the future.”

Anderson made his Lancashire debut in 2001. He took 443 first-class wickets for the county in 112 appearances, plus 83 List A wickets in 61 matches and 50 T20 wickets in 40 appearances. His 50 wickets in the 2026 Championship at an average of 17.68 earned him Lancashire’s Championship player of the year award. The county finished second-bottom in Division Two and exited both limited-overs competitions in the group stage.

Paul Farbrace, Lancashire’s incoming director of cricket, said he had told Anderson the club would not extend his contract after a meeting with the chief executive, Richard Kenyon, on 19 October. Farbrace said the club wanted to rebuild its squad to secure promotion and then challenge in Division One over the next three to four years. “Lancashire Cricket can confirm that, following a remarkable 25-year association with the Red Rose, Sir James Anderson’s playing career with the club will come to an end at the conclusion of his current contract,” read a statement from the county.

The former England captain Nasser Hussain said Anderson’s departure was “a hugely sad way” for the bowler to leave the club. “I’d say most counties in the country would take Anderson, even at the age of 44,” he wrote for Sky Sports. “I’d rather not focus in on how it ended, both for England and for Lancashire – I’d rather be thankful that we’ve had 26 years of Anderson giving it all for England and Lancashire.”

They wallow in Trump gunk 24/7. They say it’s necessary

The Guardian Sun, 25 Oct 2026 12:00:04 GMT

Joanna Coles and Michael Wolff spend most of their days thinking about the president’s follies for their podcast, Inside Trump’s Head. Someone’s gotta do it

For a couple of journalists who spend such an inordinate amount of time sloshing around the putrid inner recesses of Donald Trump’s mind, they come across as remarkably chipper.

Michael Wolff, chronicler of the 45th and 47th president, and Joanna Coles, chief creative and content officer of the Daily Beast, are just about to record the 168th episode of their runaway podcast, Inside Trump’s Head. Now in its 15th month, the thrice-weekly show is attracting an expanding audience as it digs down into Trump’s unique blend of megalomania, narcissism and insatiable lust for fame.

We are sitting in Coles’s office on the fifth floor of the IAC building, the shiplike Frank Gehry structure in Manhattan where the Daily Beast is headquartered. Coles, dressed sharply as you would expect from a former mentor on Project Runway in snakeskin shoes, jeans and white jacket, is having her trademark shock of white hair groomed for camera.

Wolff, who has styled himself more in the mould of a country gentleman in sumptuous brown corduroy suit (of which more later), seizes on the hair arranging to unleash his own trademark: the Wolff monologue.

“I don’t have any hair,” he laments. “I used to. You should see the author photo of my first book – I looked like a 70s porn star, heavy moustache and heavy hair. All gone now …”

The pair are fond of ending each other’s sentences. And they bicker a lot, like those long-married couples in When Harry Met Sally. “Do be quiet!” Coles snaps at him in a mock schoolma’am’s voice. “She really was a kind of pest,” he snipes back, recalling the early days of their friendship.

Underneath the crotchety patina, though, it’s clear they adore each other.

In the fickle world of Trump-focused media, the Daily Beast’s podcast seems to be enjoying an enduring appeal. Since its launch in August 2025, its audience in audio form has tripled to 1.5m downloads a month, while it now exceeds 5m monthly full-episode views on YouTube. The lion’s share of its supporters are in the US, but it also has a healthy following in Canada, the UK and Australia.

Part cod psychology, part celebrity gossip, part Shakespearean tragedy, the podcast leads us to places that more traditional Trump reporting rarely goes. The title is indicative. As Coles puts it, “we go deep into the dark matter inside Trump’s head”.

The 168th episode, whose recording I attend, takes in Trump’s belligerent UN general assembly speech happening that day and his later fawning reception of China’s President Xi Jinping. But it is fair to say that fans of the podcast don’t come to it for geopolitical analysis.

An average episode will delve into such matters as: the defenestration of senior women in his administration, including the short-lived press secretary Katie Zacharia and ambassador to Greece, Kimberly Guilfoyle; Trump’s weight (they call him the “all-you-can-eat president”); Melania’s mysterious disappearing act (Wolff and the first lady have form, having locked horns in a long-running legal dispute); and the outsized role of executive assistant Natalie Harp, whom Wolff flagged as an issue well before the White House correspondents’ pack.

They have also tackled the portentous question: does the president wear diapers? “There was no odor that surrounded him,” Wolff revealed in one show, drawing on his olfactory reporting skills from when he trailed after Trump during the 2024 presidential campaign.

There is no mincing of words in the pod, no on-the-one-hand-this-on-the-other-hand-that. Coles brings the sharpness of her Fleet Street training to bear in analysing Trump, as well as her skills as a forensic interviewer well-versed in the seamier side of celebrity lifestyles. Wolff can inject the observations of a book and magazine writer and the knowledge he gained from the extraordinary access given to him at the start of the era, when he was invited to spend weeks inside the first Trump White House.

His language on the podcast is spicy. Wolff has variously described Trump on air as “that fat fucker” and a “fucking asshole”, while Coles likes to highlight what she is convinced is the president’s declining mental faculties.

Trump’s top team returns fire with equal gusto. Steven Cheung, the White House communications director, has on umpteen occasions slammed Wolff as “a lying sack of shit” and a “fraud”, while Coles is a “retard” and a “blithering idiot”.

Faced with such blowback, the duo are unapologetic about their choice of subjects or words, dismissing Cheung’s attacks as “performative”. “We talk how people talk, about their friends, about their bosses,” Coles says. “We are not trying to put a glass wall between us and politicians, we’re trying to understand them as people.”

Trump has often claimed that he has made a fortune for the “fake news” media, and such bragging would appear fair comment when it comes to Inside Trump’s Head. Coles estimates that a third of the Daily Beast’s content and traffic is entirely dependent on him.

As for Wolff, Trump has been a veritable cash cow. According to Forbes, Wolff made $13m just in the first year of Fire and Fury. Will he say exactly how much he has profited from all four books?

He hesitates, then says, “No.”

Coles, true to form, finishes his sentence. “Well, you have made a lot of money,” she says. “There’s your 18th-century mansion in Amagansett.”

“It’s 19th-century,” he retorts. “And it’s a farmhouse.”

“What about your hand-sewn Savile Row suit, it’s Anderson & Sheppard isn’t it?” she presses, referring to that sumptuous brown corduroy affair he is sporting.

Wolff silently concurs. A bespoke Anderson & Sheppard suit, as worn by King Charles and Daniel Craig, can easily set you back $9,000.

The podcast’s unashamed technique of examining Trump in the round, with all his personal flaws and foibles, is not without its critics. The New York Times columnist Frank Bruni last month wrote an opinion piece that berated media outlets that focus on Trump’s appearance rather than on the damage he is doing to the world. Though he didn’t mention the podcast, Bruni did mention “cankles”, a Daily Beast favourite.

When I raise the Bruni argument – that what matters is Trump’s anti-democratic actions not his inner psychology – it sparks off another Wolff monologue.

“Trump is the most unique politician anyone has come across,” he says. “He’s so unique no political reporter can cover him. That’s our conceit: to probe what the traditional media is not covering. They cover Trump as they would an ordinary politician, and his politics as an ordinary function of cause and effect. But Trump is completely outside of the familiar ecosystem of the presidency.”

He’s only half done. “You can analyse Trump’s policies all you like, but what he is doing has nothing to do with policy. It has everything to do with himself, with his self-aggrandizement. To understand him, you have to look at his character, how this guy thinks, what are his fundamental motivations.”

The seeds of Inside Trump’s Head can be traced back to the start of Wolff’s decade-long engagement with its subject. The two men had some contact in the early 2000s when Wolff was writing a media column for New York magazine, but it was not until May 2016 that he and Trump went head-to-head.

In the course of an interview during Trump’s first White House bid, Wolff asked him why he was running for president. Trump replied: “To be the most famous man in the world.”

Wolff recalls: “I thought at that moment, my God! This is going to be a trip.”

Ever since that exchange Wolff has been on an epic voyage of discovery to get to the bottom of Trump’s bottomless desire for fame. “It’s not just a character flaw that he craves all this attention. It has become Trump’s strategy. ‘How do I stay the most famous person in the world?’ That is literally the question he asks himself when he wakes up every day.”

Trump’s attention-seeking is one of the central themes of the four books that Wolff has written about him – starting with the bestseller Fire and Fury that took readers into the chaos of Trump 1.0, and most recently last year’s All or Nothing that marked his return to office. It is also what inspired Coles to create Inside Trump’s Head as part of her plan to reinvigorate the Daily Beast after Barry Diller, the billionaire chairof IAC, invited her and Ben Sherwood to take over its helm in 2024.

Coles and Wolff have been friends for 25 years, after she left her West Yorkshire roots and relocated as a Guardian reporter from London to New York. It was Wolff who gave her a leg up into American media, helping her leave the Times of London to which she had defected and secure an editing job at New York magazine.

(This seems a reasonable moment to make a full personal disclosure. I have been friends with Coles since we worked together in the Guardian newsroom in London in the 1990s. I have also known Wolff since I myself moved to New York for the Guardian in 2006, and I have on occasion written about him. The last time I did so I reported on the Trump-related interviews he conducted with Jeffrey Epstein, during which Wolff gave the convicted sex offender PR advice on how to handle the scandal spiraling around him. Wolff emailed me having read the piece. “Jesus, Ed, you’re a nitwit,” he said.)

The Coles-Wolff friendship hasn’t always been easy. They’ve had intermittent feuds along the way, in which they have avoided speaking to each other for a couple of years, though neither can remember why. “I feud with a lot of people,” Wolff concedes.

I wonder what price the two of them are paying for what they are doing. There are many journalists who have covered Trump for the past 10 years, myself included, who know only too well the toll it takes on one’s mental health, repeatedly grappling with his lies and darkness. But few have devoted themselves to the task as round-the-clock as they have. In one podcast, Wolff admits: “There are very few conversations I ever have that are not about Donald Trump.”

What’s the collateral damage of all that wallowing in Trump gunk?

“Good question,” Wolff says. “I would fall back on that, as a writer, to get this story, to get this character, is once in a lifetime. You have the opportunity to have a voice in history. You don’t walk away from this so readily.”

“I’m British, so I don’t even think about my mental health,” Coles quips in that schoolma’am’s voice. She carries on: “We are at a pivotal moment for the global world order. Growing up in Europe, in the shadow of the second world war, you had tremendous confidence in America as an ally. All that is changing because of one man. I would feel depressed if I weren’t trying to understand this as much as I can.”

With the midterm elections fast approaching, the tone and focus of the podcast is inevitably shifting towards Lame Duck Trump. Aren’t they worried that we are nearing the end of this extraordinary epoch, of the “government of one” as they like to frame it, and the journalistic riches it brings?

Coles puts on a brave face. “We are interested in people and power. Whatever comes next will be interesting, because Trump has blown off the doors and allowed us to see inside the mechanics of power, and you can’t put the doors back on.”

The last question I direct to Wolff. Having sacrificed (at great personal gain) 10 years of his life to Trump, can he see the US, the world, ever recovering from this trauma? Will we ever be post-Trump?

“We’re going to get to the other side of this, yes,” he says, beginning his final monologue. “I absolutely believe that the unique Donald Trump will not come again. When he leaves, everyone is going to sigh with relief, even the Republicans.”

He’s not done yet.

“It’s a fascinating thing. Nobody, except his fanbase, likes this guy. I mean, Trump is a fat fuck, even to those closest to him.”

This comedian jokes about deportation … but it is happening for real

The Guardian Sun, 25 Oct 2026 12:00:04 GMT

Despite job offers, Jaishree Malik has had visa renewal and extension requests delayed and denied, and she is not alone

Jaishree Malik bounds on to the Cheeky Monkey comedy club stage and brandishes an envelope – it is a letter from the Irish government. Would the audience like to hear what’s in the letter?

“Yeah,” the first rows reply. She repeats the question, prompting a louder response. “Yeah!”

Malik extracts typed A4 pages and begins to read. “I wish to advise you that under section 3 of the immigration act 1999, the minister for justice, home affairs and migration is proposing to make a deportation order in your case.”

A nervous laugh ripples across the audience, then there’s a pause. “Oh,” says someone.

Malik beams. “Don’t worry, it’s not for you.” She resumes reading. “The reason for this is because you have remained in the state without permission […] you are therefore a person whose deportation would, in the minister’s opinion, be conducive to the common good.”

For the audience in the basement of the International bar in central Dublin, the penny drops: the letter is real. Malik, 25, is facing deportation to her native India.

“Did you know you were friends with a criminal?” she asks. “I’m sorry you had to find out this way.” She cracks a few more jokes, then: “In case you can’t tell, I’m fucking furious about this.” She concludes her set to whoops and applause.

Malik is not being deported - she is leaving voluntarily - but she may be the only immigrant to turn her deportation order into comedy. Plenty of others share her anger at a system they say has become harsh and arbitrary.

The Irish government has toughened border enforcement and rules on migration, asylum and naturalisation amid a housing shortage and strain on public services partly attributed to immigration. Placards at anti-immigration protests declare that “Ireland is full”.

The justice minister, Jim O’Callaghan, has said the authorities wish to curb population growth that is seven times the EU average. Critics say the welcome mat has been withdrawn unfairly from deserving cases, including students from Gaza denied visas despite scholarship offers from Irish universities.

Others, such as Malik, have had visa renewal and extension requests delayed and denied despite job offers. “It’s Kafkaesque. Why would I read The Trial? I’m living it,” she said in an interview, referencing the novel about a protagonist pitted against unreasoning bureaucracy.

From Gurgaon, near Dehli, Malik moved to Ireland in 2022 on a student visa to pursue an M. Phil (Master of Philosophy) in literature at Trinity College Dublin. She had a job on campus during her studies advising prospective and current students. After graduating she obtained a visa that let her stay and work for two years through the Third Level Graduate Scheme and continued working at Trinity with international exchange students.

She moved to another job in Trinity and applied to the department of justice to extend her visa, pending confirmation of a new one, but a delay in processing the application led to Malik losing that job in February and entering legal limbo. The department told her she had no right to work while the application was being processed.

She submitted additional information to bolster her case and, while awaiting a ruling, subsisted on savings and channelled her anxiety at open mic comedy nights. Malik had dabbled in comedy at Trinity but never previously performed around the city.

“Your best material comes when your life is falling apart. But the first time I was so scared. I was reading bits from my phone. It wasn’t landing very well, I didn’t know where to pause. But I got a lot of good feedback. All the comedians were absolutely lovely.”

Malik refined her act and incorporated her exasperation when the department of public works offered a job that she could not accept because of the visa imbroglio. “It’s so absurd. I’m being offered a job by the government that I can’t take because of the government.”

Some audiences think she is playing a character, she said. “They come up to me and say, ‘Oh, that’s so funny’. Then I explain and they’re like, ‘Oh wait, it’s actually real?’”

Ivana Bacik, a legislator and leader of the Labour party, said Malik’s case reflected a hardening of immigration policy. “It’s impacting on lots of people and indeed lots of employers because they’re losing good people.”

The department of justice was using “spurious reasons” to deny visas to Gaza students, said Bacik. “I believe there’s much more compassion and warmth towards inward migration among Irish communities and it’s not reflected in the ministry’s approach.”

A group that represents the Gaza students said the “breakdown” started this summer. “We were refused for documents we were never asked to provide, such as a bank statement and proof of intention to return,” it said in an emailed statement. “We were then told to appeal with original documents by post, and as you know, Gaza is destroyed and there is no postal service.” The students have taken test cases to Ireland’s high court.

A department of justice spokesperson said he could not comment on the court cases but that screening and verification were integral to the immigration system and that there had been no change in policy towards Palestinian students. “Each visa application is assessed on its own merits.”

For Malik, the battle to remain in Ireland ended with the deportation letter sent on 5 October. She will leave next month but continue performing until the end.

“I am very angry but when I get up on stage and I make people laugh, it sort of disarms the anger and the political stuff. If I can go up there and make you laugh about something so powerful it makes it less powerful and it becomes the joke. That is the jester’s privilege.”

Ireland is not immune to xenophobia and racism but audiences have been supportive, said Malik. “I’m talking about visas, yes, but under this I am still a person. I’ve made a lot of Irish friends who are basically family and they’re all outraged on my behalf.”

She has not fully absorbed the fact she must leave, she said. “I don’t think it’ll hit me until I’m on the plane.” She is bracing for “reverse culture shock” once back in India.

In the meantime, Malik is preparing to shed her possessions, close her bank account and pack before heading in the early hours of 14 November to Dublin airport. “My flatmate drives and she’s offered to take me even though it’s a very inconvenient time. That’s a very good flatmate. Shout out to the flatmate.”

As a young man, magazines were my window to the world. That wonder will be lost when all the shops have gone

The Guardian Sun, 25 Oct 2026 12:00:03 GMT

The closure of former WH Smith stores around the UK is sobering on many levels. The publications they sold were there to be perused, to broaden horizons

Towards the end of the 1970s, the brief but spectacular career of those punk rockers and folk devils the Sex Pistols was followed by The Great Rock’n’Roll Swindle, a rather tawdry drama-documentary. It recast their rise and fall as a huge scam, summed up by a slogan on a T-shirt worn by their former manager Malcolm McLaren: “Cash from Chaos”.

Back then, that motto was a neat representation of his personal brand of cultural mischief. But the culture always takes unexpected twists and turns – and 50 years on, an almost-identical maxim seems to be defining the fate of an increasing chunk of the British retail economy. While Andy Burnham pledges to restore life to town centres, a private equity outfit is busy buying up national retail chains and then shutting down scores of their outlets, while seemingly operating in line with its boss’s most celebrated quotation: “Where there’s chaos, there’s opportunity.”

Those words came from Jamie Constable, the owner of a set of businesses that includes Modella Capital, which specialises in “distressed investing” and “aggressive restructuring”. In 2024, Modella bought the craft supplies chain Hobbycraft – insisting on its “real commitment to bricks-and-mortar retail”, but then shutting 18 shops and triggering 600 job losses, while leaving redundancy costs to the taxpayer. Months later, it acquired the discount outlets branded as The Original Factory Shop, only for the entire chain to collapse. But its most ambitious move was its recent purchase of the 480 high-street shops that previously traded as WH Smith, rebranded by Modella as TG Jones (a completely made-up name, which it said would “keep that sense of a family business”), and the rapidly announced closure of up to 150 of them.

In September, 19 branches breathed their last, in such varied locations as Bath, Southend, Cardigan, Redhill and the Essex new town of Basildon. This month, the shutters are permanently falling in – among 23 places – Pinner, Truro, Inverness and Leek in Staffordshire. Thanks to their shortsighted folding into previous WH Smith premises, the closure plan will inevitably mean the loss of many local post offices: by early 2027, 70 will have gone. It will inevitably accelerate the decline of printed newspapers. But for me and many others, the key tragedy in this story is all about magazines, those gloriously tactile creations that played a crucial role in making many of us who we are.

I say that as someone who fell in love with this form of publishing as a child, via a weekly educational magazine called Look and Learn – stuffed, as I recall, with comic-strip versions of Dickens stories, and stuff about space exploration. By my early teens, I was an avid reader of Sounds, the Melody Maker and NME, the so-called weekly music papers that were really magazines whose ink came off on your fingers. Much to my amazement, between my 19th and 26th birthdays, I ended up successively working for all three – until, in 1995, I joined the now defunct company Emap Metro, which set enormous store by its mastery of glossy fortnightlies and monthlies.

Some of these names may mean precious little to younger readers, but spark a Proustian rush among older ones: Q, Smash Hits, Select (which I edited for three years), Sky, the metal and hard rock title Kerrang!, Big, Neon, FHM. Most have now closed, but three of the old stable are still standing, under different ownership: Kerrang!, which mostly lives online; the film bible Empire; and Mojo, the lovingly produced music magazine that I am thrilled to still write for.

Thirty years ago, we all knew that there was no better medium for in-depth interviews, or high-end photography. The management constantly asked us who our intended reader was, and what the future was likely to entail. Even the smallest cover-lines were pored over, as if the mere mention of Placebo or DJ Shadow might attract scores of newbies. And though a lot of us didn’t listen, we were told to never, ever put our magazines in sealed plastic bags (which, in line with a longstanding convention, would contain “free gifts”), for fear of losing the kind of punter who liked to browse before they bought.

And therein lies the TG Jones tragedy. The business has rightly acquired an utterly grim reputation, but is – or was – one reliable place to still find shelves full of printed content worthy of endless curiosity. And now? The culturally omnivorous twentysomething in Rickmansworth will no longer chance upon the latest edition of the cutting-edge music monthly the Wire, and thereby be inducted into a world of esoteric electronica and contemporary avant-garde jazz. The student-age customer in Ormskirk tiring of production-line pop may know nothing of the more substantial music covered by Mojo’s excellent competitor Uncut.

Would-be radicals will be unable to browse the printed iteration of Tribune; film freaks may be completely unaware of the in-depth, art-house wonders of Sight and Sound. Publishers will fall over themselves to alert us to subscription offers, but for a lot of people, they will be prohibitively expensive.

As George Orwell once put it, the UK is “a nation of stamp-collectors, pigeon-fanciers, amateur carpenters, coupon-snippers, darts-players, crossword-puzzle fans”. Products that reflect that enduring aspect of our national character are still at the core of magazine publishing, and why some titles still sell enviably: at the last count, for example, BBC Gardeners’ World sold a monthly average of 164,807 copies, while Country Living shifted 107,596. The broad women’s and fashion sector is also still here. It isn’t all over, by any means.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

after newsletter promotion

Still, one can easily imagine a Mark Zuckerberg-esque voice scoffing at all this as so much stone-age nonsense, and claiming that what printed magazines deliver can easily be either replicated or superseded on the internet. Experience often suggests otherwise: witness the fate of the once-independent online music magazine Pitchfork, bought out by the corporate publisher Condé Nast in 2015 and bizarrely folded into the workings of the men’s title GQ nine years later: a classic case of what we now know as enshittification. But there is an even bigger point here about how we now engage with the things we like and love, summarised in a forthcoming book titled Circulation: How Culture Moves in the Age of Algorithm by the Nashville-based US music insider David Macias, with a foreword written by Dan Clancy, the CEO of the livestreaming platform Twitch.

His argument is about music, but its logic applies across the cultural, recreational and sporting board. “The algorithm is great at finding me new music in the limited style I listen to,” he writes. “But it is really bad at showing me something new and different. My listening has become homogeneous, even though I can pick any album ever created.” This is the tedious prospect that the demise of the magazine will only accelerate – so after the high-street chaos has died down, we could be faced with an awful silence, broken only by the leakage from headphones playing the same things over and over again. And to speak the language of the insatiable capitalist, where will anyone find money in that?

John Harris is a Guardian columnist
