Stephen Fry: ‘Sherlock Holmes altered the course of my whole life’

The Guardian Sun, 25 Oct 2026 12:00:02 GMT

Nearly a hundred years after Arthur Conan Doyle’s last Sherlock Holmes story, the writer and broadcaster unravels the mystery of the detective’s enduring appeal

It has become quite the fashion for contemporary writers to have a go at reinventing past classics. We’ve seen it done with imperishable literary heroes like Bond, Jeeves, Poirot and Winnie-the-Pooh. This is a relatively new phenomenon. But not in the case of Sherlock Holmes, where the practice is almost as old as the man himself.

Sherlock Holmes was the conception of Arthur Conan Doyle, a Scottish doctor down on his luck who had turned his hand to fiction to make up for a worrying lack of success in attracting patients to his surgery. Conan Doyle could never have guessed that the first Sherlock Holmes story he wrote, A Study in Scarlet, published in the 1887 issue of Beeton’s Christmas Annual, would in a few years propel him and the characters he created to literary fame. The personalities and characteristics of Holmes and Watson became as familiar to late Victorians as their own friends and families. The readership was worldwide and spread across all ages and classes.

Conan Doyle himself – frustrated by the burdensome discomfort of what he felt had become something of a millstone around his neck – killed off his creation by having Holmes apparently plummet to his death in Switzerland’s Reichenbach Falls, pulling his arch-enemy Moriarty down with him into the roaring cataract. The public outcry was swift and over­whelming. Grown men and women wept openly, black armbands were adopted, and a host of angry readers wrote abusive letters to Conan Doyle’s publishers, to the Strand magazine and to Conan Doyle himself. He grudgingly bowed to public pressure and unearthed a story set before Holmes’s plunge into the abyss – The Hound of the Baskervilles. But only after the clamour still refused to subside did he at last bring his hero back to life in The Return of Sherlock Holmes, presaging a new stream of short stories and a full-length novel, The Valley of Fear. He was to continue writing Sherlock Holmes adventures right up until 1927, although he never set a story later than the eve of the first world war.

During his lifetime, stage productions (he collaborated on the first himself) and silent films were produced, and after his death in 1930 the great post-Conan Doyle Holmesian caravan began to rumble into full life.

Now, you should know that the Sherlock Holmes body of work written by Arthur Conan Doyle himself is called by Sherlockians “the Canon” (coincidentally and happily an anagram of Conan). The Canon comprises four full-length novels and five collections of short stories.

In all, 60 canonical stories. How many have been written since? I don’t believe it is possible to count. I know I have written one myself. Conan Doyle’s son Adrian Conan Doyle, along with the great Golden Age mystery writer John Dickson Carr, wrote a collection of new stories under the title The Exploits of Sherlock Holmes. After that, the stampede was on, in all media, of course. The Hollywood films starring Basil Rathbone as Holmes and Nigel Bruce as Watson began in 1939 with the canonical The Hound of the Baskervilles, but soon began to move the pair into all kinds of modern settings. By the 1940s, they were doing their bit for the homeland by pitting themselves against the Nazis. The Conan Doyle Estate was open to allowing and authorising such variations, which soon became an established and legitimised part of the whole Sherlock Holmes enterprise. Between 2014 and 2023 Holmes emerged from copyright and entered the public domain.

Most Sherlockians I have come across will, like me, cite Jeremy Brett as their favourite Holmes, but one feels there will always be a new kind of Sherlock for every age. I had the honour of playing Sherlock’s brother Mycroft in Guy Ritchie’s Sherlock Holmes: A Game of Shadows, with Robert Downey Jr and Jude Law as Holmes and Watson, and the pleasure of reading the entire Canon for Audible. Along with the publication of my own Holmes pastiche, these were the completion of some kind of a lifelong dream. The closing of a very strange circle.

I can say without the slightest fear of exaggeration that Sherlock Holmes altered and determined the whole course of my life. Let me explain.

I had been entranced by the Sherlock Holmes stories from the earliest age. I read and reread the entire corpus of stories avidly and before long I had joined, as their youngest member to date, the august Sherlock Holmes Society of London. This eccentrically aristocratic institution had Lord Gore-Booth as chair and the Marquess of Donegal as editor of its magazine, the Sherlock Holmes Journal. I managed to get permission from my housemaster to leave school one weekend, travel by train to London and attend a society meeting, at which I was scheduled to read a paper. The subject of my disquisition? Well, I had noticed with excitement one day the parallels between Sherlock Holmes’s description of Professor James Moriarty (“He is extremely tall and thin, his forehead domes out in a white curve, and his two eyes are deeply sunken in his head”) and TS Eliot’s description of Macavity the Mystery Cat (“his eyes are sunken in. His brow is deeply lined with thought, his head is highly domed”). The society was being very kind in letting me address them on this topic: any fool could see that Eliot had based his Macavity entirely on Moriarty, it was hardly news. I thought I had discovered a great literary secret. At any rate, the event went well, but the sequel did not.

I stayed in London, sitting in cinemas from dawn till midnight and watching any number of films. By the time I came to and hopped on a train back to school, a full three days later than had been agreed and sanctioned, I found that I had been officially declared missing. My parents and the police were informed, and the hunt was on. The fat was truly in the fire, my number finally up. The school expelled me. That expulsion led to other expulsions and disasters, which culminated in my landing in prison; I shan’t go into too much detail: Moab Is My Washpot, the first volume of my autobiography, is also happily still in print, and the full story can be read there.

Anyway, all these ructions finally got me thinking straight and determining to change my ways and try for Cambridge, the university on which I had always set my heart. I did get there, where I met my friend Hugh Laurie and found myself set on the course of writing and performing which has filled my life ever since. None of which could have happened without that Sherlock Holmes Society evening and its cascade of consequences back in the early 70s.

But I still haven’t quite addressed the most pertinent question. Why? Why do these characters – Holmes, Watson, Mrs Hudson and Mycroft (along with that hapless cast of professional bunglers, sceptics and sincere admirers from Scotland Yard) – seem to attract reinvention and retelling so much more than any other fictional creations? And why the Game? How did that arise? The Game, I should explain, is what Sherlockians call the tradition of Holmesian scholarship that makes the very serious and straight-faced assumption that Holmes and Watson were real and that they actually did live at 221B Baker Street and that everything Watson writes about (although he makes plenty of mistakes in consistency and continuity) truly did historically happen.

Sign up to Bookmarks

Discover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories. Literary delights delivered direct to you

after newsletter promotion

But I repeat: why? This doesn’t happen with Poirot, Father Brown or Lord Peter Wimsey. What’s so special about the denizens of Baker Street?

Well, one can begin by making the surely undeniable statement that Sherlock Holmes is one of the most fully realised and enduring fictional characters ever created. Very quickly, his complex and rounded personality, the details of his intellect, his manners, his dress, his habits, his appetites, techniques and methods combined to create a place for him in the public consciousness of a kind that had never before been experienced in literature.

Holmes’s world is also vivid and tangible. Everyone who has read even a handful of stories will have their own clear picture of the Baker Street rooms, the fireplace, the test tubes, the violin case, the pipe rack, the fog at the window … we all have our images, reaffirmed or modified by countless films and television adaptations certainly, but unmistakably real. So real, indeed, that even as the stories were still being written and published, tens of thousands around the world behaved as if Holmes and Watson truly lived and breathed. From as far as Japan and South America came letters addressed to 221B Baker Street begging for Holmes’s assistance. Some even wrote to Buckingham Palace and Downing Street to urge the king and prime minister to award Sherlock Holmes a knighthood.

But there is, I think, another reason for the astonishing connection that Holmes made with the public on his arrival and that he continues to make in all the multiplicity of his incarnations today. And that is need. The world needed him in 1887 and the world needs him now.

With the great rise in literacy from the middle of the 19th century onwards, it perhaps seems inevitable that a new kind of fiction should arise that tried to solve the puzzle of the lately arrived Big City – most especially the biggest by far in the world, London. The daunting size of the metropolis was something quite new in human history. Society was transforming itself from a knowable hierarchy into a bewildering network. It could be seen structurally as like a great web, interlinked and complex, mastered only by those sensitive enough to understand, touch, feel and identify every node and every twitch on the filament. In fact, by a Sherlock Holmes.

And after Holmes, of course, ten thousand more detectives sprang up, all with their own USPs, their own special ways of clearing up mystery and caging the monsters. But so, too, did a strange breed of 20th-century heroes who offered a similar promise of bringing light and order to the darkness and chaos of modernity, but in their case without bothering to think much. I mean, of course, the comic book and film superheroes. Our infantile side (and there was never an age in our history that so encouraged and coddled our inner child as the present) seems to have embraced magic, flying, invisibility, X-ray vision and all kinds of impossible superpowers. It seems to me fair to suggest that Superman and Batman, unlikely as it may seem, follow in the great detective’s footsteps and owe him their being. He was surely the first caped crusader, for all that his cape was constructed of good tweed. They, like him, answered a need.

Why so many have moved from valuing the real and achievable powers that Holmes exhibits – achieved through his own self-training, study and practice – to valuing imaginary, unearned, randomly achieved magical superpowers is another question. But fortunately the appetite for Holmes and real deductive talent is undiminished, too. We can have both kinds of hero, after all. On television alone, for every Superman and Deadpool, there has always been – as well as a new Sherlock for each new generation – a Columbo, a Monk or a Ludwig reaffirming the power of the Sherlockian method and re‑establishing the primacy of mind over mayhem. Holmes’s cigar ash, footprints and almost invisible telltale particles are the forerunners of the crime lab’s mitochondrial DNA, epithelial particles and microfibres, and his magnifying glass gives way to today’s scanning electron microscope. But the principles are quite unchanged. Which is why he is the presiding spirit behind every CSI operative and why the modern Scotland Yard criminal database (the Home Office Large Major Enquiry System) has initials that spell out the name HOLMES.

Like London and the wider human world, the world of Holmes and Watson is a work in progress, capable of being modernised and made over in countless ways, but always, underneath it all, entirely its noble and magnificent self.

Sherlock, a collection of new stories with an introduction by Stephen Fry, is published by Simon & Schuster. To support the Guardian, order your copy at guardianbookshop. com. Delivery charges may apply.

From five-fingered trainers to the shoeless shoe: what’s with all the freaky footwear?

The Guardian Sun, 25 Oct 2026 12:00:01 GMT

Guardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link. Learn more.

‘Ugly’ shoes, once the preserve of the catwalk, have gone mainstream. Why are so many people taking a walk on the wild side?

Until recently, a busy commuter train would be packed with people wearing low-key, unobtrusive shoes. An elegant and inoffensive pump, a sporty trainer or a polite and basic ballet flat, they were the type of shoes that said background extra rather than main character energy.

But now change is afoot. Deliberately strange designs are reaching new heights of desirability. Polarising rather than pretty, these shoes tend to be flat, a little bit orthopaedic and, according to the internet, “ugly”.

From Vibram’s glove-like FiveFingers, which punctuate each toe, to barely there mesh shoes that leave the foot looking like a boned and rolled ham at Christmas, fashion’s new favourite shoes are leaning into the ludicrous. Welcome to the new era of freaky footwear.

“We are now at a liberating place where more people can have fun with their shoes,” says Dal Chodha, a writer and lecturer at Central Saint Martins fashion school in London. He finds this trend “thrilling”, saying it “forces someone to embrace the jolt of something that feels ugly or absurd”. While previously these designs were confined to the catwalks, they are becoming more common on the streets.

According to the fashion search platform Lyst, demand for cloven hoof-like Tabi styles, designed to split the hallux (big toe) from the rest of the toes, has increased fourfold since 2022. Meanwhile, FiveFingers are up 57% year on year.

Shoes that were once reserved for taking out the bins or nipping round the corner for milk are now increasingly being worn to the office – and even weddings. Simone Rocha has created supersized Crocs and smothered them in pearls and gemstones, while Etro joins Dior and Valentino in reimagining Birkenstocks’ “anti‑fashion” cork footbed clogs.

This summer, the hype for a pair of Gardanas, £38 earthworm-coloured French gardening clogs, led to lengthy waiting lists (and not only for the green‑fingered). Celine sells a similar mossy-coloured pair for £670.

Meanwhile, on the high street everywhere from John Lewis to Zara is championing the “Frankenshoe”, such as sneakerinas, an amalgamation of a sneaker and a ballerina flat. These new cross-breeds include the snoafer, a marriage between a sneaker and a penny loafer.

Heels haven’t completely disappeared, but they have been re-envisioned as deflated balloons and even broken eggs. In American designer Tory Burch’s latest lineup, she inverted the heel itself, creating the illusion of a flat mule while simultaneously elevating the wearer. A stubby “nipple heel” measuring half an inch is now the sought-after height.

Valerie Steele, chief curator of the Museum at the Fashion Institute of Technology in New York and author of Fetish: Fashion, Sex & Power, says society has a long history of strange shoes. She points to medieval poulaines, a shoe with an elongated toe that showed the wearer’s social ranking. Some were so long they had to be fastened to the knee to prevent tripping. Chopines, towering platform shoes worn by women from the 15th century, were also used to denote status, while in ancient Greece sex workers are reputed to have worn sandals with “Follow me” carved into the soles. Steele says today’s purposely strange designs let the wearer “play with elements of ugliness”, allowing someone to make a fashion statement without committing to a whole look. “Shoes are far away from your face, so you can experiment without looking ugly,” she says.

Chodha, who as a teenager wore Nike Air Rift trainers featuring a split-toe design, now favours a “potato” shoe. As the name suggests, this style of footwear isn’t dissimilar to a freshly dug maris piper. Even M&S has got behind the spud style. A £45 bulbous, soft suede pair has become one of its fastest-selling options for autumn.

For some, provocation is part of the appeal. “Anyone who is resisting standard forms of beauty or propriety or practicality in their choice of footwear is in some way embracing a punk spirit,” Chodha says. They also offer an opportunity to “challenge what and why we think something is ugly”.

Barbara Janeczek, curator manager at Lyst, says designs are becoming more extreme as “fashion has an incredible ability to normalise the previously unwearable”. She describes today’s iterations as “exposing, dividing or framing the foot in ways we’re not used to seeing”.

Tiffany Hsu, chief buying and group fashion venture officer at the luxury e-tailer Mytheresa, prefers the term “talking point shoes” rather than ugly, explaining that the style is “designed to create a reaction and bring something unexpected to a look”. Lars Byrresen Petersen, founder of a popular shoe meme account @ LarsLaLa, favours the word “extreme”. Some of his most liked posts are where he has compared shoes to condoms and mops.

The popularity of the trend can be pegged to the “wrong shoe theory”, a term coined by stylist Allison Bornstein in 2023. This styling trick involves purposely wearing an unexpected shoe (think a kitten heel with tracksuit bottoms, or flip-flops with tailored trousers) to make a look more interesting. Bornstein says a shoe that is a little “off” works because “it signals that there is some intention and choice, and therefore it gives your look personality”.

Some view the trend as a backlash against the uniform pageantry of the Maga aesthetic. Republicans love a nude pointy-toe stiletto almost as much as the presenters of Fox News. “When politically there is a big right swing, you have a lot of people that through their clothing want to say, ‘I’m not that,’” Steele says. A freaky shoe can be like a “secret masonic handshake”, she adds.

Sign up to Inside Saturday

The only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.

after newsletter promotion

The hoof-type Tabi shoe was first thrust into the spotlight in the 1980s, when Martin Margiela featured the subversive riff on a 15th-century Japanese sock design in his debut collection. Now the Tabi-ification extends to trainers, ballet flats and Mary Janes across various brands. Byrresen Petersen, who has been wearing the style “every day for the past 10 years”, isn’t thrilled about their new universal appeal. “People who aren’t familiar with the shoe’s history are just wearing them for the shock value,” he says.

While some freaky shoes conceal the foot, it’s the toe‑bearing styles that are really captivating fashion. Similar to Hollywood’s naked dressing trend, they offer a quick flash of foot or even a full-frontal view of each toe. It’s a trend as divisive as Curtsy’s toe separator inspired heels– where each toe is embraced in its own thong strap.

Steele says feet and shoes have long been fetishised, as the outline of a foot can be compared to a miniature version of the human body. Toes can be squeezed together to create “cleavage”, while the round curve of the heel is considered similar to the bum. Steele says it was once thought to be “erotic” to wear a slingback. “You were letting your ‘butt’ hang out!”

It’s a trend growing against the backdrop of the mainstreaming of foot fetishes. The photo-sharing site Wikifeet, which ranks celebrities’ feet for their beauty, gets nearly 20m views a month. (Rihanna and Margot Robbie score five stars while Michelle Yeoh currently sits at a one.) Selling foot pics has become a lucrative side hustle for many, including the singer Lily Allen, who shares hers on OnlyFans, a subscription-based site most commonly featuring porn. Allen, who posts under the username FTSE500, has said she makes more money from #feetpics than she does from Spotify streaming. On social media, the phrase “No free feet pics” plays into the idea, with users carefully cropping photos so their exposed toes aren’t on display.

While “potato shoes” are prevalent in menswear, toe-framing styles are less so. Saint Laurent recently horrified viewers when it sent male models down the catwalk wearing transparent PVC Oxford brogues. When Alexander Skarsgård wore them on the red carpet, they quickly became clouded with condensed perspiration. “I asked myself, ‘Why torture women with plastic shoes, but not men?’” Anthony Vaccarello, who helmed the brand at the time, remarked on the idea behind them.

Steele points out that masculinity has been historically associated with heavy boots: “Men’s fashion generally emphasises sexuality through tightness or padding, not so much through body exposure.” Naked toes suggest vulnerability and, “Men don’t want to look vulnerable. They’d rather look armoured.”

Why are shoes getting so freaky right now? Chodha says that, like the miniskirt in the 60s, these styles are rebellious and liberating. They can be viewed as an extension of the writer Leandra Medine’s “man repeller dressing”, where the wearer prioritises their own likes and comfort over the diktats of the traditional male gaze. Others view it as a rejection of millennial “girlboss” culture, a movement that glamorised a relentless work ethic associated with spike heels and polished looks, which is now considered toxic by gen Z.

Or could it be connected to the economic moment? A recent report warned that the UK was at risk of “a lost generation”. From a lack of job opportunities to the housing crisis and increasing fears over the use of AI, many young people are deeply anxious about their future. As a result, some are embracing a “soft life”, prioritising comfort and a focus beyond the 9-5. Grounding rather than grinding – a five-finger shoe that connects the wearer with the soil beneath them fits the moment. The writer Liana Satenstein has described that particular shoe as “an orgasmic exhale for the foot”.

“There’s a sort of jouissance to the walk young people walk,” says Chodha. “I don’t think young people are marching or stomping, because, of course, they all feel so disengaged with the world.” While their predecessors furiously click-clacked around in skyscraper heels, today’s twentysomethings are more likely to be found padding around slowly with a matcha in hand. Chodha says that the heeled stomp “feels out of step with the time”.

Where next? “Once everyone gets comfortable with the weird thing, you have to find something weirder,” says Janeczek, who credits “fashion’s one-upmanship” for playing a role in fuelling the trend for weird shoes. Chanel has offered a pilot run of what that might look like, challenging the very definition of what constitutes a shoe. Its “shoeless shoe”, first seen during its catwalk show in Biarritz in France in April and later worn by Margaret Qualley to a London film premiere, features just a heel cap, bearing its double CC logo, leaving the bare foot to walk without any protection at all.

Flex those toes, the time has come to let them loose!

This is how we do it: ‘Our fertility doctor told us we were having too much sex’

The Guardian Sun, 25 Oct 2026 11:00:00 GMT

Ines and Ross shared a high sex drive, but things calmed down a bit after their daughter was born

How do you do it? Share the story of your sex life, anonymously

double quotation markOur desire hasn’t diminished, but I’m content with a cuddly, loving shag these days

Ross and I had been dating for four months when I asked if he wanted children. I’d memorised a script, but I was so anxious I was visibly shaking as I asked him. It felt so vulnerable, and what if he said no? I’d have to end the relationship.

That year, I went through three rounds of egg freezing after being told my anti-Müllerian hormone levels were so low I might never be able to have a baby. I met Ross just before starting the first round, but I didn’t tell him because I didn’t want to scare him off. It also played on my mind that Ross was 28 and I was 36.

After Ross reassured me he did want children, he hugged me and said: “This is inappropriate, but I have a boner.” He called it a romance boner.

Two months later, he referred to “our kids” in conversation.

Six months after that, we decided to start trying. The fertility doctor told us we were having too much sex. Apparently having sex every other day gives the sperm time to properly develop, but we’d been doing it four or five times a day: once before work, when we got home from work, before dinner and again before bed. I’d never been with anyone whose sex drive was as high as mine.

After we miscarried our first child, sex became less about experimentation and more about comfort. And now we have a 10-month-old daughter, we just don’t have the energy to do it like we used to. Rather than four times a day, we have sex four times a week, and it’s more vanilla. But our desire hasn’t diminished, and I’m content with a cuddly, loving shag these days. We still hold hands and touch feet while we sleep.

Although there are some days when we joke that we’re more like workmates now we’re a team getting things done, we’re just as close as we always have been – it’s just a different kind of closeness.

Seeing how wonderful he is with our daughter has made me love him even more. I say to her: “I picked your dad wisely.”

On our first date, Ines made a joke about being older, but it wasn’t an issue for me. We were just two people who were very compatible and had a lot of common interests. But the age gap probably sped up the process of having a child. When Ines told me she had frozen her eggs and I was welcome to leave if that wasn’t what I wanted, I gave her a big hug and said I’d love to stay.

On our second date, I baked Ines a red velvet cake and she opened the door in a bathrobe. The sex was amazing – the best I’d ever had. I came more than 10 times that night. It became a game to make Ines orgasm as many times as possible – I get a lot of pleasure from her pleasure. Although her drive was higher than mine at the start, mine increased to match hers because the sex was so good.

Although we were too sad to have sex after the miscarriage, we were still very open to each other. We got married soon after, which was a helpful distraction, and slowly our sex life returned to normal. When we first had sex after our daughter was born, we took it slowly because I was afraid of hurting Ines. Now we’re parents, we don’t have time for two-hour oral sex. It has gone from a marathon to a sprint, but it’s always very intimate. We’re often too tired, and it feels too weird to have sex with the baby in the room, so we have to be more sneaky, making the most of the time when she’s asleep.

I stopped initiating sex to take the pressure off Ines; so she doesn’t feel as if she’s letting me down by not wanting sex. Looking after our daughter is our priority. Although we love sex, we don’t owe it to each other. I’ve made it clear that, despite letting Ines take the lead, I still desire her. There’s intimacy outside sex too – dancing in the kitchen to our wedding song, or taking the baby out when one of us needs a rest. Names have been changed

‘I’d rather live through something publicly than escape it privately’: Jack Antonoff on survivor’s guilt and still singing love songs after his breakup

The Guardian Sun, 25 Oct 2026 10:00:00 GMT

Whether he’s playing the role of soul-baring artist or starry producer, the Bleachers frontman strives to keep his integrity intact. He weighs in on Ed Sheeran, his love of working on ‘high-stakes’ albums and why he’s standing by the songs about his marriage

Sitting in the restaurant of a Denver hotel, in the middle of a US tour with his band Bleachers, Jack Antonoff shrugs. “There’s this intense need to figure me out,” he frowns, “and I don’t really know where it comes from, because I keep explaining all of it.”

He has a point. For the last 12 years, Bleachers have released a succession of albums packed with Antonoff’s strikingly personal and frank songs. Being strikingly personal and frank was the whole point. Antonoff had previously been guitarist in Fun, a pop-rock band who went supernova with their 2011 single We Are Young. Despite co-writing a song that sold 10m copies in the US alone, Antonoff says he “hated” the experience “because I wasn’t the leader, they weren’t my words, and I needed to write a song that if I fucking died tomorrow would be my life story”.

He says he insisted his then-record label release said song I Wanna Get Better as Bleachers’ debut single “to let people know what they were in for”. It depicted Antonoff literally screaming in anguish, “losing my mind” with grief in the wake of his younger sister’s death, aged 13, from a brain tumour. You can tell it set the confessional tone of Bleachers’ oeuvre just by looking at some of their other song titles: I’m Ready to Move On, Everybody Lost Somebody, Stop Making This Hurt, Self-Respect, I Can’t Believe You’re Gone, We Should Talk.

Their latest album, Everyone for Ten Minutes, offers his audience what you might call the Jack Antonoff origin story: there are songs about his teenage years spent traversing the US in his parents’ minivan, touring down-at-heel punk venues with an emo band called Outline, which by his own account was a pretty hair-raising experience (“Teenagers, in a van, drinking a lot, smoking pot, taking psychedelics, smoking what we thought was hash but turned out to be black opium,” he laughs, “I’m amazed we survived”), to which his parents only agreed because his sister’s illness meant “they could not give a fuck about anything that didn’t really matter. When something serious, existential is going on in your life, you get a little less stressed about a parking ticket or grades, you know?”

If Bleachers were the only thing that Jack Antonoff did, then it would all seem terribly straightforward. But, of course, they aren’t the whole story. Around the same time he started the band, he met Taylor Swift at an awards ceremony, bonded over a mutual love of 80s synth duo Yazoo and embarked on a creative collaboration that ultimately led Antonoff to become perhaps the most in-demand pop producer on Earth: he’s worked not just on 11 Taylor Swift albums, but with Sabrina Carpenter, Lorde, Lana Del Rey, St Vincent, Kendrick Lamar and Gracie Abrams, among a host of others. He is in the vaunted position of being a blue-chip pop mega-producer who also makes soul-baring, Bruce Springsteen-influenced angst-rock, and insists neither activity takes precedence over the other in his career.

“I’m in a very narrow group of people who truly do both, probably,” he nods. “Usually someone’s slumming it on one side: songwriters or performers who think they can produce a record but then have to really care about someone else’s work in a deep way, or producers who think: ‘Now it’s my turn!’ but don’t have that thing you can’t even describe that drew you to write your own songs and fucking sing them in front of people since you were a kid.”

Indeed, for all his protestations that he’s really terribly straightforward, Jack Antonoff seems anything but. Rather, he seems like such a mass of complexities and contradictions that you sometimes get the impression he might be trying to puzzle them out himself, in front of you. He’s clearly very driven, but he worries his drive is bound up with “survivor’s guilt” over his sister’s death, “about not going for things or using my time when someone you love didn’t get time, which is not the best way to live – there’s a difference between joyfully seizing the moment and something that’s predicated on anxiety”.

He decries the constant chatter of opinion on the internet: “I don’t give a fuck any more, it’s like, the very act of engaging negatively on the internet is inarguably such a fucking low-vibrational joke, and I think artists for too long over the past decade have read into it and there’s less than nothing there.” But equally he says he enjoys making “super high-stakes albums … helping to architect and guide something that everyone is going to have an opinion on, that people love to have the hottest opinions on”.

He thinks his role in making some of the biggest records of the century so far is widely misconstrued as shadowy and machiavellian (“He’s annoyingly, inescapably, maddeningly everywhere … the designated steward of Tasteful Pop,” protested one piece on music website Pitchfork, which went on to accuse him of “musical manspreading” and suggest he had “extreme Main Character Energy”). “One of the great misconceptions of how it works in my world is that I write songs and hand them to, like, a pop star, which I’ve never done once in my life,” he says, but declines to discuss how it actually works because “it doesn’t really matter”. Besides he’s sick of people constantly trying to explain everything online. “You’re on your phone all the time being explained something,” he says. “You’re being explained what’s happening in this country, you’re being explained how a train works, it’s like an information dump and it’s killing people’s imaginations. ‘Do you want to sound like Jack Antonoff? Here’s how he did it!’ It’s made me want to allow people to imagine the magic of it all.”

Certainly, in the context of 21st-century pop, he’s a very odd fish. He is obviously someone who moves with enviable ease among the pop aristocracy: he apparently ended up working on Kendrick Lamar’s multiple Grammy-winning 2024 album GNX when he popped into the studio to visit a friend and “didn’t leave for three years”; Bruce Springsteen isn’t just an influence but a friend, collaborator with Bleachers and mentor (best advice thus delivered by The Boss: “Don’t live in the dream, let the dream live in you”). But Antonoff both looks noticeably more like someone who might have spent his teens playing gigs in anarchist book stores on drugs than someone who co-wrote, say, Sabrina Carpenter’s Please Please Please – close-cropped hair, tattered skate pants, Sonic Youth T-shirt – and often sounds more like a chippy indie outsider than someone who recently enjoyed chicken nuggets with caviar at Taylor Swift’s wedding.

Certainly, he is more free with his opinions than you might expect from someone who operates at the top table of pop, a world where artists tend to have any capacity for controversy media-trained out of them. He’s currently engaged in a war of words with Live Nation over gig ticket prices (he is proud that Bleachers’ tickets are “as low as they can physically possibly be”). “Live Nation keep missing the point, because every time I say something, they’ll call my people and say: “Let’s have a meeting.’ You don’t get it, I don’t want to fucking talk to you people, I want to make it clear that I’m not fucking OK with you turning the most sacred thing into the world into some weird free-market piece of shit … the idea that if you’re rich, any ticket you want is yours at any time and if you’re not, you have to go through this demoralising online experience where you get whacked and kicked and fucked around.”

When I meet him, his social media channels are filled with abuse from commenters angry that a Jewish artist has made a point of saying “free Palestine” onstage at Bleachers shows: he points out that he was saying it long before the recent Ed Sheeran/Macklemore controversy blew up but says he has “felt way more emboldened to say it now, because it’s not in any way a strange, uncomfortable or controversial thing to say, it’s a deeply human thing to say. If you think it is [controversial] you’re lost in some other sauce that is so crazy. They’re going to let some fucking promoter tell me what I can say? Don’t book me. I’ll play for free outside. [Ed Sheeran] missed a massive, beautiful opportunity there: just cancel the whole fucking tour, then play for free outside each venue, raise a bunch of money, rather than let a fucking billionaire tell you what to do. The reason it’s not an anomaly or niche issue is because we all live in a world where billionaires are constantly telling us what to do. So stand the fuck up.”

Sign up to The Guide

Get our weekly pop culture email, free in your inbox every Friday

after newsletter promotion

Of course you could argue that Antonoff has more freedom to be unguarded than the artists he works with. Bleachers enjoy a curious kind of success – their albums sell respectably rather than astronomically and they’ve never come “even close”, Antonoff points out, to having a huge crossover hit. Yet they are capable of filling out Madison Square Garden with an audience that Antonoff says aren’t there to see “that producer’s band”. His own celebrity is largely by proxy, thanks to the company he keeps in the recording studio – his 2023 wedding to actor Margaret Qualley took place amid a scrum of fans and paparazzi, but that seemed to have less to do with the bride and groom than the fact that Taylor Swift was in attendance.

Recently, the gossip pages have been alive, first with his former partner Lena Dunham’s memoir Famesick, which suggested that one of the reasons their romance floundered was because Antonoff was more invested in shepherding Lorde through her Difficult Second Album than their relationship, and latterly with news of his marriage’s collapse. That came as a surprise given that Bleachers had released an album thick with loving peans to Qualley and to marriage a matter of weeks before their split was announced: one of them, You and Forever, even came with a video starring the couple together.

Antonoff thus currently finds himself on tour, singing songs about a relationship that’s now over. When I mention it, he first interrupts me – “Oh, I can imagine what you’re going to say: it’s bizarre” – then clarifies my point: “Songs which I wrote recently,” he nods. “I obviously was really worried about this specific thing, I sat long and hard with it and thought: ‘If I change the setlist …’ and in my gut there was a unanimous jury that said, ‘No, this is the deal. The deal I’ve made with my audience is that I’m going to tell you honestly how I feel and I’m going to risk at any moment having to stand behind it for fucking ever.’

“Anyone could relate to the terrible sadness and pain, but there’s a great power to it also,” he says. “It’s actually been really beautiful. I mean, for people to come together, to know what I write a song about, to know how that must feel for me now, to know what that song means to you as an audience member, to just hold it all and sort of celebrate. I don’t rewrite the past, I have no shame about the things I’ve said. My life has been dedicated to making it impossible for me to rewrite the past, because I’m standing there, singing about how I felt during the good times, so when the bad times hit I can’t look myself in the mirror and pretend that those times didn’t exist. I would rather live through something publicly than even escape it privately.”

After we speak, on stage at Colorado’s Red Rocks Amphitheatre, there is indeed a fraught emotional charge to Bleachers’ performances of Dirty Wedding Dress and You and Forever. Antonoff follows the latter by playing I Wanna Get Better alone on acoustic guitar. The audience – who, as he promised, are an odd combination of twentysomething women, middle-aged couples and a smattering of grizzled Deadheads in tie-dye T-shirts, none of whom look as if they’re there to see Taylor Swift’s producer in the flesh – bellow along, so loudly that they’re in danger of drowning him out entirely. For a moment, in the spotlight, Jack Antonoff does not need figuring out.

Bleachers are touring the UK and Ireland, 23 November to 4 December; tour starts Kingston upon Thames. Their album Everyone for Ten Minutes is out now.

The hill I will die on: The email sign-off is archaic – it needs to go. No regards, Tom

The Guardian Sun, 25 Oct 2026 08:00:56 GMT

The torture of the inbox is made insufferably worse by the dated cliches at the beginning and end. Enough!

If email were a person, it would be an adult dressed in a teenager’s clothes, desperately trying to stay relevant. Despite being 55 years old and having been surpassed by numerous developments in communication technologies, its functionality remains largely the same as when it was first widely adopted. Unfortunately, so does the etiquette surrounding it.

Whereas other forms of communication have long since dispensed with unnecessary textual tassels, email communication styles still lean closer to telegram than a text. Since I last checked, almost no one relishes receiving a new email – unless it’s informing you of a significant cash windfall that means you can, in fact, now quit your job and stop using it altogether. Yet, for some reason, many people start their responses with “Thank you for your email!” I would put this forward as one of the least convincing sentences in the English language.

At the other end of the page is one of the most common yet totally unnecessary habits of the digital age: the email signoff. For those who haven’t yet realised, I’m here to tell you that you don’t need to sign your name at the end of an email – I can already see it’s from you. I know your name. Outlook has gone to extraordinary lengths to tell me your name. It’s in my inbox, the “from” field and the thread, and I probably begrudgingly addressed my last email directly to you.

And then there is whatever form of final flourish you see fit to precede that with. To me, the whole concept of “regards” – kind, best or otherwise – is archaic and overly formal, not far from sealing the whole thing with a wax stamp and dispatching it via horse. But worse are the new ways of signing things off. “In solidarity”, “Keep dreaming” and the ultimate Covid-era classic: “hope you’re staying positive and testing negative”. This reaches its logical conclusion with the use of “KR” as a signoff. We have begun to admit that we don’t actually feel enough “kind regards” to type the words any more – and yet, the convention rolls on.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

That’s to say nothing of email signatures, which now routinely exceed the length of the emails they are attached to. Name, job title, mobile number, office number, LinkedIn profile, logo, environmental disclaimer, confidentiality notice, statement about working hours and a quote from Maya Angelou. All appended to an email saying: “Running 5 mins late!”

However, I appreciate that we must retain some means of expressing digital distaste, such is the harsh reality of the world of work. Therefore, the only use of the word “regards” I will permit is the one placed at the end of an email to communicate blunt and absolute hostility towards the recipient.

With absolutely no regards, Tom

Tom Gill is a freelance journalist and consultant from London, based in Melbourne

How cocaine conquered the UK: in pubs, festivals and workplaces the drug has become an everyday habit

The Guardian Sun, 25 Oct 2026 07:00:55 GMT

Previously considered a middle-class drug, price drops have made cocaine more widely available, and created a new set of problems

Cocaine-linked crimes on the rise in Britain as consumption surges

Ageing users and record deaths – the data behind Britain’s £9.8bn-a-year cocaine habit

Lisa* is watching Scissor Sisters at a festival in the Lake District, a can of cider in hand, dancing along to the music on a sunny afternoon.

The 30-year-old has a few days off from her job as a veterinary nurse in Gateshead, where she lives with her fiance. She loves going to festivals, especially as “I love meeting new people,” she says.

She is confident and makes friends at the festival very easily. The reason for that? “I’m on a bit of coke,” she says.

It is a crime largely hidden in plain sight – and one many people would barely consider a crime. However, it could land her a maximum sentence of seven years in prison, though for a first offence it is more likely to be a police caution. But she’s unlikely to be caught, especially at a festival, where over the course of the weekend numerous people admit to the Guardian to taking cocaine – or trying to get hold of it – and are seen openly taking it.

By many estimates, use of the class A drug is soaring. Wastewater analysis suggests people in England consumed 123,000kg of cocaine in 2024-25, a rise of 26% since 2021. That’s equivalent to roughly 2.5bn lines of cocaine, at an estimated street value of almost £10bn.

Cocaine is a powerful and addictive stimulant that causes euphoria, overconfidence, restlessness and paranoia. A Guardian investigation has found a 10% rise in recorded crimes where the drug was mentioned since 2019.

Research from wastewater samples in 2022 carried out by Imperial College London and released earlier this year found that cocaine use spiked during major sporting and music events, heatwaves and bank holidays.

Its reputation as a middle-class drug still stands, though it has become more available across different demographics, as prices have dropped year-on-year and reached “historically low levels” last year. That wider use brings wider problems.

Cocaine was thought to have been a major factor in the 2021 widespread disorder at Wembley stadium during the Euro 2020 final, when thousands of ticketless fans breached safety barriers to get access to the ground. Lady Casey’s independent review later that year found that “excessive consumption of alcohol and cocaine” were fuels of a “febrile atmosphere”.

More than half of fans who responded to a survey in the aftermath of the incident said they had seen open drug use at Wembley stadium or on the way from the station.

“People were taking cocaine in front of us [and] my sons cried for most of the game,” one person quoted in the report said. A safety official was quoted as saying: “Drug usage was noticeable. It took four or five stewards to try and hold someone down – more than the number it usually takes when fans are drunk.”

It has also become a drug of choice for the far right.

Cocaine was a factor in the 2024 summer riots when some of the perpetrators of violence were found to be in possession of it or have taken it before the riots erupted. Two rioters also later pleaded guilty to selling it. Open cocaine use was also seen at the Unite the Kingdom rally, a far-right anti-immigration protest in London last year.

But cocaine was – and still is – a party drug, popular at nightclubs, student house parties, middle-class dinner parties and now in the pub.

At a West Ham pub in east London, a pub manager explains she cleans cocaine residue off surfaces in the toilets most mornings. It is a pub for people who live and work in the area and for West Ham fans who are regulars on match days.

“It is just staggering the amount and the accessibility of it,” she says.

“It seems to be so blended with the concept of a night or even a day out for a lot of people ... It has been very normalised [and it’s] just a thing that you can quite blatantly and overtly do.”

She says the ubiquity of cocaine has become “significantly worse” over the past five years.

While other drugs are more obvious – they have a strong smell or leave their users visibly intoxicated or even incapacitated – cocaine can be harder to spot, which is a problem for publicans.

There can be telltale signs though, she says, such as when a punter appears to be getting agitated, leaves the pub and then comes back some time later, going straight to the toilets. “I’ve had real idiots, and they’ve been very blatant, and it’s been easy to kick them out.”

The manager believes people often take cocaine in an effort to “sober up” so they can continue drinking, “which obviously does not actually work but a lot of people believe it does”.

“Now you’ve got the impaired judgment from alcohol but you’ve also got the alertness from cocaine. That for me is a really big problem because that’s when you get potentially very volatile behaviour. That’s probably the point that I would call the most dangerous, both in terms of people behaving erratically, but also because they don’t realise how drunk they are. They are – at that point – a danger to themselves in terms of me having to call an ambulance or something.”

Cocaine use becomes particularly obvious when punters get into fights. “I had a 60-something-year-old man beat up a 70-something-year-old man in the toilet, knock his teeth out, because he said that the other guy had allegedly called him a cunt,” she says. “Now I understand that there are egos involved and that people can be volatile – and there’s all kinds of silly petty rivalries going back decades amongst some of the customers – but you’re not telling me that’s a normal reaction.”

She says she has spent years working in hospitality, managing different venues, and she thinks the problems that come from cocaine use can be seen in both cheap chains and expensive country gastropubs.

“But technically none of us can talk about it because none of us can admit that drug-taking takes place on our premises,” she says. “Everyone’s scared of losing their licence.”

What wastewater analysis cannot reveal is whether more people are taking cocaine, or more is being taken by those who are habitual users, or both.

For some people, cocaine is simply a part of life, something taken every day, even while at work.

The first time Will* took cocaine was at about the age of 15. “I remember it being stimulating, like I felt kind of chatty. I felt a lot of my social anxiety-based inhibitions fade away and, in the space of that, I was really confident and felt kind of unstoppable, in a sense.”

Things quickly escalated to him dealing the drug. “I was a 16-year-old with like half a fucking kilo of cocaine in my bedroom.”

He began selling to friends and friends of friends, though he admits he was an “atypical” dealer. He was from a relatively wealthy family in Essex, surrounded by teenagers with a lot of disposable income.

“That would pay for my usage of it,” he says, earning as much as £7,000 in a weekend.

“But then over the last like 20 years, it has developed much more into a coping mechanism,” the 37-year-old says.

A carpenter in TV and film, he has used it to help with long hours, being the first on set and the last to leave. It is so common among his colleagues that he says parts of the industry “basically run themselves on cocaine”.

He has “successfully hidden it from professional relationships so easily” and says people he interacted with at work would have no idea he was taking coke in the workplace.

“It can really seem like a good idea but it ultimately isn’t. [It’s fine] until you realise that you’ve built the physical dependency and then you go a day without it and you’re like dragging yourself through mud.”

At one point he counted up and realised he had spent £35,000 in one year on cocaine. He says: “I was like, oh my god, that’s a lot of money.”

He has managed to cut down on his use substantially, from “spending thousands of pounds a week doing cocaine every single day to someone who’s spending maybe £120 to £180 a weekend”. But even still, he thinks he will probably never stop taking it.

“I’m trying to be in control of it as opposed to being fully sober, because I don’t really see myself as someone who is ever gonna be fully sober.”

*Lisa’s name has been changed. Will spoke to the Guardian on the condition of anonymity. His name has also been changed.

Don’t call me ‘mumsy’ – the contempt behind that word makes me livid

The Guardian Sun, 25 Oct 2026 06:00:55 GMT

It means to be drab, homely or old-fashioned – ‘motherly’, essentially. Why can’t we have some respect for mothers, instead of deriding them?

A recent newspaper headline – “Sorry Radley! These dated handbag brands will make you look mumsy – here’s where stylish A-listers and Royals are shopping instead” – reminded me of a word I despise: “mumsy”.

My list of words that make me want to throw things is varied and long, but “mumsy” is near the top. The quality of being mumsy means to be drab, homely or old-fashioned, essentially “motherly”. Something about the casual misogynistic contempt it carries makes me livid. So livid I might even use “that voice”. You know. The scary mum voice that turns misbehaving children in supermarkets into stone.

“Mumsy” crops up in fashion coverage, which in autumn is unduly focused on the new school-run “style rules”. Articles about how to look chic at the school gate and short-form videos about “what the cool mums are wearing” add to this feeling that the last thing you, as a mother, would want to appear as is what you actually are: someone’s mum.

Of course, it’s understandable, and totally normal, to not want to be entirely defined by your reproductive status. Few of us want our entire identities to be “mother”. I still remember the shock I felt when a health professional first referred to me as “Mum” instead of by my name. It can feel as though you have ceased to be a person in society’s eyes. Add to that the fact your body’s changed because you’ve made and birthed a whole human being, and that you are now responsible for that other human being’s every want and need, drastically limiting the time you have to attend to personal style and grooming, and it can feel hard to know who you are now.

These conflicting feelings are never a reason to deride mothers in general, though, or to act like “I’m not a regular mom, I’m a cool mom”. There’s a reason Amy Poehler’s comic Mean Girls catchphrase has proved so legendary. There’s something inherently ridiculous about working to deny something that you so irrevocably are and will always be. The harsh reality that dawns on you as you transition from not-mother to mother is that you are for ever changed. You can try to dress it up all you want, but the fact is that you’re someone’s mum now.

New theories of matrescence tell us that this change is a lot more complicated than suddenly wearing really naff jeans, although you might be doing that too (or be simply too sleep-deprived to give a toss that you’re wearing really naff jeans. Or using the word “naff”, which is probably also mumsy). The concept of mumsy changes according to the era you are living in. In the 1990s, all the mums wore high-waisted Levi’s 501s, which we even came to call “mum jeans”. This came to be co-opted by fashion brands, albeit using the slightly less mumsy sounding “mom”. I wouldn’t have been caught dead in mum jeans. What am I wearing now, as I type this? That’s right, a pair of vintage 501s. It all comes back round eventually. The teenagers I pass on the school run every morning would never.

I look at how their baggy jeans are soaking up the puddles and pigeon piss all the way up to their knees and am not nostalgic. This must have been the sort of zen that my own mum felt; I feel confident in my personal style. That doesn’t mean that fear of mumsiness doesn’t try to stalk us all regardless. The anxiety around this question is palpable on forums such as Mumsnet: what shape of jeans should we be wearing now? Are coloured trainers fashionable?

I’m not going to pretend that I don’t care at all, but I would think less of someone who uses the word “mumsy” about other women. I will never forget, long before I had a child myself, one writer I know saying of another that her work was “a bit mumsy”. The writer in question wrote brilliantly and hilariously about parenthood, and also about a lot of other things. I found the way that “mumsy” was used to reduce and deride her intelligence and the quality of her work deeply unpalatable. I also recall an editor saying that she hated seeing the word “mum” in print. I suppose she preferred the more literary sounding “my mother”, which has its place but, let’s be honest, it’s not how most of us speak.

It made me realise that it isn’t just fashion, then, that is resistant to mumsiness but culture more generally, and that’s only going to change when mothers and the work they do are afforded the respect they deserve. As it stands, to become a mother is to not only be confronted with biological reality and structural sexism, but to somehow navigate this without dressing, writing or sounding too much like a mother. Perhaps, like the fashion writer Frankie Graddon, whose Substack’s strap line is: “I’ve had a baby, not a style crisis”, the solution is to simply be “Mum-ish”. Whatever. You can prise my 501s from my cold, dead hands.

‘That’s the way the city works’: how the UAE changed the face of Andy Burnham’s Manchester

The Guardian Sun, 25 Oct 2026 06:00:54 GMT

The story of the emirates’ presence in Manchester winds from the Arab Spring to some of the most deprived places in England – with complicated results

Emirati-linked firms’ ownership of Manchester land ‘up 39%’ in 10 years

When Hosni Mubarak, Egypt’s long-ruling dictator, was toppled from power in the Arab spring protests of 2011, his downfall sent shock waves across the Middle East. It also helped change the face of modern Manchester.

Mubarak’s successor, the Muslim Brotherhood leader Mohamed Morsi, was a sworn enemy of the United Arab Emirates, whose rulers feared the advance of Morsi’s Islamism.

The UAE, a key western ally, was concerned that David Cameron’s UK government was not strong enough on the Muslim Brotherhood and warned ministers it could pull billion-pound arms deals if Britain did not act.

A secret Whitehall unit was hastily established to keep the oil-rich emirates on side. Lucrative investment deals were offered in private meetings later revealed by the Guardian.

One of these would turn Abu Dhabi’s now crisis-stricken ownership of Manchester City football club into a much deeper stake in the city itself.

Fifteen years after the Egyptian revolution, a Guardian analysis can reveal a stark rise in the amount of land and property owned by the UAE government or Emirati developers in Manchester over the past decade – extending to the size of 260 football pitches at its peak in 2023.

Manchester City’s owner, Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed al-Nahyan, has built an extensive portfolio outside the club, including the UK’s biggest indoor arena, an “upper-upscale hotel” that opened last month, a suite of apartment blocks and investment in world-leading university research through a firm run by Khaldoon al-Mubarak, the City chief executive.

The cheating scandal at Manchester City has put the spotlight on the wider influence of Abu Dhabi in the city, the growth of which helped power Andy Burnham to Downing Street.

Through interviews with key past and present local politicians and officials, new data analysis and an examination of public records spanning more than a decade, the Guardian can now tell the story of how the oil-rich state’s influence has grown, what it has meant for Manchester, and how it has fuelled concerns about the city becoming “a northern version of London”.

Ten years ago, the sight of the murky-green Rochdale canal was a sign you had strayed too far out of Manchester’s lively Northern Quarter and should turn back. Now drinkers and diners gravitate to the area, pulled in by trendy waterside bars serving up £6.90 pints and an artisanal bakery where a single croissant costs £7.50.

That transformation began in summer 2013, when David Cameron’s government sought to defuse tensions with the UAE and asked Manchester city council to draw up three investment proposals for the super-rich emirates.

One of these resulted in a £1bn deal called Manchester Life, under which the council sold a prime slice of city centre land to Abu Dhabi for £5m to build 6,000 homes, along with a right of first refusal on other projects.

Richard Leese, the leader of Manchester city council at the time, told the Guardian: “That was a UK government-brokered deal and we were obviously seeking a very significant investment for what would in total have been a £1bn scheme.

“Housing development in and around the city centre and Ancoats in particular had stopped and been stopped for several years. At that time there were no [other] developers who were either willing or able to do it.”

In a press release, Leese hailed the partnership as a “world-class exemplar of regeneration” and “a platform for the delivery of more than 6,000 new homes”.

However, only 2,039 homes have been delivered by Manchester Life – a third of the total promised – with a further 2,839 homes being built by other developers. The total of 4,878 new properties is nearly 20% short of the 6,000 envisaged.

Despite the council’s longstanding policy of at least 20% of new developments being for social and affordable housing, only 8% of these 4,878 properties fell into that category – and none were provided by Manchester Life.

A five-minute walk from the new Abu Dhabi-funded apartments, which are home to the city’s first Michelin-starred restaurant, the nave of a former Methodist church is stacked high with emergency food for those living on surrounding streets.

The short walk to the Etihad Stadium includes some of the poorest areas in the second most deprived local authority in England. Within only half a mile, there are four charity food banks or distribution sites, one of which has a plaque marking its opening by Burnham in 2021.

“It’s bound to cause resentment,” said Mark Blake, the chief executive of Manchester Central Foodbank, of the sudden influx of shiny apartments, expensive eateries and well-paid tenants. “When it’s in your face and is during a cost of living crisis it potentially could lead to some unrest. I think it should be a real concern.”

Parking has become a flashpoint, with reports of cars being vandalised after being left on council estate streets by those living or dining at the Abu Dhabi-funded properties. Tenants of the swanky apartments are encouraged to leave food to local food banks in donation boxes in each of the luxury blocks.

“People are feeling all these cultural divides that are played out through the proxy of housing and everyday issues around parking,” said Alan Good, a Lib Dem councillor for Ancoats and Beswick. “Residents tell me they look at the shiny new towers and there’s a resentment – a feeling that they’re not benefiting from what Manchester is benefiting from.”

Good said he felt Manchester was becoming a “northern version of London” as an “insane” property crisis compounded the misery for the city’s 20,000 people on the social housing register.

Dr Matthew Stallard, a University College London researcher and chair of trustees at Manchester Central Foodbank, said there was an uncomfortable disconnect between the city’s reputation nationally – with “Manchesterism” becoming a byword for a thriving metropolis with an eye on broader social benefits – and the reality for many in the city.

“If you look at central Manchester and all the skyscrapers and you go out in every direction by a mile and a half or two miles, you’re then in some of the most deprived neighbourhoods in the country. In Ancoats, it’s a very clear line where the money is and where the money’s not.”

In summer 2016, Burnham was keenly aware of Greater Manchester’s housing crisis. He told the Salford Star that if elected, he would stop large property firms benefiting from multimillion-pound taxpayer-funded loans from the mayoral authority.

There were concerns, he said, that the Greater Manchester combined authority (GMCA) fund had “been used to provide loans to large companies, which should have used their own finance instead, and that is too focused on city centre and luxury schemes”.

Barely a year later, Burnham signed off a £55m loan to Jersey-registered property firms owned by Sheikh Mansour, scion of one of the world’s wealthiest families with a reported fortune of about £300bn.

GMCA said its loans fund was available to all developers who met the lending criteria and that the loans had been repaid in full. But these decisions are now being investigated by councillors on GMCA’s scrutiny committee.

There are awkward questions for Burnham, too. Weeks before the loans were approved, he enjoyed hospitality from City’s owners in a meeting that came to light only last week after disappearing from public records. The prime minister initially said he had had only one “significant” meeting with the club’s bosses – in 2021 – but a further five have since emerged.

Burnham said last week he had asked GMCA to conduct a “manual trawl of everything, as I want everything possible to be out there”. He added: “There’s no question about that – full transparency.”

There appeared to be little transparency, however, when it came to the council’s long-term relationship with Manchester City’s owners.

In December 2015, it signed a 10-year “collaboration agreement” with Abu Dhabi giving the emirates first refusal on land near the city centre. A specific clause in effect gagged the council’s democratically elected politicians from announcing the deal without written approval from Sheikh Mansour’s firm.

Other Manchester developers only discovered this years later. “It’s blatant partiality on a massive scale. It stinks,” said one property consultant. A council spokesperson defended the clause as “a standard agreement between two parties that ensures announcements or information releases are agreed by all parties”.

All of the property, now worth an estimated £350m, is ultimately owned by Sheikh Mansour via Jersey-domiciled subsidiaries, with the super-rich Emirati receiving the rent paid by the hundreds of mostly young professionals who live there.

The council said it had received nearly £3m as part of an undisclosed profit-sharing agreement and a further £17.6m in council tax. However, the precise return to the taxpayer – and the terms under which the deals were struck – remain unknown.

Leese, 75, stepped down as council leader after 25 years in December 2021, becoming honorary president at Manchester City two years later. When approached by the Guardian, he denied the Abu Dhabi deal was shielded from scrutiny and defended his appointment at Manchester City.

“This was something that happened after I retired from the council. Whether it would have been appropriate when I was on the council, I would have questioned that,” Leese said.

One senior former council officer, who worked in the property and development team, described the culture in this period as “Kremlin-like” or akin to “a medieval court” where officials could show “no dissent” towards the decisions of the Labour leadership.

“When you’ve got a council that’s 99% one party, there wasn’t really room for discussion,” they said, adding that they felt some senior leaders got “blinded by schmoozing around” with Abu Dhabi executives and others.

Leese denied he got too close to Manchester City, the team he supports, or gave them favourable treatment as council leader. “There are a lot of players in Manchester that the city council is close to,” he said.

“That’s the way the city works – in partnership.”

Manchester city council has strongly denied claims of a “sweetheart deal” with Abu Dhabi after researchers at the University of Sheffield concluded it had “sold the family silver too cheaply” by giving the land to Abu Dhabi at a cheaper rate than comparable developments.

In 2017, three years after the first Abu Dhabi deal and the year Burnham became Greater Manchester mayor, council leaders made another huge bet. They paid £42m for a hollowed out retail park next to the £1bn Manchester Life development, described at the time as the biggest ever land purchase in Manchester city centre.

Its price was at least six times higher per acre than the adjacent land sold for £5m to Sheikh Mansour – and it would later be identified as the permanent future home of Burnham’s No 10 North.

This former retail park was also a partnership with Abu Dhabi. Again, the terms were shielded from scrutiny as members of the public were excluded from council hearings – but inside the town hall, the fallout was significant.

A senior council property officer, Dominic Hayes, resigned abruptly in March 2018 over concerns about the deals the council was doing with Mansour’s group. He listed a series of complaints in an email to the council chief executive, Joanne Roney, who the previous year had succeeded the all-powerful Howard Bernstein when he retired after 29 years in charge.

In a tense meeting days after the resignation, a senior council figure, Eddie Smith, is said to have told colleagues that Hayes had thrown them “under a bus” and that the leadership was furious. According to contemporaneous notes by a colleague, seen by the Guardian, Smith said Hayes had made “not acceptable [and] possibly dangerous” criticisms of a Manchester City board member who was a key figure in the Manchester Life deal.

Smith is then said to have commented: “You don’t criticise the council’s relationship with the football club in this organisation and hope to survive.” Smith, who left the council in 2020, denies making the comment.

Yet Hayes’ concerns were serious enough to warrant an internal investigation into governance at the council. It found that anxieties about the council’s deal-making were not limited to just one officer.

A second senior employee told auditors they were concerned that the council had “overpaid” for the rundown retail park, according to an official record of the meeting. That officer raised concerns that the Abu Dhabi-led project was “driving the master planning for a site they didn’t own”.

When Burnham became prime minister in July, the site was tipped as the permanent home for No 10 North. As scrutiny of the Abu Dhabi link grew in October, these plans were quietly shelved.

Council sources noticed a change of approach under Leese’s successor, Bev Craig, when she became council leader in December 2021.

Craig ordered a review of the Manchester Life deal to make sure it was “all legal, all above board”, she told BBC Radio Manchester this month, adding: “The answer was yes.”

One of the reviews commissioned by Craig, who succeeded Burnham this year as Greater Manchester mayor, was published in July. It found that while the deals with developers such as Abu Dhabi had delivered “significant benefits”, there were “weaknesses in documentation, monitoring and assurance”, particularly around the profit-sharing nature of these deals.

Prof Jonathan Silver, a University of Sheffield researcher who has analysed the Manchester Life deal, said the growing buy-up of land and property by Emiratis raised “major concerns about the fragility of the ‘Manchester model’ and its reliance on attracting flows of international finance, whatever the cost”.

Silver said there were “urgent questions” about what would happen to the hundreds of homes in the Manchester Life developments if Sheikh Mansour was forced or decided to sell Manchester City in light of the cheating scandal.

Leese remains confident the Abu Dhabi deals were a huge success for the city. Asked whether he would have handled the partnership any differently given the concerns raised by academics and others, he said: “No. Nothing that I can think of. It is a phenomenally good deal for Manchester.”

Additional reporting: Carmen Aguilar García and Michael Goodier

'Culture is stagnant, so politics is stuck' | Playwright James Graham – Radical Thinking – podcast

The Guardian Sat, 24 Oct 2026 06:45:25 GMT

Are we doomscrolling our way into a democratic crisis? That’s what the playwright James Graham fears may be happening, as he suggests that our algorithms have led us into ‘a massive crisis of the new’ and are preventing us from imagining a different future

Aditya suggested reading (and watching) list for James Graham

James Graham has written a shaming amount. I’ve listed below three

1. Dear England: about England’s football team

https://www. bbc. co. uk/iplayer/episodes/m002qktz/dear-england

2. Sherwood: mentioned in the conversation, set in the village where James Graham grew up in the shadow of the miners’ strike

3. Quiz: set on the British quiz show, Who wants to be a millionaire, where a contestant wins a million quid

On cultural stagnation:

A lot of people say culture is stuck, although few sketch out the political consequences of that stagnation as well as James Graham does in our chat.

Many also disagree on why:

For ‘it was the algorithm that did it’, read Filterworld: How algorithms flattened culture by Kyle Chayka

For a wider ranging explantaion look at Blank Space: A Cultural History of the Twenty-First Century by W. David Marx

Wildwood Out now If Pixar was a chocolate bar, it would be a Mars, while Laika – whose new film Wildwood incorporates themes of war and child abduction – would be something like Green & Blacks. Darker and with more esoteric flavours, this stop-motion animation is not so much for the nursery school crowd, but for discerning pre-teens and adults alike. Ghosts: The Possession of Button House Out now The beloved BBC TV comedy gets a big-screen outing, with Simon Farnaby’s trouserless Tory MP ghost, Jim Howick’s dead scoutmaster, shot by a member of his own troop, Ben Willbond’s closeted second world war officer and the other regular cast members all returning. Ali G: Who Iz I? Out now Twenty four years after Ali G Indahouse opened at No 1 at the UK box office, Sasha Baron Cohen revives his alter-ego for a followup, making his directorial debut in the process. Morgana Robinson also stars. Catherine Bray

Suede, Manic Street Preachers OVO Hydro, Glasgow, 28 October; First Direct Bank Arena Leeds, 30 October; touring to 12 November Christmas comes early for people of a certain vintage with a penchant for evergreen British rock bands in the shape of this co-headline tour. Jasmine Myra Norwich Arts Centre, 27 October; Earth, London, 28 October; St George’s, Bristol, 29 October Alto saxophonist-composer Jasmine Myra is on the rise within the cinematic spiritual jazz orbit of Manchester’s Gondwana Records, a visionary operation devoted to the soulful lyricism and storytelling she espouses. This tour will be a fascinating insight into just how far the very promising Myra is instrumentally ready to go. John Fordham

London Symphony Orchestra/Pappano Barbican Hall, London, 29 October The LSO is the latest major international institution to commission British composer Hannah Kendall, a distinctive, ambitious voice in contemporary classical music. Her new work I Have Discovered the Secret of Death features Grammy-winning mezzo Fleur Barron. Its world premiere is paired with Tchaikovsky’s impassioned Fifth Symphony. Antonio Pappano conducts. Flora Willson

Wilhelmina Barns-Graham Tate St Ives, to 3 May A big part of St Ives’s modernist boom in the early 2oth century, Barns-Graham (work pictured above) quietly became one of the UK’s most important artists of her era with an emotional take on abstraction, celebrated here with 170 works from throughout her career.

LS Lowry MK Gallery, Milton Keynes, to 28 February This big celebration of the life and work of one of England’s best-loved artists is the first institutional show of his grimy, gritty industrial painting for 13 years, and marks 50 years since his death.

The Rupture: No Condition Is Permanent Talbot Rice Gallery, Edinburgh, to 13 February Attempting to respond to a time of unprecedented political, social and economic change, this exhibition brings together a huge cast of international artists to reckon with our increasingly broken systems.

The Way We Live The Box, Plymouth, to 21 February This exhibition looks at the idea of the home, and what it means to a variety of artists including the likes of Do Ho Suh, Rachel Whiteread and recent Turner prize winner Jasleen Kaur. Eddy Frankel

The Lives of Others Adelphi theatre, London, to 9 January Director Robert Icke adapts the Academy award-winning film set in East Berlin, 1984. Macbeth Liquid & Envy, Oldham, to 7 November While Oldham’s Coliseum theatre is being restored, it is staging work in imaginative locations around town. This site-specific take on Macbeth is set in a real-life nightclub, invoking a world of 70s gangsters, casinos and shifting social codes. MG

Hansel & Gretel and the Witch Northern Stage, Newcastle upon Tyne, 29 October to 1 November Choreographer Liv Lorent and her company BalletLorent have really cornered the market in fairytale family shows with a bit of edge and a lot of imagination. Susan Calman Touring to 20 November The Glaswegian standup has presented a slew of TV programmes and done a Strictly shift in the decade since her last tour, but new show Tall Tales – which combines showbiz stories with meditations on grief and depression – proves this glam career pivot has done nothing to dent her twinkly misanthropy. Rachel Aroesti

Michael Kiwanuka - Fudge Out now Originally due for release last autumn, this fifth album from the Brit-nominated Kiwanuka was delayed after he suffered a haemorrhagic stroke after returning home from a tour. John Legend - Muse Out now After dabbling in music for children with 2024’s lullaby-centric My Favourite Dream, the Egot winner returns to more grownup themes on this entirely Pharrell-produced 11th album. The One About Matthew Perry Netflix, 27 October A moving film recounting the life and career of the late Friends actor charting his rise to TV stardom and lifelong battles with addiction, as well as the tabloid scandals that accompanied his fame.

How Houdini Made Magic Podcast TV’s favourite illusionist Derren Brown tells the story of one of magic’s most iconic figures, Harry Houdini, in this 10-part series. Brown builds a fascinating picture of how Houdini fashioned himself a modern celebrity image.
