The Best Laptops

Wired October 24, 2026

All products featured on WIRED are independently selected by our editors. However, we may receive compensation from retailers and/or from purchases of products through these links. Learn more.

I’ve been reviewing laptops for well over a decade, sometimes testing more than 30 devices per year. Not all are winners, and many should be avoided, no matter how slick the marketing or how cheap the discount. Good news: It’s my job to recommend laptops that fit your budget and won’t make you regret your purchase six months later. These are my favorite laptops that I’ve tested myself and would highly recommend you buy.

For more guidance, also see my recommendations in specific categories, such as the Best MacBooks, Best Gaming Laptops, Best Chromebooks, Best Budget Laptops, Best Windows Laptops, and Best 2-in-1 Laptops. My guide on How to Choose a Laptop may also help if you’re undecided.

Updated October 2026: I’ve updated my recommendations after testing all the new Nvidia RTX Spark laptops, as well as the new Googlebooks. The Surface Laptop Ultra has replaced the Dell XPS 14, and I've added back the Acer Chromebook Plus Spin 514 at its discounted price.

Amazon

Dell (8 GB)

HP (X2 Plus, 32 GB)

Amazon (2560 x 1600)

Apple

Amazon

Walmart

Apple

When friends or family ask what laptop to buy, I always start with the MacBook Air. It is far more powerful than its compact size suggests. It’s a shame about the recent $200 price increase from $1,099 to $1,299, but even at that new price, it remains my top pick because it nails the big picture. Everything from the trackpad to the speakers is of the highest quality, and it delivers all the performance and battery life the average person needs.

With the latest M5 chip, its GPU matches the M3 Pro MacBook Pro, easily handling everything from gaming to video editing. That’s not at all what the MacBook Air is designed for, but the performance is there when you want to dabble. It’s what makes it feel like a do-it-all machine, all contained in a fanless chassis that’s still one of the thinnest laptops you can buy. Oh, and did I mention it’ll last well over a full workday away from the wall socket and perform just as well on battery as when plugged in? In almost every aspect, it’s the gold standard.

While the lower price of the new MacBook Neo might be tempting, the MacBook Air is the better choice for anyone working at a computer all day. With its superior performance, extra memory, faster storage, and Thunderbolt ports, you will never have to question if you have the right tool for the job. (And unless you already know you need a MacBook Pro, you probably don’t.)

Dell

Dell (8 GB)

Dell (16 GB)

Best Buy (16 GB)

Speaking of price, I have to mention the new Dell XPS 13 next. I like just about everything about this laptop, whether it’s the compact size, the excellent build quality, or the gorgeous screen. It’s not OLED, but it’s sharp, bright, and color-accurate. It also includes a 120-Hz refresh rate, which makes animation and motion on the device look super smooth. The XPS 13 is filled with features like that, which don’t normally end up in a laptop at this price. While it doesn’t have what I’d call powerhouse performance, the Intel Wildcat Lake chip inside gets the job done for basic, day-to-day computing tasks. That translates to great, all-day battery life, competitive with the MacBook Air. Just don’t try to play games, edit high-resolution video, or take it to engineering school.

The XPS 13 is especially good for those who want a compact device to travel with. With its tiny bezels, it’s still one of the best laptops to use on a plane. But even beyond that, it’s just one of the best laptops you can buy under $1,000 right now. The Dell XPS 13 is primarily being talked about as a budget laptop, thanks to its $700 starting configuration. But that model comes with only 8 GB of RAM, which limited performance in my testing. You’ll probably just want to avoid that 8 GB model. Most people will want the upgraded 16 GB model, which you can get for $900. It’s the best hardware you can buy for under $1,000.

HP

HP (X2 Plus, 32 GB)

HP (Core Ultra 7)

Best Buy (X2 Elite)

If you want a Windows laptop that still feels high-end but has a bit more performance, I would point you to the HP OmniBook Ultra 14. It might be the prettiest Windows laptop you can buy right now. The device is beautifully built and incredibly sturdy, with a thin chassis, an oversized haptic trackpad, and polished metal edges. I also appreciate the three Thunderbolt 4 ports split between both sides for convenient charging, as well as the surprisingly good speakers. I tested the high-end model, which features a fast Snapdragon X2 Elite, 32 GB of RAM, and a gorgeous 2880 x 1800 OLED display. The screen offers near-perfect colors, excellent brightness, and astounding HDR performance. It doesn’t get much better than this. It’s usually quite expensive, but we’re finally seeing discounts that bring it to a more reasonable price. There’s also an Intel model with a very efficient, powerful chip that would be a good choice. I’d go with whichever is cheaper right now.

Lenovo

Amazon (2560 x 1600)

Lenovo (1920 x 1200)

And lastly, for something with a larger screen, I’d recommend the Lenovo IdeaPad Slim 5x. It’s a particularly good alternative to the 15-inch MacBook Air, at a much lower cost. These days, you can buy the upgraded model with the 2560 x 1600 OLED display (and 165-Hz refresh rate) for $1,000, on sale at Amazon. While it’s slightly thicker than the MacBook Air, it leaves more room for extra ports including HDMI, USB-A, and an SD card slot. And while the Snapdragon X2 Plus isn’t quite an M5 killer, I was happy with the performance and battery life provided. Lenovo also sells a cheaper version directly, but it has a lower-resolution IPS screen that I haven’t tested. The $30 it costs to upgrade the display to a higher-resolution OLED is well-worth it.

HP

HP (14-inch)

Amazon

While “cheap” means something different to everyone, the best budget laptops generally fall under $750. This is where Windows truly shines, offering great specs for less money. Thanks to the latest processors from Qualcomm and Intel, these laptops now offer battery life that rivals Apple. The best affordable laptop I’ve checked out is the HP OmniBook 5. The model I tested has a Snapdragon X processor, 16 GB of RAM, 512 GB of storage, and a 14-inch OLED screen. Discounts fluctuate frequently, but HP always has some version of the OmniBook 5 with a Snapdragon CPU at under $700. The specific discounted configuration seems to change every few days, though, so shop carefully. I'll be testing the latest model soon, which switches to Intel processors and starts at $699.

I also recently tested the new HP OmniBook 3, which uses the same chip as the OmniBook 5. It frequently sells for less than the OmniBook 5 by at least $100 or so. HP is selling this configuration of the 14-inch model for under $550. While the OmniBook 3 is a good alternative, the OmniBook 5 is much thinner and looks more modern. Neither laptop has a particularly great touchpad, though, which is easily the biggest flaw in both laptops. Between the two, the OmniBook 5 is the better buy if you can afford it.

Apple

Amazon

Apple

The MacBook Neo is Apple’s new entry-level laptop. It initially started at an aggressive $599, but that price has recently been raised to $699. Even at that price, the laptop shines when it comes to the display. It offers the best screen you can find at this price, bringing the macOS experience to an unprecedented value, even at $699 (or $799 for the 512 GB model). Apple clearly prioritized the front-of-screen experience, delivering a premium feel across the display, build quality, and keyboard. While the 8 GB of RAM, outdated ports, and slower SSD are notable drawbacks—making the MacBook Air a far better choice for remote workers—the Neo is an extremely premium-feeling laptop available for students, travelers, and casual users. Thanks to the lower-powered A18 Pro chip, though, performance does take a hit. So, be careful about buying this laptop if you work at a computer all day.

Given how good some of these budget laptops are, it’s a bit harder to find a place for Chromebooks. Perhaps that's why Google introduced the next evolution of the platform, so to speak: the Googlebook. The first batch has been released into the world, and I've tested a number of them. Googlebooks are similar to Chromebooks in use case, but they run entirely on Android and include some exclusive Google Gemini features. I like the close integration with Android, but Googlebooks ended up being a bit of a letdown, mostly because they're so expensive. The Acer Googlebook 14 and Dell XPS Googlebook are the two standouts in my book, as both use a Snapdragon X-series chip to deliver really great battery life. The XPS Googlebook is particularly pretty, as the chassis is nearly identical to the XPS 13. But $999 is a tough price to swallow. It ultimately has some of the same limitations as Chromebooks, as you can't download applications from the web and are forced to rely on the Google Play Store. The Acer Googlebook 14 is probably my top pick, as it comes in the cheapest at $899. Even that isn't exactly what I'd call a “budget laptop,” though.

Acer

Best Buy

That's why I strongly recommend the Acer Chromebook Plus Spin 514, especially when it's on sale for under $700 (which is frequent). It uses an efficient (and responsive) MediaTek Kompanio Ultra that delivers excellent battery life. For most people, I wouldn't recommend spending over $500 on a Chromebook because if you're paying more, you should consider the MacBook Neo or the HP OmniBooks, which offer more than a Chromebook's limited scope. But the Acer Chromebook Plus Spin 514 might be the best combination of display, touchpad, and battery life at this price, making it a good choice for the right person—so long as you know what you're paying for.

Truly cheap Chromebooks come with bigger compromises, especially in display quality, touchpad feel, and battery life. If you really need something dirt cheap as a starter laptop for a kid or as a secondary device, I'd recommend the Asus Chromebook CX14. It has a modern design, enough ports, a good keyboard, and decent storage.

Apple

Amazon (M5 Max)

Amazon (M5 Pro)

Apple (M5 Pro)

While the laptops above are great for most people, content creators and gamers need extra performance. For the former, the 16-inch M5 Max MacBook Pro is the ultimate choice. It combines immense power with surprising portability and fantastic battery life—a rare feat. The M5 generation is the most impressive yet, with a greatly expanded GPU and significantly boosted on-device AI processing thanks to a more efficient Neural Engine and faster memory bandwidth. While it is one of the most powerful AI laptops available, the MacBook Pro isn’t for everyone; it is built specifically for professional creatives and engineers running heavy, demanding applications. It’s become more expensive in 2026, though, and the competition from the Windows side is finally heating up.

Microsoft

Amazon

Microsoft

I'm talking primarily about the launch of Nvidia's new RTX Spark “superchip” and the new laptops that use it. To be clear, despite Nvidia's involvement, these aren't gaming laptops. Like the MacBook Pro, they're designed first and foremost for running heavier creative applications and on-device AI. The Surface Laptop Ultra is a great example, which has a lot in common with the standard 15-inch Surface Laptop. But the differences internally are substantial. The Surface Laptop Ultra uses a single chip that integrates the CPU, GPU, and memory together, allowing up to 128 GB of memory to be shared across the system. That's not unlike how Apple Silicon works, dramatically increasing the on-device AI performance. So, if you've been curious about running LLMs right on your laptop without relying on the cloud, these RTX Spark laptops are a great place to start. The other two RTX Spark laptops I tested, the HP OmniBook Ultra 16 and Lenovo Pro 9n, share a lot with the Surface Laptop Ultra (including performance). The OmniBook Ultra is the thinnest of the three, but I prefer the Surface Laptop Ultra's Mini-LED display and 3:2 aspect ratio.

Perhaps the most common use for extra laptop performance, however, is gaming. If you plan to boot up graphically intensive games more than a couple of times a week, you will want a dedicated gaming laptop. After testing dozens over the past year, I’ve come back to the Lenovo LOQ 15 as my top pick. There are cheaper RTX 5050 models, such as the Alienware 15 or MSI Cyborg A15, but prices have been increasing on these laptops over the past few months. The Alienware 15 with the RTX 5050, in particular, has seen a $600 price jump, which makes it incredibly overpriced.

Lenovo

Walmart (RTX 5060, 512 GB)

Amazon (RTX 5060, 1 TB)

Lenovo (RTX 5050, 512 GB)

That’s led me back to the LOQ 15, which has stayed steady at $1,300 at Walmart and gives you an RTX 5060 for graphics and a bright, colorful screen. You won’t find a cheaper gaming laptop that doesn’t make some significant compromises in either performance or screen quality, both of which can sour the gaming experience. And while I wish the LOQ 15 were still selling for under $1,000 as it did at launch, it's still the best gaming laptop for the money right now. It’s really the only gaming laptop under $1,500 I’d currently buy, given where prices are.

There’s also a whole world of gaming laptops outside the budget tier, though. I’ve tested an assortment of options, and I always come back to the Razer Blade 14 and Razer Blade 16. Portable, minimalist, and extremely well-made, their sleek design means they work just as well for school or work as they do for gaming, without the bulk of a traditional gaming laptop. While you can buy more powerful options, nothing quite matches the Razer Blade. They’re expensive, but if you can afford them, they’re as premium as gaming laptops get. I’ll soon be testing the latest version of the Blade 16, which includes Intel’s new Panther Lake chips and should have vastly improved battery life.

If you choose one of the laptops above, you will be very happy with your purchase. However, if you are looking for a specific feature or a different price point, I have included a few other options below that I’ve recently reviewed and enjoyed using. Each of these recently tested laptops has at least one minor drawback, but they could still be the perfect choice depending on your needs and current discounts.

Framework Laptop 13 Pro for $1,599: We’ve always loved Framework laptops at WIRED, mainly because their internal components are so repairable and upgradable. Users can easily swap out nearly every part, including the CPU. The Framework Laptop 13 Pro uses the same internal structure as the basic Framework Laptop 13, but upgraded with a haptic touchpad, an aluminum chassis, and a brighter (and sharper) display. The result is the Framework Laptop I’ve always wanted, especially with an all-black aesthetic that hints at ThinkPad inspiration. But most of all, if you’re going to try and make a laptop last for many years, it makes sense that it would be something more premium. This one actually feels like it’s worth the investment.

Microsoft Surface Laptop 13.8 for $930: The Surface Laptop 13.8 (also known as the 7th Edition) was one of my favorite laptops throughout 2024 and 2025, primarily because of its premium build quality, great battery life, and 3:2 aspect ratio screen. And while I still love this laptop, it’s risen dramatically in price and no longer feels like a great value, especially since it’s two years old now. The 2024 model now starts at $1,200, though I’ve occasionally seen it dip under $1,000. The next-generation model with the Snapdragon X2 chips costs $1,700. I have seen that price come down as low as $1,350 on discount.

Dell 14 Plus for $1,199: There was a time in 2025 when the Dell 14 Plus was as affordable as $600. It was easily the best deal in the world of Windows laptops, primarily because the Dell 14 Plus has a 2560 x 1600 display and a smooth touchpad—two things laptops at that price typically lack. These days, it’s up to over $1,000, though for a 1 TB configuration, that is still a reasonable price. The XPS 13 is the better overall laptop, but the Dell 14 Plus offers more ports and storage for the price.

Lenovo Yoga Slim 7 Ultra for $2,250: I like this laptop quite a bit. The OLED screen is sharp, bright, and quite colorful—very similar to the HP OmniBook Ultra. It also has many of the other great features on premium Windows laptops these days, including a haptic-feedback touchpad and a very slim profile. Unfortunately, it’s only available right now in a very expensive, maxed-out configuration with 32 GB of RAM and at least a terabyte of storage. I don’t think that’s a good pairing for this ultra-light laptop. Even with half the memory and storage, though, this would be too expensive compared to the competition.

Asus Zenbook A16 for $2,200: The Zenbook A14 and A16 are Asus’ ultralight laptops, weighing just 2.16 pounds, making them some of the lightest laptops you can buy right now. This second-generation Zenbook A16 is still incredibly light and now comes with second-generation Snapdragon X2 chips. It’s unique for its portability, and the Qualcomm chips deliver great battery life and performance. However, given the dramatic price increase, I’d suggest buying the 2025 model instead, which consistently comes in under $1,000.

Alienware 16X Aurora.

Alienware 16X Aurora for $1,950: Another solid gaming laptop with the typical Alienware flair. Its standout features are its higher-resolution display and great build quality. The price fluctuates frequently, though, and in most cases, the LOQ 15 is the better option (unless you really want that higher-resolution screen).

Acer Swift 16 AI.

Dell 14S: This is the 2026 successor to the Dell 14 Plus, which I recommended above. This is a solid laptop with a premium design and a highly reflective OLED display. It also performs well, thanks to the latest Intel Core Ultra Series 3 chip. But it’s far too expensive right now. Until the price comes down, I prefer just about every other Dell option, including the Dell 14 Plus, Dell XPS 13, or Dell XPS 14.

Lenovo LOQ 15 Essential: This is a “new” model that came out this year, even though it uses a CPU from 2023. But honestly, this is just too expensive. I’ve seen it on sale for under $1,400, but even then, the standard LOQ 15 costs about the same and has a far superior display.

MacBook Pro M5: It’s not a significant step up from the MacBook Air in performance, and it’s much thicker. You’re paying for the Mini-LED screen and extra ports. Unfortunately, it got the biggest price bump, up $300 to $1,999. It’s not a bad laptop, but you’re better off with the MacBook Air or a more powerful M5 Pro/Max configuration.

Acer Swift 16 AI: This is one of the few laptops you can buy with the powerful, efficient new Intel Core Ultra X9 chips. However, the Acer Swift 16 AI takes an experimental approach with its oversized trackpad, making it very difficult to use. Even at a discount, you’ll find it frustrating.

Asus TUF Gaming A14: There’s a lot I like about this gaming laptop. The design is portable yet modern, and the display is sharp. And while the TUF Gaming A14 is impressive technically (using the interesting AMD Strix Point chip), the lack of a discrete graphics card doesn’t provide enough gaming performance to justify its very high price. I haven’t tested the options with dedicated graphics cards, but they tend to be more expensive than counterparts from Lenovo, Acer, or Alienware.

Asus Vivobook 14: I recommended this laptop a lot throughout 2025, but it doesn’t hold up as well these days. While the Vivobook 14 has great battery life, the HP OmniBook 5 14 offers a much better display and similar specs, making it a better laptop.

How Much Should You Spend on a Laptop?

If you’re shopping for a laptop, you probably already have a budget. But some context might help put things in perspective. The cheapest laptops cost around $200, but laptop prices can range as high as $5,000. Meanwhile, the average amount people spend, according to the best data we have, is around $750. That lands decidedly in the midrange, splitting between the more expensive devices that are more than $1,000 and the budget-tier machines you find below $700.

When we talk about pricing, it’s often the “starting” price of the laptop, meaning the lowest-priced configuration. This is really important to consider, as you want to compare devices apples to apples as much as possible. For example, a cheaper laptop might start at $750 with 256 GB of storage, while a more premium laptop might start at this same price but come with 512 GB or even 1 TB of storage. Increasingly, you can find some really decent laptops around this price, some of which we’ve listed.

If your budget needs to be under $750, though, there are still good options. Laptops below this price tend to come with compromises. Most commonly, it’s the quality of the display and touchpad that suffers, as these are things you can’t gauge from a spec sheet or reference photo. Or it might be a performance-related issue, such as the 8 GB of memory in the MacBook Neo. If you’re shopping for something under $500, Chromebooks often give you the best bang for your buck.

So, why spend more? Well, there are two primary reasons. First, you might want a more premium design, perhaps one that has a more daring aesthetic or high-end components. Take the MacBook Pro, for example. It starts at $600 more than the MacBook Air but comes with a brighter mini-LED screen, significantly better speakers, and more ports. The second primary reason to spend more than $750 or so is to get more performance. Whether for gaming or content creation, laptops with discrete GPUs cost more, which is why it’s hard to find a worthwhile gaming laptop for less than $1,000. If you’re buying a gaming laptop, plan to spend a few hundred bucks more.

What Are the Best Laptop Brands?

Unlike the smartphone world, the biggest laptop brands have been around for more than 40 years. Besides Apple, four laptop brands stand out for adopting the latest technology and trends while providing reliable support and service.

Lenovo is the biggest PC brand in the world, at least in terms of global shipments. It’s perhaps most well-known for its familiar sub-brands like ThinkPad and Yoga, but it also isn’t afraid to take risks with more experimental designs and advanced technology. Lenovo has also made a name for itself in the gaming space with its Legion laptops, known for balancing performance and features at competitive prices.

Asus has quickly become a favorite, notable for the sheer number of laptops available in the consumer market. The company takes a similar approach to Lenovo, which has led Asus to innovate quickly on new technology and designs while also launching premium laptops at more affordable prices than its competitors. Gaming, in particular, is a space Asus has come to dominate, with the ROG Zephyrus, Strix, and TUF brands leading the way.

Dell and HP are generally more conservative, but both have recently undergone significant rebranding. In 2024, HP replaced its Spectre and Envy lines with the OmniBook name. Meanwhile, Dell briefly retired its well-known Inspiron and XPS sub-brands in 2025, though it has since reversed course and brought the XPS line back.

Other notable laptop brands include Microsoft Surface, Samsung, Acer, LG, and MSI, though none have the same global footprint as the top four.

How Do I Choose the Right Laptop?

If none of these laptops resonate with what you're looking for, that’s OK! There are far more laptops than we have time to test. To help you make smart choices, we put together a complete laptop buying guide. We also cover the CPUs and GPUs you need to know. We recommend sticking to these guidelines:

RAM: We recommend 16 GB of RAM. That’s become the new standard, even in more affordable laptops. Upgrading to 32 GB is even better, so you won't have to worry about running out of memory, especially if you’re a gamer or video editor. The recent memory shortage has led to some dramatic price increases, largely based around configurations of RAM. Apple’s launch of the 8 GB MacBook Neo this spring has led to the return of high-end 8-GB Windows laptops as well, such as the Dell XPS 13.

CPU: For Windows laptops, you have three CPU brands to choose from: Intel, AMD, or Qualcomm. Intel’s Core Ultra Series 2 launched in late 2024 and delivers a huge boost to battery life. It also has the best integrated graphics of the three. Core Ultra Series 3 is just now rolling out and, based on my testing, is extremely impressive in performance and efficiency. While AMD chips are primarily used in gaming laptops, they’ve struggled to gain ground on Intel elsewhere.

Qualcomm’s Snapdragon X chips, however, have seriously challenged Intel over the past year with their ARM architecture, offering some of the best battery life we’ve ever seen on Windows machines. The second generation, Snapdragon X2, was announced last fall and rolled out slowly throughout 2026. They improve performance, but in many cases, they've led to more expensive laptops, while previous-gen laptops are still available that cost less.

Starting this year, there's also the choice of Nvidia’s new RTX Spark platform, which gives you the option of 18-core or 20-core CPUs. More on that in the GPU section below.

Apple Silicon is what powers all the modern MacBooks, the latest of which is the M5 chip. Read our in-depth guide on Which MacBook to Buy for more information

Graphics: Want to play AAA PC games, edit video on your laptop, or run local AI models? You’ll want some powerful graphics on hand. At this point, Nvidia is the primary option. The RTX 5090 launched in 2025 is still the most powerful new GPU available, but the 5040-series still remains a good option.

Integrated graphics have improved significantly over the years, though, especially on processors made by Apple, AMD, and Intel, such as the Apple M5 or the Intel Core Ultra X9 388H. Nvidia's RTX Spark platform uses a single “superchip” that provides unified memory to both the CPU and GPU to improve AI performance.

Screen: The display depends highly on the size of the laptop. A 1,200-pixel resolution (HD+) screen on a 13- or 14-inch laptop looks sharp enough to get by, but you’ll want more pixels on larger displays, such as a 2560 x 1600, 2880 x 1800, or 3840 x 2400. While IPS screens are good enough for most people, OLED and Mini-LED are becoming more common, offering better color accuracy, deeper contrast, and excellent HDR performance.

Connectivity: We generally recommend at least two USB-C ports, along with one HDMI and one USB-A port for legacy devices. (Remember that nearly all laptops today use one of those USB-C ports for the power adapter.) Thankfully, most laptops still have headphone jacks, but always check, because a few models have dropped them. Lastly, make sure it supports Wi-Fi 6E or newer. Even if you don’t have a Wi-Fi 6E or Wi-Fi 7 router yet, you'll likely have one in the future (see our Best Routers or Best Mesh Systems guides if you need a new one).

Battery life: Battery life is extremely competitive these days, with Apple, Qualcomm, and Intel all making highly ambitious battery-life claims. Most laptops with the latest chips (and without discrete graphics) will get you more than 10 hours of battery life, or many more if your workload is lighter.

Intel vs. AMD vs. Qualcomm

As mentioned, in Windows-based laptops, there are three primary options for CPUs: Intel, AMD, and Qualcomm. All three companies offer good processors, but it really depends on the type of laptop. For premium laptops, you’ll want something like the Intel Core Ultra 258V or Qualcomm Snapdragon X Elite. Meanwhile, for budget laptops, Snapdragon X is the best choice. And for gaming laptops, I’d recommend something from AMD, such as the Ryzen AI 9 365. All three companies have announced next-gen chips for 2026, and there’s some exciting stuff coming soon.

Intel’s latest chips, known as either Core Ultra Series 3 or codename Panther Lake, are slowly rolling out in new laptops, such as the Dell XPS 14. These chips represent a massive leap forward in both CPU and integrated graphics performance. While highly impressive, they will soon face fresh competition from upcoming AMD and Qualcomm releases.

Qualcomm made a major impact in 2024 with its Snapdragon X chips. Similar to Apple's M-series, these ARM-based processors prioritize efficiency to drastically improve battery life. This has been a game-changer for Windows laptops across different price points. The Qualcomm Snapdragon X Elite is the highest-end option for performance, but the Snapdragon X Plus and base Snapdragon X still offer equally strong battery life, despite showing up in much cheaper laptops. The sequel was unveiled in late 2025, and now in 2026, we’re seeing those laptops roll out. Unfortunately, like Intel’s latest chips, laptops with this next-gen silicon tend to be significantly more expensive than their predecessors.

AMD has grown into a competitive player in the gaming laptop space. Its latest processors, including the Ryzen 9 9950X3D and 9900X3D, are the most powerful gaming chips you can find in a laptop. Unfortunately, it’s still hard to find many laptops supporting these killer chips. AMD also offers its Ryzen AI 300 H and HX chips, which are more commonly found in gaming laptops. While they also offer a mainstream Ryzen AI 300 series, these chips aren’t found in many laptops and currently fall short of the battery life offered by Intel and Qualcomm.

Nvidia's RTX Spark platform just hit the scene, promising to deliver power and efficiency especially when running AI-based operations. It's not as ubiquitous as Intel, AMD, or Qualcomm chips, but it's something to watch for.

How I Test Laptops

I have been reviewing laptops for well over a decade, and WIRED contributor Chris Null has been testing them for 25 years. We test each laptop we review in a variety of situations, including both synthetic benchmark tests and real-world use cases. We make comparisons against similar equipment. We don’t just look at the specs—our reviews evaluate performance, usability, portability, and price to help you find the right laptop for your needs.

We put every laptop through a gauntlet of tests before writing a review and assigning a rating.

Hands-on use: We evaluate the exterior of the device. We compare how thin and light it is against other laptops. We repeatedly open and close the lid to test the quality and ease of the hinge. We push on weak points like the keyboard and lid to test build quality. We also extensively test the keyboard and touchpad for comfort and precision. By using each laptop as our daily driver for days or even weeks, we can spot real-world quirks—like awkward port placement, excessive bloatware, or unexpected problems that may make the laptop difficult to use—that you won’t see on a spec sheet.

Sights and sounds: Once we boot up the device, it’s all about the sights and sounds. The screen is paramount, as it’s your window into everything the laptop has to offer. While you can tell a lot about brightness, color, and contrast just by looking, we go beyond subjective testing. We use a Spyder colorimeter to precisely measure brightness, contrast, color saturation, and accuracy. For HDR-capable screens, we also test peak brightness with HDR content. Finally, we evaluate the webcam and speakers to ensure they are ready for your video calls and streaming sessions.

Performance testing: Finally, we test performance. We always evaluate a laptop based on what it’s intended for—we don’t expect a $500 budget laptop to run like a gaming powerhouse, or a gaming rig to get 18 hours of battery life. Our testbed includes more than 20 synthetic benchmarks, which we constantly adapt based on the device's CPU and operating system. These include tests within Geekbench, PCMark, 3DMark, Procyon, GFXBench, Puget Bench, Superposition, Cinebench, and various gaming-related tests such as 3DMark and Cyberpunk 2077. While we don’t generally report raw scores, we pay close attention to what they tell us. We also monitor fan noise, surface temperature, and overall battery life during these tests.

It’s a lot, I know. But we’re thorough, because we want to stand by our recommendations and ensure that the laptops we rate highly are worth the money.

Review: Ray-Ban Meta Audio

Wired October 24, 2026

All products featured on WIRED are independently selected by our editors. However, when you buy something through our retail links, we may earn an affiliate commission.

8/10

I am very lost in Los Angeles. I’m also sweating because I'm running as fast as I can, slapping my hands against the wet glasses frame on my face to boost the volume of the pulsing techno beats blasting into my ears—and anyone else’s if they happen to be nearby. It’s only the second time I’ve gone on a run in the city, and I decide to let myself get completely off course.

“Hey Meta,” I pant. “I need to get back; tell me where to go.”

The music dims, and the AI agent barks turn-by-turn directions in my ears. After getting turned around a couple of times, I eventually make it back. The navigation wasn’t perfect, but it got me where I needed to be.

This feature has long been available in Meta’s smart glasses. But now I’m wearing the new Ray-Ban Meta Audio, camera-free glasses the company announced in September. The only big change between these and Meta’s other glasses is the lack of a camera, but losing that one feature makes a world of difference.

It makes sense that Meta started with cameras on its glasses. After all, its primary breadwinner is Facebook, a visual platform driven by all the photographs and memes your uncle can use AI to generate. The platform is designed to capture content and beam it to the world—sometimes whether people like it or not.

It took waves of privacy controversies for Meta to finally ditch the cameras. People have found the camera-enabled glasses creepy, calling Meta’s products “pervert glasses” because they have been used by weirdo pickup artists to record people without consent. Some users also shared techniques for removing the indicator light on the glasses designed to let people around the wearer know they’re recording. (Meta released a software fix for this that disables the cameras entirely if the indicator light has been tampered with.)

It didn’t help that the company tried to put facial recognition technology on the glasses, which it denied at first, then later admitted to, and removed. In September, the company was sued for its facial recognition systems. (Meta insists that all the very public pushback did nothing to encourage it to release audio-only glasses.)

Ray-Ban Meta Audio

Rating: 8/10

All products featured on WIRED are independently selected by our editors. However, we may receive compensation from retailers and/or from purchases of products through these links. Learn more.

All that goes away when cameras are removed. The Meta Audio glasses don’t record audio either, except for when you’re using the AI chatbot. Those requests are then saved in the Meta AI app. There is the ability to do live language translation, but it requires going into the Meta AI app first. It’s a shame it took Meta this long to remove the cameras—even with what feels like such a key feature missing, it makes the glasses all the better.

I’ve been wearing the Burbank style. I personally prefer the rounder Clubmaster, and when a friend saw me wearing them for the first time, he laughed and said, “Those are a little thick.”

The frames may be thick, but the Ray-Ban Meta Audio might just be the perfect running glasses. They’ve got transition lenses that adjust quickly to sunlight. The speakers deliver solid sound quality, letting you blast music while also piping in crucial ambient sounds, like that car barreling toward you. Call quality is great, too, and people I’ve spoken with over the phone haven’t noticed I’m speaking through my glasses. That said, the sound does leak out and doesn’t have the best bass response.

They’re lightweight—43 grams for the Burbank model and 47 grams for the Clubmaster, noticeably lighter than the 51.5-gram camera-equipped Gen 3 Wayfarer. A 12-hour battery life means all-day wear is truly viable. It’s nice not to worry about battery life or deal with earbuds or headphones.

I also like that I can walk around peacefully without people thinking I’m recording them. There are legitimate reasons to have cameras on smart glasses. (Anything with augmented reality features will need them.) But removing cameras entirely is the right choice for people who want to use smart glasses for anything that isn’t capturing content.

Frankly, these are probably the only smart glasses I’d willingly spend my own money on. I’ve tried a lot of smart glasses, especially this year. Just about all of them end up back in their case, tossed into a drawer at my desk. Maybe somebody (cough Google cough) will beat Meta eventually. For now, the Ray-Ban Meta Audio are the only smart glasses I actually want to keep on my face.

Which iPhone Should You Buy (or Avoid) Right Now?

Wired October 23, 2026

Apple

Apple

Apple

Apple (Pro)

All products featured on WIRED are independently selected by our editors. However, we may receive compensation from retailers and/or from purchases of products through these links. Learn more.

Apple sells seven iPhone models, from the $699 iPhone 17e to the $1,999 iPhone Duo, but which iPhone is best for you? This is a good time of the year to buy an iPhone if you need to upgrade, since Apple just released its flagship models. (We don't expect the more affordable iPhone 18 models until spring 2027.) We've tested nearly every model and outlined their strengths and weaknesses so you can get the right one for you.

Check out our other Apple buying guides, including Which iPhone 18 Models to Buy, Which iPhone 17 Model to Buy, Best iPhone 17 Cases, Best MagSafe Accessories, Best MagSafe Chargers, Best MagSafe Wallets, and Best Apple 3-in-1 Chargers. Wondering what's new in iOS 27? We have details on that, too.

Updated October 2026: We’ve added more details on the iPhone Duo and links to our reviews and other related coverage now that it's available.

But First, Sell That Old iPhone!

If you’re upgrading from an iPhone, you can trade it in to Apple for a small discount. Before you do that, check whether you can sell it elsewhere for more money. iPhones hold their value incredibly well, particularly if they’re in mint or good condition. We have a guide that runs through the process of selling your phone, and we generally recommend you use websites like Swappa, Gazelle, or Back Market.

We also have a handful of setup guides you should follow:

Buying From Apple vs. a Carrier

Most people in the US purchase iPhones from carriers, which means the devices are locked to that network. If you bought an iPhone from Verizon, you can't easily switch to another carrier without breaking a contract and paying extra fees. It also poses headaches for travelers who want to use international SIM cards or eSIMs.

The easier approach is to buy directly from Apple, though there are some things you should know:

Connect to any carrier later: Choose this option for the most hassle-free experience. You get an unlocked iPhone, then all you need to do is transfer the SIM card or eSIM from your old iPhone to the new one to get started. This might be painless, though you may need to contact your carrier if the iPhone can't complete the eSIM transfer. In the US, Apple hasn't included a SIM tray since 2022's iPhone 14.

Choose a carrier: If you choose a carrier through Apple. com, you will get an unlocked iPhone, no matter which carrier you choose (except if you purchase with AT&T on an installment plan). The downside is that Apple doesn't have the same offers as the carriers, so you may lose out on a deal. However, carrier offers often require new lines, trade-ins, or an upgraded plan, and the savings come in the form of bill credits, so these deals aren't as amazing as they may seem.

Finance: You can finance your iPhone either with Apple's credit card via monthly installments or as Apple iPhone Payments via a Citizens One loan. You need to choose a carrier here, but Apple confirmed these devices are all unlocked. You have to fill out a credit application to see if you qualify. If you opt to finance through a carrier on Apple. com, only the T-Mobile and Verizon models will be unlocked. The AT&T and Boost Mobile options are locked iPhones, so it's no different from buying it on an installment plan directly from those carriers.

Apple Upgrade: Buying directly from Apple also nets you access to the Apple Upgrade leasing option. Is it worth it? Broadly speaking, no. Most people do not need to upgrade to a new iPhone every year or two. It's expensive, and you must return your leased iPhone in good condition to avoid additional charges. AppleCare is not included, as it was with the discontinued iPhone Upgrade Program.

What Is Apple Intelligence?

The most hyped-up feature from the iPhone 16 range was Apple Intelligence, which rolled out in iOS 18.1. This is Apple's suite of AI features, following the wave started by the likes of ChatGPT and Google's Gemini. Apple Intelligence is available on the iPhone 15 Pro/Pro Max and newer, including the iPhone 16e (not to mention select iPads and MacBooks).

What exactly is Apple Intelligence in the first place? It's a collection of features that draw on the power of large language models to introduce “smart” capabilities. For example, in the Voice Memo and Notes app, you can now start a recording and get a real-time transcription. You can even record a call and get the transcription saved in the Notes app. Siri has been redesigned to understand when you misspeak and can even plug into ChatGPT for more powerful responses to open-ended questions. There are writing tools available throughout the operating system that let you change the tone of your emails or proofread text so you don't make an unnecessary typo on Threads.

This is just a small sampling. We've boiled down many of the Apple Intelligence features here, and additional features keep rolling out in iOS updates. For example, Genmoji—which lets you create your own emojis—debuted alongside the AI image-generation app, Image Playground, in iOS 18.2. In iOS 27, Apple added the revamped, conversational Siri AI assistant. Siri now understands personal context and can retrieve information from your messages, emails, and photos. It can also act on your behalf to draft a message with a particular tone or find a good restaurant for your partner's birthday dinner. Here's everything you can do with Siri AI.

If you don't care for Apple Intelligence and want to turn it off, you can! We have a helpful guide detailing the exact steps.

What Is MagSafe?

Magnetic MagSafe wireless charging is available on the iPhone 12, iPhone 13, iPhone 14, iPhone 15, iPhone 16, iPhone 17, and iPhone 18 models (except the iPhone 16e), and it allows you to magnetically attach various accessories to the back of the iPhone. (iPhones support Qi2, which is the open standard, whereas MagSafe is proprietary; you can use Qi2 accessories just like MagSafe.)

You can get first-party accessories like Apple's MagSafe Wireless Charger, which sticks to the back for faster charging. Or snag the MagSafe Wallet so you can keep your credit card attached to your phone. There are plenty of third-party accessories (you'll find quite a few in our guide), and MagSafe doesn't just have to be charging accessories like power banks or wireless chargers. There is a wealth of useful tools, from wallets, tripods, and camera cages to notepads and ring lights that can attach to the back of the iPhone and add extra versatility.

If you plan to use a case, get one that has MagSafe embedded inside to ensure a strong magnetic connection with Apple's accessories (non-MagSafe cases can interrupt MagSafe and make the magnetic connection weaker). All of the cases in our case guides are MagSafe-tested. And yes, a case is a smart investment because iPhones are made of glass, and glass breaks, even if Apple uses ceramic to strengthen it. We cracked an iPhone 16 Plus after a 4-foot drop to the pavement—that model's ceramic glass was supposed to be twice as strong as previous iPhones, too! Ouch. See our favorite cases for the iPhone 17, iPhone 16, iPhone 15, and iPhone 14 ranges.

The iPhone 17 is nearly the perfect phone, and it's what most people looking for a new iPhone should buy right now. With this model, Apple finally upgraded the screen's refresh rate to 120 Hz. This might not sound like the snazziest feature, but you'll immediately notice everything feeling smoother and more responsive as you use the phone, especially if you're coming from an iPhone with a 60-Hz display. The slightly larger display can also hit up to 3,000 nits of peak brightness, which means you shouldn't have any trouble reading it in sunny conditions, and the new anti-reflective coating should also help cut glare. It's protected by Apple's new Ceramic Shield 2 glass, which supposedly is three times more scratch-resistant than before.

More excitingly, the selfie camera has been upgraded to 24 megapixels (binned down to 18 MP). It's the same across the entire iPhone 17 lineup (excluding the iPhone 17e), and Apple is using a square sensor for the first time. It's smart and helpful because you can keep holding your iPhone firmly in portrait orientation, but digitally switch to landscape or portrait orientation when taking a selfie without having to rotate the phone in your hand. It'll also automatically zoom and rotate orientations when it detects more people in the frame (Apple calls it Center Stage). You can also natively shoot video with the front and rear cameras simultaneously with Dual Capture.

Storage was bumped to 256 GB (finally!), and the ultrawide camera was upgraded to 48 megapixels, delivering sharp results even in low-light conditions. There's a slightly bigger battery, too, and the results have been very impressive, easily lasting through a full day with more than six hours of screen-on time. I only wish Apple added a telephoto zoom camera here—Android phones at this price are starting to see more optical zoom options, like the Google Pixel 10 and Samsung Galaxy S26, and it would make this iPhone more versatile. (At least the “optical-like” 2X zoom is decent.)

All in all, this is one of the most well-rounded and feature-rich iPhones in years, even if it doesn't feature the fun Camera Plateau design of the pricier iPhone Air or Pro models. Sadly, Apple increased the price of the iPhone 17 (and every other older model) by $100 when it unveiled the new 18 Pro lineup. If you're wondering why there isn't an iPhone 18, that's expected to debut in early 2027.

There's a single camera on the back—it's decent but not as versatile, and it struggles the most in low-light conditions. This iPhone doesn't have the ultrawide-band chip, which allows for precision guidance when hunting for your AirTag. (You can still locate your misplaced item, just with more vague instructions to its location.) Oh, and the screen is stuck at 60 Hz, so it doesn't feel as responsive as the other iPhones here.

It's powered by the A19 chip like the iPhone 17, except with one fewer graphics core, so there's a small hit to performance. However, I booted up Genshin Impact and didn't have much trouble playing it, even after maxing out graphics; you'll just see more stutters here and there.

I appreciate that Apple has installed its Ceramic Shield 2 glass to protect the screen, meaning improved durability, and there's a bump in base storage to 256 GB. Battery life has been reliable, easily lasting me a full day even with heavy use, but the biggest upgrade is the addition of MagSafe. A strange omission on the iPhone 16e, this capability means you can take advantage of the wealth of magnetic MagSafe accessories on the market, whether you want faster wireless charging or just an easier way to mount the smartphone on a tripod or car mount.

Apple still sells this 2024 phone but has increased the price to $799 and discontinued the larger iPhone 16 Plus. I would try to find it for cheaper at other retail channels if possible—I wouldn't pay $799 for the iPhone 16. (There is no new iPhone 17 Plus model; Apple replaced it with the iPhone Air.)

The 6.1-inch iPhone 16 can get you through a day, but heavy users may need a top-up before bedtime. It features the Action Button, which replaced the mute switch on older iPhones, but you can bring that functionality back or customize this button to do something else. There's also Camera Control, which launches the camera and doubles as a shutter button. A light amount of pressure on this button lets you switch camera modes or photography styles, and you can slide your finger to cycle through them. (I hate this secondary function, so I always disable it: Settings > Camera > Camera Control > Customize and toggle off Light Press and Swipe.)

The iPhone Duo may have dominated the headlines recently, but Apple's true flagships are the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max. If you want the best battery life on a smartphone, this is it, particularly the Pro Max, because it packs a denser battery. You can easily make it through two days on a single charge. The smaller Pro generally had around 40 percent left by bedtime. These are also the most powerful smartphones, with the Apple A20 Pro chip backed by an improved vapor chamber design for cooling—ensuring the smoothest performance even when you're playing a AAA game like Control.

The Dynamic Island is a little smaller this year; it can now display three activities, making it a little more useful. There's no orange color option, but Apple is offering a lovely new burgundy. Perhaps the biggest enhancement is with the already versatile, triple 48-megapixel lens camera system, thanks to a new variable aperture in the main lens. Changing the aperture gives you more control over how much light you let in, allowing better low-light performance, and allows you to capture that coveted bokeh effect for blurred backgrounds or narrow it down to keep more of the scene and background in focus. It also adds enhancements to the already excellent video capture capabilities.

This minor refresh over the iPhone 17 Pro also comes with a price bump (an extra $100 across the board), and some handy new features in iOS 27 (though the iPhone 15 Pro and newer will get these, too). The revamped Siri AI is far more capable than previous versions, with more contextual understanding of what's onscreen and the ability to delve into your messages, emails, and photos.

Apple

Apple

Breaking the trend of incremental annual updates, the iPhone Duo is Apple's first foray into foldables, and it's astonishingly good for a debut. Instead of the book- and flip-style foldables that have dominated the market so far, Apple went with a passport-sized form factor, similar to Samsung's recent Galaxy Z Fold8 (our current pick for the best folding phones). The Duo sports a 5.4-inch screen on the outside, but unfolds to reveal a 7.6-inch display inside that feels like an iPad Mini. You might even try working on it.

With a tough titanium frame, a precision hinge with magnets for that satisfying snap-shut, and an IP68 rating, this is one of the most durable foldables on the market, but not the slimmest or lightest (it's bigger and heavier than Samsung’s Fold8). But Apple has minimized the main screen’s crease with a special display stack and a matte-finish nanotexture screen.

There are trade-offs with folding phones, and the Duo drops Face ID (Touch ID is in the side power button instead) and makes do without a telephoto lens (you get a 48-megapixel primary camera and a 48-megapixel ultrawide). On the upside, it has the biggest iPhone battery ever, promising 24 hours of mixed use. You can expect to have around 40 percent in the tank after an average day's use.

Apple's take on the software is what we’re most excited about, as it finds unique ways to take advantage of the new form factor and encourages third-party apps, like Slack, to optimize for the folding format. However, it may take a while for all your favorite apps to be properly optimized. Controls are stacked vertically, there's plenty of split-screen support, and transitions are typically smooth. Features like Kid Cue, which helps you catch your kid's attention for photos, and enhanced StandBy support, which lets you use the outer screen as an alarm clock while the inner display gently pulses with light to wake you, will set this iPhone apart. Apple Pencil support is coming later this year.

Whether it's worth the considerable premium, when the iPhone 18 Pro models are more capable (on paper), depends on what you want from a phone. First-generation devices are never perfect, so it may be sensible to wait for the sequel.

The iPhone Air is the first model of its kind. Borrowing from other Air models—the original MacBook Air and iPad Air—it's the thinnest iPhone ever made at a mere 5.6 mm and one of the lightest at 165 grams. The difference is palpable, especially considering its large 6.5-inch screen. Use the iPhone Air for a day, and the iPhone 18 Pro will feel like a brick.

It's not for everyone. Think of it like an early-adopter iPhone, as the design innovations no doubt informed the folding iPhone Duo. But there are a few too many compromises considering the price. Namely, the camera system. We're all used to multi-camera setups on our smartphones, and a single-lens design for a $1,100 handset is too limiting. It sports the same 48-MP main camera as the iPhone 17, though the cheaper iPhone sometimes delivers sharper results. You can use the 2X “optical-like” zoom, but that's it. There's no ultrawide and no telephoto camera. I even tried to take a close-up photo of a flower, and the lack of a macro mode meant I couldn't move the iPhone Air as close to the subject. Thankfully, it has the same great 18-MP selfie camera as the rest of the iPhone 17 lineup.

The other major compromise is battery life, though this depends on how you use your phone. I was pleasantly surprised by the iPhone Air's runtime, which often hit more than five hours of screen-on time. That's better than I expected. With average use, it lasted me a full day, and I didn't feel too anxious about it dying on me. However, on busier days, I needed to top it up in the afternoon. If you're a heavy user, relying on various battery-sucking apps like Maps or gaming, the iPhone Air's battery won't impress.

This, alongside the iPhone 17e, has Apple's custom C1X modem, which is more power efficient, and one of the ways Apple can max out the battery life on the Air. The downside is that it doesn't support millimeter-wave 5G (mmWave). It won't impact you much since the dominant form of 5G is sub-6 (we have an explainer here), but mmWave is deployed in dense urban areas and high-traffic areas like airports and stadiums. It's weird to not have it on a flagship smartphone in 2025.

If you barely use the camera and are regularly near a charger, there are plenty of cheaper smartphones that will serve you well. But if you must have an iPhone and want to try a super-thin and lightweight device, I think you'll be happy with the iPhone Air.

Apple no longer sells the iPhone 17 Pro and iPhone 17 Pro Max, but you can find them at alternative retailers. As long as you're not paying MSRP (anything close to what the new iPhone 18 Pro models cost), they're great buys. Note that new options often sell out fast.

They are some of the thickest iPhones in recent memory because Apple stuffed them with big batteries. For the first time, we didn't always need to charge an iPhone every single day. We routinely hit close to seven hours of screen-on time and had 30 or 40 percent left, depending on the device. Outside of battery and screen size, these two iPhones have the same features.

The second biggest upgrade in the iPhone 17 Pro models wasn't a sexy topic: thermal conductivity. Apple switched to aluminum and added a vapor chamber cooling system to manage heat better. By dissipating heat across the back of the devices, these iPhones stay cooler for longer and eke out more from the A19 Pro chipset. We played Assassin's Creed Mirage for more than an hour, and while the iPhone was warm, it had no hot spots. We saw no stutters or lag at max graphical settings, a step up from its predecessors. Meanwhile, the iPhone Air got uncomfortably hot in one spot, and we saw more stutters after prolonged play. If you plan to play demanding games on your smartphone or tackle processing-intensive tasks, buy one of the Pro models.

The cameras didn't just get a fun new redesign on the back. Apple upgraded the telephoto to 48 megapixels, so now every rear camera is 48 MP. It zooms up to 4X, though you can get optical-like quality at up to 8X. If you're wondering, yes, the iPhone 16 Pro offered 5X optical zoom, but the larger sensor and higher megapixel count mean you'll get sharper, brighter zoom photos on the iPhone 17 Pro. If you capture a lot of video with the rear cameras, that's another reason to buy these iPhones, because they offer some of the best native video quality on a smartphone. (We have plenty of examples in our review!)

The iPhone 17 Pro or iPhone 17 Pro Max are still plenty powerful for most folks. The new 18 Pro models slightly strengthen already strong areas of these phones (see above for what has been upgraded). But only the 17 Pro models come in orange!

While last year's iOS 26 debuted the divisive Liquid Glass, iOS 27 and iPadOS 27 focus squarely on quality-of-life improvements, with a redesigned and much improved Siri AI assistant, easier Shortcuts, and lots of little tweaks to enhance speed and stability.

Siri AI doesn't just look different—now resembling a glass orb—it can also understand your personal context, pulling info from your messages, emails, or even photos, and helping you draft messages or find the right wine to pair with your dinner. Siri can also now pop up in the camera app to help you choose your next book or split a bill with friends.

Apple says iOS 27 is faster than ever, with app launches up to 30 percent faster, newly captured photos in your Photo Library loading up to 70 percent faster, and AirDrop transfers completing up to 80 percent faster. For more details, read our guide on the top features in iOS 27 and how to download it.

Avoid These iPhones

The iPhone 14 and older iPhones are probably available somewhere, but you shouldn't take the bait. They don't have the processing power to keep up with the latest software, and even if they do, they will have a much shorter software shelf life or lack modern features like USB-C. The only older iPhones worth considering at the moment are the iPhone 15 or iPhone 16 series, even better if it's the Pro models, if you can find them at low prices. The iPhone 16e is also another option, though only if you can find it at a steep discount.

The iPhone XS, iPhone XS Max, and iPhone XR are cut off from receiving the iOS 27 update, so they're especially ones to avoid. Without software support, your device will slowly become less secure and could become a slow, buggy mess.

The iPhone's Charging Port Is USB-C, Not Lightning

The iPhone 15 range ditched the long-standing Lightning port for USB-C, and it's in every iPhone since. This is the same charging port on iPads, MacBooks, Android phones, Windows laptops, and many more personal tech gadgets. USB-C is often called the “universal port” because it can technically handle various responsibilities. For example, you can plug in external displays and extend the iPhone's screen or connect the same USB-C accessories you might be currently using on your laptop, like SD card readers. Sadly, it does mean your Lightning accessories won't work unless you get dongles.

You can read more about what the port does here, but there are two important things to note:

The iPhone 15, iPhone 15 Plus, iPhone 16, iPhone 16 Plus, iPhone 16e, iPhone 17, iPhone 17e, and iPhone Air support the USB 2.0 standard just like the iPhones before, so you'll max out at 480 megabits per second of data transfer speeds.

The iPhone 15 Pro, iPhone 15 Pro Max, iPhone 16 Pro, iPhone 16 Pro Max, iPhone 17 Pro, iPhone 17 Pro Max, iPhone 18 Pro, iPhone 18 Pro Max, and iPhone Duo support the USB 3.0 standard and are capable of up to 10 gigabits per second of data transfer speeds.

What’s the Deal With eSIMs?

All iPhone 14 and newer devices completely ditch the physical SIM tray in the US, meaning you can no longer just pop your physical SIM inside to turn on cellular connectivity. Instead, you'll have to rely on an eSIM. You can read more about them here. This tech has been available in iPhones since the iPhone XS and XR, but now you have to use it. Apple has also started switching more global models to eSIM only, like the iPhone Air.) When you're setting up your new iPhone, you'll automatically be asked to transfer your number from your previous iPhone, and the whole process should take a few minutes without any hassle. (eSIMs are more secure than physical SIMs.) Once you transfer your number, your physical SIM card won't work anymore.

There's a chance you may still run into some issues, especially if you're coming from an Android phone (or want to switch back to an Android phone). You'll have to check with your carrier to get your cellular connection working again. It shouldn't take long, but it's not as simple as popping in a physical card.

How to Replace Your iPhone's Battery

If you don't want to spend the money to get a new iPhone, consider a fresh battery. If the biggest issues with your aging iPhone revolve around how long it lasts in a day, replacing the battery might make it feel brand-new. (Apple's iPhone 16, 16 Plus, and 16e have an easier-to-replace battery.)

Replacements for older iPhones are $89, and $99 or $119 for newer models. If that doesn't do the trick, read our guide on ways to fix your iPhone's problems or our guide on selling your iPhone to get the most money for it.

What Is the Action Button and Camera Control Button?

The Action Button debuted on the iPhone 15 Pro models, and it's now standard on every iPhone in the lineup. It sits above the volume rocker on the left edge of the phone. It effectively replaces the old Mute Switch, but think of it as just a configurable button. You can have it still control the mute function of the phone, or customize it (Settings > Action Button) to trigger the flashlight, a Voice Memo, or even launch an app or Shortcut.

Camera Control is another newer addition that debuted on the iPhone 16 series. On the right edge of the phone below the power button, press it to launch the Camera app, and you can press it to capture a photo or start recording a video. A light tap and swipe can move through different camera lenses or modes, but I found this annoying. (You can configure it by heading to Settings > Camera > Camera Control.) Press and hold this button, and you'll trigger Apple's Visual Intelligence. It'll use the camera to identify subjects in front of you, very much like Google Lens, so you can ask questions via Google or ChatGPT about what you're looking at.

Elon Musk Just Dumped Another $76 Million Into the Midterms

Wired October 23, 2026

Elon Musk gave his personal political committee, America PAC, more than $76 million in the first two weeks of October to boost Republicans in the final stretch of the midterms, according to a pre-election report the PAC filed Thursday evening with the Federal Election Commission.

The group spent nearly $43 million in the first two weeks of October, and entered the campaign’s last leg holding nearly $47 million in cash.

The Texas Senate race dominated the new spending. It drew $15.2 million, double what the PAC spent there all summer. That spending included $12.4 million to attack Democratic candidate James Talarico and $2.8 million to promote Republican Ken Paxton.

Daily filings since then show $9.1 million more against Talarico, bringing the PAC’s spending against him this cycle to nearly $28 million, about 40 percent of everything it has spent supporting or opposing candidates. The PAC also shifted toward online ads, spending $11.4 million on digital ads in the same two weeks, which is close to what it spent on mail and texting combined.

All told, Musk has given more than $445 million to Republican political groups this election cycle, according to WIRED’s analysis of FEC filings, making him the biggest known individual donor in the midterms. More than $165 million of that has gone to America PAC since July alone.

America PAC declined to comment.

Musk—who has several companies, including Tesla and SpaceX, based in Texas—has also been posting online about the race. On Wednesday, Musk posted on X that “there is something deeply wrong with Talarico,” then called him “a creep” and claimed, without evidence, that he “would vote to take away your kids and transition them.” Earlier this month, Musk amplified a false claim that Talarico had been treated at a mental health facility. Talarico shot back the same day: “There is something deeply wrong with a political system that allows one trillionaire to buy his own personal US Senator.”

The Texas race remains a toss-up. An Emerson College poll of 1,000 likely Texas voters, conducted October 17 to 19, found Talarico at 48 percent and Paxton at 46 percent, within the poll’s 3-point margin of error.

The stakes for Musk reach well beyond Texas. If Democrats win the House, the lawmakers in line to lead its committees have signaled they will investigate his role in the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE), his companies’ federal contracts, and what Zoe Lofgren, a California Democrat, called an “astounding” number of conflicts of interest. Unified Democratic control of Congress would pose even more problems for him.

Silicon Valley Democrats added another target on Friday: restrictions on SpaceX’s Starshield satellite service in Ukraine. In a letter to the White House demanding an investigation, Representatives Sam Liccardo, Jimmy Panetta, and Ro Khanna vowed that the next Congress “will closely scrutinize federal funding awarded to Mr. Musk’s businesses.”

How Many Billions Would It Take to Hold Meta Accountable?

Wired October 23, 2026

Earlier this week, a New Mexico judge ordered Meta to pay a $25 billion fine for violating consumer protection laws dating back to the Cambridge Analytica scandal. $25 billion is a massive fine, the largest Meta has ever faced, but it still had us folks at WIRED wondering: Would Meta even feel the pain?

A quick recap of the case: Filed in 2021, the suit alleged that the company violated the state’s Unfair Practices Act by lying to Meta users about the way it handled their data. (Later, New Mexico’s attorney general also made claims against Meta’s content moderation policies.) In September, a jury ruled in favor of the state. Then came the multibillion-dollar penalty.

“This ruling, and the Attorney General's approach to enforcement, makes it all but impossible to do business in the state of New Mexico,” C. J. Mahoney, Meta’s chief legal officer, said in a statement. “At its core, this lawsuit seeks to impose a tax on speech to enforce new rules for what people can say online. We are confident we will prevail on appeal.”

Meta’s legal troubles have proliferated so much this year that it’s hard to keep track of them. Earlier this year in New Mexico, a jury ruled that the social media company should pay $375 million for violating the state’s Unfair Practices Act. That trial was related to child safety. A second phase of the case resulted in Meta being ordered to pay $567 million.

Meanwhile, a Los Angeles County superior court found Meta—and Google-owned YouTube—liable for harming a user’s mental health with the addictive design features of their apps. The plaintiff, a young woman, was awarded $6 million; Meta is on the hook for the bulk of that payment. Then in August, Meta settled a landmark federal case brought against the company by the majority of US states. This suit, once again, centered on addictive features in its apps that were alleged to be harmful to kids. As part of that settlement, Meta will pay the states between $17 and $18 billion over 10 years.

Added up, that’s a lot of billions. And yet: It’s still just the cost of doing business for Meta. Reuters reports that in the most recent New Mexico trial, the state’s attorneys originally asked Judge Francis Mathew to award the state between $35 and $45 billion. That would’ve been significant for the state, but would that extra $20 billion have kneecapped Meta? Nope.

Even if Meta was forced to pay the total maximum fine of the New Mexico ruling—a whopping $219 billion, or $5,000 across 43 million violations, reduced by the judge to $25 billion—the company would have felt only a mild sting. As of writing, Meta is worth around $1.7 trillion. Its stock took a hit on Thursday, but that was due to a confluence of factors, like Meta’s earnings report on Wednesday, the company’s massive capital expenditures on AI, and AI stocks dragging overall.

At this point, with no immediate monetary damage to Meta, it would take an accumulation of events to force some kind of change, legal experts tell me. For one, Meta has a clear perception problem: Juries are ruling against it, protesters have railed against it, even its own employees have been more vocal about the company’s internal policies.

Every time Meta doesn’t settle a case, the evidence presented during trial can be scrutinized by the public and used in future cases against Meta, says Corban Rhodes, partner at DiCello Levitt, the outside law firm representing New Mexico in this case. “This trial included more than 100 exhibits that we were able to put into public record, things that had been kept secret for more than a decade since Cambridge Analytica,” Rhodes told WIRED.

One such item is a 2018 email that then COO Sheryl Sandberg sent to a few colleagues days after the Cambridge Analytica scandal broke. Sandberg wrote, “The single biggest issue we face—and I really need everyone to know this—is that there were a MILLION developers with access to the data. We are going to have many, many, many more moments like this in the next month and year.”

There are early signals that private insurers may start balking at having to cover the cost of a tech company’s legal defenses. Some experts are suggesting that insurance companies could even end up being de facto governance for AI, as they “inject responsibility into how AI is designed, developed, and deployed as a condition for obtaining insurance.” Meta learned this firsthand in March, when a Delaware judge ruled that insurers do not have a duty to defend Meta against the literal thousands of lawsuits being brought against it.

There’s no well-defined number at which Meta suddenly becomes vulnerable—the company is unlikely to ever fold from legal penalties alone. But problems could crop up if shareholders or board members stop seeing the company as some inanimate entity and start to focus on the individual directors or officers who have been making bad decisions, says Brian Quinn, a law professor at Boston College Law School who studies corporate law, M&A, and transaction law. Like, say, the people who keep appearing in lawsuits.

“The way that indemnification law is written right now, the fact that a person in a company was found to have violated a law doesn’t necessarily make them liable. It can be believed that they were acting in good faith, or in the best interest of their company,” Quinn says. “But problems start to arise if shareholders say, wait a minute, there’s not only evidence that this director or operator is violating the law, but it has appeared in the same set of facts seven times now.”

After a huge accumulation of these kinds of results, Quinn says, some angry shareholders might stand up and say the corporation should no longer be able to indemnify those directors. That’s when you might see change, because Meta’s executives would no longer be as protected.

Finally, since litigation is often behind the curve on society-disrupting technology, Meta’s legal woes are likely far from over—especially as it wades deeper into AI. “Regulators and courts have for a long time been focused on the impact of social media 1.0 and 2.0, and I think we’re moving on from that era,” says Rhodes. “I expect the next wave of litigation will be focused on AI.”

This is an edition of Steven Levy’s and Lauren Goode's Backchannel newsletter. Read previous newsletters here.
